title: Batch: a dev environment that works
description:
The rest of inventory-tng-o1uj that does not need a decision from the project owner, formed 2026-08-29 after PR #40 made writes work again.

Four issues: the Django admin rendering unstyled (o1uj.1, P0), nginx holding a dead upstream address after the backend restarts (o1uj.2), a configurable trusted-origin list (o1uj.7), and the missing test that would have caught o1uj.6 in the first place (o1uj.8).

TWO OF o1uj's CHILDREN ARE DELIBERATELY NOT HERE. o1uj.3 amends decision 0013 point 3, which is a security decision and a person's to make; o1uj.4 decides whether a cross-origin arrangement is supported at all, which changes what configuration this project ships. title: Batch: make the writes work again
description:
Two issues, formed on 2026-08-29 out of one sitting spent trying to run the application on the project owner's own machine.

inventory-tng-o1uj.6 is the defect that made it unusable: nginx forwarded the host without its port, so Django rebuilt a different origin from the browser's and refused EVERY write with a CSRF origin failure. The other is the documentation that sitting produced -- Podman as an equal to Docker, a heading for the first sign-in, corrected ports, and three worked examples to follow.

They ship together because they came from the same afternoon and neither is much use without the other: the walkthroughs cannot be completed while writes are refused, and the fix is hard to notice without a session to run against it.

BOTH ISSUES' PARENT WAS MOVED HERE from inventory-tng-o1uj, the dev-environment epic, which holds five further issues that are NOT in this batch. scripts/check-batch.sh reads parentage as batch membership, so an issue cannot be in both at once.

The guard half of o1uj.6's original description -- making CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS configurable -- was split out as inventory-tng-o1uj.7 rather than landed here. It touches settings, .env.sample, compose.yaml, the chart and their docs, and none of it is needed to make writes work.
close_reason: All children completed

title: Every write is refused: nginx drops the port, so Django's CSRF origin check fails
description:
Found on 2026-08-29 by driving the volunteer flow end to end in a browser
against the compose stack: pick a volunteer, scan the location label, scan an
item label, press Save. This is almost certainly what the project owner
reported as a CORS error after signing in -- the message Django returns says
"Origin checking failed", which is what most people would call that.

THE SYMPTOM. Every write fails. Reads all work, sign-in works, TOTP works, the
batch builds correctly on screen, and then Save answers:

    POST /api/stock/transactions -> 403
    {"detail":"CSRF Failed: Origin checking failed -
      http://localhost:8080 does not match any trusted origins.","code":"forbidden"}

So the single-page app cannot save a batch, which is the thing the application
is for. Decision 0011's whole QR flow -- scan, cart, Save -- is unusable on the
stack the README tells a new contributor to run first. Nothing else in the
inventory can be changed either: the same check refuses every POST, PUT, PATCH
and DELETE, so the administrative screens cannot write either.

THE CAUSE, proven rather than reasoned. Three facts.

1. frontend/nginx.conf.template proxies with `proxy_set_header Host $host` in
   all three of its proxying locations (lines 92, 119 and 129 of the rendered
   config). nginx's `$host` is the host WITHOUT the port -- that is its
   documented behaviour, and `$http_host` is the variable that keeps it.
   So Django is told the Host is `localhost`, not `localhost:8080`.

2. Django builds the origin it will accept from its own view of the request.
   Asked directly, inside the running container:

     Host: 'localhost'       -> good_origin http://localhost        match: False
     Host: 'localhost:8080'  -> good_origin http://localhost:8080   match: True

   against the browser's Origin of http://localhost:8080.

3. CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS is [] at runtime, and the name appears NOWHERE in this
   repository -- not settings.py, not .env.sample, not compose.yaml, not the
   Helm chart. So there is no second chance after the host comparison fails.

Together: nginx drops the port, Django therefore computes the wrong origin, and
nothing is configured to forgive the difference.

WHY IT WAS NEVER CAUGHT, which is the part worth keeping. On a deployment the
browser reaches the ingress on 443 and the Origin header carries no port, so
`$host` and the origin agree and every write succeeds. The bug only appears
when the port is not the scheme's default -- which is every local setup and no
deployed one. The browser integration suite does not catch it either: its specs
sign in and read, and nothing in frontend/integration/ posts a batch.

TWO FIXES, and they are not alternatives so much as one fix and one guard.

* `$http_host` in place of `$host` in the three proxy_set_header lines. This is
  the actual defect and the one-line correction. The template's own comment
  block already says the Host header has to stay the browser's, so the
  intention was right and the variable was wrong; correct the comment with it.
  Check the same reasoning against vite.config.ts, which documents the same
  requirement for the dev server and gets it right by not overriding the host
  at all.
* Make CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS configurable and set it explicitly in compose.yaml
  and .env.sample. Even with the header fixed this should exist, because the
  moment anybody runs the frontend on a host name that is not what Django sees
  they will land here again with no knob to reach for. It also belongs with the
  sibling issue about Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, since a genuinely
  cross-origin arrangement needs both and neither is present.

TESTS, and this is where the real gap is. The unit tests drive Django's test
client, which does not go through nginx and so cannot see this at all. What
would have caught it is a browser test that SAVES -- the integration suite has
the fixtures for it already (seed_integration_data mints a volunteer, an item, a
location and a label). Add one spec that scans the location, scans the item and
presses Save, and asserts the ledger moved. The nb8 epic's notes make the same
point about asserting things that happen outside Django: drive the real stack,
not the test client.

VERIFY BY RUNNING IT. After the change, the manual walkthrough is: sign in at
:8080, pick a volunteer, scan DEM0000002 (the seeded location label), scan
DEM0000001 (the seeded item label), press Save, and the batch should clear and
the on-hand count for LiteBeam AC Gen2 should move. Today it 403s at the last
step.
close_reason: nginx now forwards $http_host, so Django rebuilds the origin the browser actually used. Verified end to end: the same Save that answered 403 answers 201, and the ledger moved.

title: The Django admin loads with no styling at all under compose
description:
Found by the project owner running the app on 2026-08-29, reported as "the
admin page has NO styling at all", and reproduced and root-caused the same day
against the compose stack on this machine.

WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE. http://localhost:8080/admin/ (and :8000/admin/) renders as
raw browser-default HTML. Measured in the page rather than described: the
computed font-family on body is "Times New Roman" and the computed background
is rgba(0, 0, 0, 0). All five stylesheets the admin asks for answer 404:

    /static/admin/css/base.css
    /static/admin/css/dark_mode.css
    /static/admin/css/nav_sidebar.css
    /static/admin/css/dashboard.css
    /static/admin/css/responsive.css

WHY. Three facts that are individually reasonable and together are the bug.

1. compose.yaml sets DJANGO_DEBUG to true by default (the ${DJANGO_DEBUG:-true}
   on the backend service).
2. settings.py adds WhiteNoise to MIDDLEWARE only under `if not DEBUG`. The
   comment above it says why -- in development Django's staticfiles app serves
   them and collectstatic has not run, so WhiteNoise would only warn about a
   missing directory.
3. The compose stack runs gunicorn, not runserver. The staticfiles app only
   serves anything through runserver's handler.

So the one arrangement the comment in settings.py does not account for is the
one the quickstart ships: DEBUG on AND gunicorn. Nothing serves /static/ and
every admin asset 404s. The files themselves are present and correct --
backend/Dockerfile runs collectstatic at build time, and
/app/src/staticfiles/admin/css/base.css is in the image at 24538 bytes.

PROVEN BOTH WAYS on this machine, same stack, same image:

    DJANGO_DEBUG=true   (the shipped default)  -> /static/admin/css/base.css 404
    DJANGO_DEBUG=false                         -> /static/admin/css/base.css 200

That is the whole diagnosis; there is nothing left to investigate.

WHY IT IS WORTH MORE THAN IT LOOKS. The admin is not decoration here. Decision
0013 routes admin/login/ to allauth, and guides/administrator.md sends an
administrator into the admin for the things the app cannot yet do -- notably
identifiers, which inventory-tng-gz2 records are reachable from nowhere else.
An unstyled admin has no sidebar, no nav and no layout, so those tasks are hard
to complete rather than merely ugly, and it is the first impression anybody
gets of the project.

THE FIX IS A DECISION, NOT A LINE. Options, and the trade is real:

* Add WhiteNoise unconditionally and let it serve from STATIC_ROOT whenever the
  directory exists. Closest to what the deployed image already does, and makes
  the compose stack resemble production, which is what compose.yaml says it is
  for. Costs a collectstatic in any DEBUG-on flow that wants admin CSS.
* Key the condition on the server rather than on DEBUG -- the real distinction
  is runserver versus gunicorn, and DEBUG is standing in for it badly.
* Set DJANGO_DEBUG=false in compose.yaml. Smallest edit, but it trades the
  Django error page away, and that page is worth a lot in the stack somebody is
  using to find bugs. Probably the wrong one.

Whichever is chosen, settings.py's comment states the reasoning that is now
wrong and has to be corrected with it, and DEVELOPERS.md's Option A is where a
developer would look for the consequence.

A TEST IS WHAT KEEPS IT FIXED. Assert that a request for an admin static path
answers 200 under the settings the compose stack actually runs. The unit tests
drive Django's test client, which never exercises WhiteNoise, so this one has
to go through inventory_tng.wsgi.application -- the same trap the nb8 epic's
notes record as the iqff.1 defect recurring.
close_reason: WhiteNoise now loads when STATIC_ROOT exists rather than when DEBUG is off. Verified in the stack: the admin renders styled under the compose default, and all five stylesheets answer 200.

title: EPIC: An app the owner can run and use on their own machine
description:
Raised by the project owner on 2026-08-29 and given priority over the feature work in flight. The reasoning is theirs: the project is at the point where USING the app is the cheapest way to find the usability and cosmetic faults that matter, and that is only true if it runs on their laptop without a fight. Every child here is something that was hit while trying to do exactly that, in one sitting, following the repository's own documentation.

Nothing in this epic is speculative. Each child was reproduced against the compose stack on that machine and root-caused before it was written down, and each says what was observed as well as what to change.

WHAT WAS ALREADY DONE in the same sitting, so it is not duplicated as a child: README's quickstart was rewritten to cover Docker and Podman as equals, to give both command sets, to add a Sign in for the first time section, and to send people to port 8080 for everything; DEVELOPERS.md gained a Podman section carrying the one prerequisite Podman has that Docker does not. scripts/check-docs.sh passes on both.

THE ORDER IS BY WHAT BLOCKS USE. The admin having no styling is first because an administrator cannot do the identifier work guides/administrator.md sends them into the admin for. The 502 is second because it punishes the develop-and-restart loop every time. The rest are smaller.
close_reason: All children completed

title: Backend pods can never become Ready: the probe's Host is refused
description:
Found by a deployment review of docs/deployment.md on 2026-08-22, reading the chart rather than a cluster.

infra/helm/inventory-tng/templates/backend-deployment.yaml probes /api/healthz with a plain httpGet and no Host header, so the kubelet sends 'Host: <podIP>:8000'. DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS is set from django.allowedHosts, which names the ingress host and not the pod IP, and settings.py has no wildcard. Django answers 400.

Verified against the real settings module: DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS=inventory.nycmesh.net gives ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['inventory.nycmesh.net'], and a probe carrying 'Host: 10.42.0.17:8000' is refused.

CONSEQUENCE, and it is the whole deployment: every backend pod starts, fails readiness at once, never joins the Service, and is killed by liveness at roughly 70 seconds. CrashLoopBackOff for ever. The ingress answers 503 because the frontend can proxy to no endpoint. 'kubectl exec' to make the first administrator lands in a container that is killed mid-command. The logs show 400 with no explanation, because DisallowedHost is only visible with DEBUG on, which must not be on.

It is silent, it looks like a database problem, and it is not.

FIX: set the probes' Host header to an allowed host -- the first entry of django.allowedHosts -- on BOTH probes. Then say so under 'Health checks' in docs/deployment.md, because the next person to edit django.allowedHosts will otherwise re-break it.
close_reason: Closed

title: The backend job has been red since before this batch
description:
CI's backend job sets only DJANGO_SECRET_KEY and DATABASE_URL, so DEBUG is False and settings.py selects CompressedManifestStaticFilesStorage. collectstatic never runs in that job, so every test that renders /api/docs, /admin/... or the MFA pages dies on 'Missing staticfiles manifest entry'.

Reproduced locally with DJANGO_DEBUG=false: test_only_an_existing_administrator_can_reach_the_grant and test_the_admin_can_still_be_read both fail. With the repository .env, which sets DJANGO_DEBUG=true, all 446 pass.

main has been failing this job since 'Require one issue per commit', and it is a required check, so nothing can merge until it is fixed.

The integration job already sets DJANGO_DEBUG: true for the same reason. The settings comment says the DEBUG split exists because collectstatic has not run in a development checkout, which is what the backend job is.
acceptance_criteria: The backend job passes on main without weakening what the suite covers.
close_reason: The backend job sets DJANGO_DEBUG so the suite runs against a checkout's storage rather than the built image's manifest, which is what the integration job already does.

title: Rework the local landing gate
description: .claude/hooks/landing-gate.sh blocks publishing until a review has been recorded, which is the opposite of the new ordering: quality gates then publish, and review afterwards against the pull request. It also assumes one review per change rather than one per batch. Move the gate onto the merge instead. Separately, its textual test matches any command whose text contains 'git' followed by the words it guards, so prose about this very workflow trips it.
close_reason: The gate now guards the merge rather than the push, keyed on the pull request head, and its command matcher no longer trips on prose. Local file, gitignored.

title: Document how work reaches main
description: New canonical section in DEVELOPERS.md covering the branch, the pull request, publishing before review, the review cycle against the PR, and why rebase is the only merge. Update its Commits section for the trailer and summary rules, replacing 'Several issues at once'. Record the reasoning in docs/decisions/0017. Everything else links here and restates nothing.
close_reason: DEVELOPERS.md gained a canonical Pull requests section; Commits updated for the trailer and summary rules; ADR 0017 records the reasoning.

title: Make Django settings environment-driven
description: Scaffold settings hardcode SECRET_KEY, DEBUG=True, ALLOWED_HOSTS=[] and sqlite. Production deploy is impossible until settings read from env. Add django-environ, .env.sample, Postgres via DATABASE_URL, and wire DRF/CORS/spectacular into INSTALLED_APPS (DRF is installed but unregistered).
acceptance_criteria: No secrets in source; DEBUG defaults False; DATABASE_URL drives Postgres; .env.sample documents every var
close_reason: Closed

title: Let a demo deployment be seeded, behind an acknowledgement it cannot inherit
description:
Found by a state review on 2026-08-30, asking what stands between this repository and a demo deployment people can use. Ali chose this route over a demo-only image and over typing the catalogue in by hand.

THE GAP. seed_demo_data refuses when settings.DEBUG is off. Its own docstring gives the reason and the reason is good: the command ships inside the backend image, so it is one wrong kubectl context away from a production pod, and the half of it not guarded by ledger_is_ours() writes into whatever database DATABASE_URL names.

DEBUG must be off in a cluster -- infra/helm/inventory-tng/values.yaml says false is the only supported answer and docs/deployment.md agrees. So the two rules meet and a deployed demo cannot be given anything to look at. Every list is empty, which README already says makes every page below it useless.

WHAT TO BUILD, and the shape is already in this repository rather than invented. seed_integration_data takes --i-know-this-creates-a-published-login, and its comments argue at length why a FLAG rather than an environment variable: a variable is ambient, so one Helm value switches the guard off for every invocation in that cluster from then on and nobody afterwards has to know it did. A flag is spent per invocation, cannot be turned on in advance by configuration, and shows up in the command that ran. That argument carries here unchanged.

So seed_demo_data gains a flag of its own -- something like --i-know-this-writes-invented-data -- which admits it when DEBUG is off. Without the flag the DEBUG refusal stands exactly as it does today, so nothing about a development machine changes and the path README hands a newcomer keeps working with no extra words.

WHAT THE FLAG HAS TO SAY WHEN IT REFUSES, because the refusal is the interface: name the flag, say the data is invented, and say it writes into whatever DATABASE_URL names. Somebody reaching for this on a real deployment should be told what they are about to do rather than which switch to flip.

AND IT WANTS DOCUMENTING WHERE A DEPLOYER LOOKS. docs/deployment.md's ten-step path from an empty cluster to a first sign-in has no step for data at all, because until now there could not be one. A demo deployment is a real case and the document is where somebody standing in front of an empty cluster reads.

TESTS: refused with DEBUG off and no flag; admitted with DEBUG off and the flag; unchanged with DEBUG on; and the refusal names the flag. The existing suite for this command is backend/src/inventory/tests/test_seed_demo_data.py.
close_reason: seed_demo_data takes --i-know-this-writes-invented-data, which admits it where DEBUG is off. The DEBUG path is unchanged, the refusal names the flag, and docs/deployment.md gained the step it never had.

title: Batch: an install that works and has something in it
description:
The three things between this repository and a demo deployment somebody other than Ali can use, identified by a state review on 2026-08-30.

inventory-tng-qe7 -- nothing has ever published an image, so every pod ImagePullBackOffs at the first install. docs/deployment.md step 2 says so outright and the troubleshooting table's first row is that failure.

inventory-tng-v7g -- the migrate Job renders with no resources, so a namespace with a ResourceQuota refuses it and helm blocks until it times out. Second row of the same table.

A third, filed with this batch: seed_demo_data refuses when DEBUG is off, and DEBUG must be off in a cluster, so a deployed demo has no way to get data into it. Ali chose the acknowledgement-flag route.

Together these are 'it installs, and there is something to look at'. What comes after -- the second factor being optional, the sign-in pages not looking broken -- is the next batch and not this one.

title: Batch: stop the batch check being red by default
description:
inventory-tng-et6o, built after ee2c measured the problem: the one-issue-per-commit job fails on 48% of pull request runs, and both causes are the documented development flow doing what it is told.

Ali's framing is the one to build against: a pipeline failure should not be a step in the development flow. If the normal way to discover you are ready is that CI stops being red, red has stopped carrying information -- and it cost exactly that in the session that found this, where a hanging test was reported as a passing suite three times because only the final run per branch was being read.
close_reason: All children completed

title: A ship-logs test deadlocks on a pipe smaller than it assumed
description:
Found on 2026-08-30 while running the suite during inventory-tng-8ljy. Present on main, unrelated to any batch in flight, and it hangs FOREVER rather than failing -- the suite stops at 93% and never returns.

THE TEST: test_a_burst_arriving_in_one_write_is_one_post_rather_than_sixty, in backend/src/inventory/tests/test_shipping.py. It writes sixty records into an os.pipe(), closes the writing end, and only then reads:

    reading_end, writing_end = os.pipe()
    os.write(writing_end, (sixty records).encode())
    os.close(writing_end)
    with os.fdopen(reading_end, 'rb') as stream:
        lines = list(shipping.reading(stream, shipping.waiting))

NOTHING DRAINS THE PIPE WHILE IT IS BEING FILLED. One thread writes, and the read that would empty it is on the line after the write completes. So the write blocks as soon as the pipe is full, and nothing will ever empty it. A textbook single-threaded pipe deadlock.

THE ARITHMETIC, measured rather than estimated:

  one record serialised          229 bytes
  sixty of them, with newlines   13,800 bytes
  the pipe on this machine        8,192 bytes
  a default Linux pipe           65,536 bytes

13,800 fits in 65,536 and does not fit in 8,192. That is the whole bug.

WHY IT IS A FLAKE RATHER THAN A CONSTANT FAILURE, which is the part worth keeping. Linux shrinks newly created pipes once a user is over fs.pipe-user-pages-soft. On this machine that limit is 16,384 pages and the user was holding 988 pipes at sixteen pages each -- essentially at the limit -- so new pipes came back at two pages instead of sixteen. Earlier in the same session, with fewer pipes open, the identical test passed in seconds.

So it passes on a quiet machine and on CI, and deadlocks on a developer's machine after a long session with containers, subprocesses and background jobs. The worst shape: green everywhere it is watched, hanging where somebody is working.

PROVEN, not inferred:

  the single test, on this branch   hangs (timeout)
  the single test, on main          hangs (timeout)
  test_shipping.py alone, earlier   passed in seconds
  fcntl F_GETPIPE_SZ on a new pipe  8192

THE FIX IS NOT TO SHRINK THE TEST. Sixty is the number the test is about -- the defect it guards is sixty posts where one was wanted, and the docstring says so. Writing fewer records to fit a small pipe would keep the test green while removing what it tests.

Drain and fill at the same time instead. A writer in a thread, or a child process, so the reader empties the pipe while it is being filled; the assertion afterwards is unchanged. A temporary file would also work and would lose something real -- the reading() helper exists because select answers about a descriptor and a text stream buffers in front of one, and a regular file is not the descriptor that behaviour is about.

WORTH CHECKING AT THE SAME TIME whether any sibling in that module writes to a pipe the same way. The three around it are smaller and pass, but they pass for a reason nobody chose -- they happen to fit -- and the same shrunk pipe would take them too if a record grew.

AND IT EXPLAINS SOMETHING THAT SHOULD BE SAID PLAINLY: while this was hanging, three separate 'the full suite passes' claims were made in this session on runs that had actually timed out at 92%. The guardrail suites and the targeted runs were real; the full-suite claims were not. A test that hangs rather than fails is exactly what turns a timeout into a misread.

title: A checker that refuses an undocumented config value
description:
Split from inventory-tng-xi9w on 2026-08-30, because documenting the values and guarding them are two commits.

Read xi9w for the audit. This issue is only the guard, and it lands after the documentation it would otherwise refuse.

WHAT IT CHECKS, and the fourth is the one that matters most:

1. Every assignment in .env.sample has a comment above its contiguous group.
2. Every environment entry in compose.yaml does.
3. Every leaf value in infra/helm/inventory-tng/values.yaml does.
4. Every variable the chart renders into a container appears in docs/deployment.md's environment-variable table.

The measure for 1 to 3 is the one a reader uses: a comment block directly above the group, no blank line breaking the two apart. A naive 'comment on the line above' rule reports three times as many failures and is wrong -- group comments covering a coherent block are correct and must keep passing. xi9w records that mistake being made and corrected.

Rule 4 is what found CLIENT_REPORT_RATE: set in .env.sample, rendered by the chart, absent from the document that lists what an operator may set. It is the rule that catches the gap mattering to somebody deploying rather than somebody reading, and it is the reason this is worth building rather than fixing the values once.

WHERE IT GOES: scripts/check-config.sh with scripts/check-config.test.sh beside it, and a line in CI's 'Guardrail checkers' job with the others. That job runs each checker's own suite and then, for the commit hook, runs the checker itself -- the same shape applies here.

AN ALLOWLIST IS WANTED, following scripts/check-docs.allow and check-telemetry.allow. Some values genuinely need no prose and the local-only variables are legitimately absent from the deployment table. Those files' own headers argue that an entry is a decision to justify rather than a way to make a build pass, and that argument carries.

TESTS, in the shape the other checkers' suites use -- a throwaway tree, a value with a comment, a value without one, a group comment covering several, a chart variable missing from the table, and an allowlisted exception.
close_reason: scripts/check-config.py with its wrapper, allowlist and a 12-case suite, wired into CI's Documentation and Guardrail jobs, and documented in DEVELOPERS.md#documentation-rules.

title: Batch: every config value says what it is for
description:
Two issues from inventory-tng-xi9w, split because they are two commits: writing the documentation that is missing, and adding the checker that stops it going missing again. Each is revertible on its own and the second is worthless without the first.

The audit is on xi9w and was done before either was filed, so neither is an instruction to go and look.
close_reason: All children completed

title: Say what every config value is for
description:
Asked for by Ali on 2026-08-30: every config value in the sample env and the config files is to be CLEARLY documented.

AUDITED BEFORE FILING, so this is a list of real gaps rather than an instruction to go and look. The measure is the one a reader actually uses: a value is documented if a comment block sits directly above its contiguous group, with no blank line breaking the two apart. A first pass counting "a comment immediately above this line" reported three times as many gaps and was wrong -- the OIDC block, and the provider client secrets, are covered by group comments that name each variable in turn, and that is good documentation rather than a hole.

=== WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING ===

.env.sample -- 5 of 40 values, with nothing above their group:

  APPEND_BURST_RATE, APPEND_SUSTAINED_RATE
      There IS a long comment about the two rate limits, but it sits above a
      different group and the blank line breaks it. Reads as unexplained.
  POSTGRES_DB, POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD
      Genuinely nothing. They follow a blank line under a comment about
      POSTGRES_PORT, which is about the port and says so.

compose.yaml -- 8 of 41 environment entries:

  POSTGRES_DB, POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, DJANGO_SECRET_KEY,
  DJANGO_DEBUG, DJANGO_LOG_LEVEL, DJANGO_LOG_LEVELS, BACKEND_ORIGIN

  DJANGO_SECRET_KEY and DJANGO_DEBUG are the two worth doing first. The secret
  key carries a literal dev-only default and nothing beside it says never to
  deploy that; DJANGO_DEBUG defaults to true here and inventory-tng-o1uj.1 is
  what that already cost once.

infra/helm/inventory-tng/values.yaml -- 20 of 54 leaf values:

  nameOverride, fullnameOverride, registry, repository, replicaCount (x2),
  port (x2), cpu, memory (x4), debug, enabled (x3), className, host

  Several are conventional Helm knobs a reader can guess. `debug` is not: it is
  DJANGO_DEBUG in a cluster and deserves a line saying what it turns on. The
  resource figures are not either -- docs/deployment.md's health-check
  arithmetic divides by the worker count and there is a test holding the two
  together, so a number changed here without reading that breaks a documented
  model.

=== AND ONE THAT IS SIMPLY ABSENT FROM THE DOCUMENT ===

CLIENT_REPORT_RATE is set in .env.sample, rendered into the backend by
infra/helm/inventory-tng/templates/_helpers.tpl, and appears NOWHERE in
docs/deployment.md. It is the ONLY variable the chart renders that the
environment-variable table omits -- checked by walking every `- name:` in the
helper against the table. Every sibling rate limit is there:
APPEND_BURST_RATE, APPEND_SUSTAINED_RATE, DEVICE_ENROLMENT_RATE and
DEBUG_TRACE_RATE all have rows.

An operator can set it, the chart will honour it, and the document that is
supposed to list what they may set does not know it exists. That is the sharpest
single item here and is worth fixing first whatever happens to the rest.

Five more in .env.sample are absent from the table and are NOT defects, for the
record, so nobody chases them: POSTGRES_PORT, POSTGRES_DB, POSTGRES_USER and
POSTGRES_PASSWORD belong to the compose database rather than to a deployment,
and VITE_API_BASE_URL is the dev server's. The table is about deploying, and
saying so where the reader might wonder is part of this work.

=== WHAT "CLEARLY" SHOULD MEAN, because a comment on every line is not it ===

This repository's existing comments are unusually good and the standard is set
by them: say what the value DOES, what breaks if it is wrong, and where the
canonical explanation lives -- not a restatement of the name. NUM_PROXIES and
DATABASE_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS in .env.sample are the models to write to.

A group comment covering a coherent group is CORRECT and should not be broken up
into one comment per line. Rule 1 applies here as everywhere: the full argument
lives once, and the config file points at it.

=== KEEP IT TRUE WITH A CHECKER, which is this project's habit ===

scripts/ already holds check-docs.sh, check-telemetry.sh, check-setup.sh and
check-batch.sh, each with its own *.test.sh, all run by CI's guardrail job. A
config checker belongs beside them, and it is what stops this issue being done
twice:

  * every assignment in .env.sample has a comment above its group
  * every environment entry in compose.yaml does
  * every leaf in the chart's values.yaml does
  * every variable the chart renders into a container appears in
    docs/deployment.md's table

The fourth is the one that found CLIENT_REPORT_RATE and is the most valuable,
because it catches the gap that matters to somebody deploying rather than the
one that matters to somebody reading.

An allowlist will be wanted for the handful that genuinely need no prose, the
way check-docs.allow and check-telemetry.allow already work -- and, as those
files argue, an entry on it is a decision worth justifying rather than a way to
make a build pass.
close_reason: Every value in .env.sample, compose.yaml and the chart's values.yaml now has prose above it, and CLIENT_REPORT_RATE has the deployment-table row it never had. The checker that keeps it true is inventory-tng-8ljy.

title: Split the batch check: structure on every push, completeness at merge
description:
Asked for by Ali on 2026-08-30, in the same breath as inventory-tng-ee2c: use that issue's findings to enforce the one-issue-per-commit rule LOCALLY rather than when the pull request run happens. Read ee2c first -- it holds the diagnosis, and this issue is only the half that builds on it.

THE SHORT VERSION OF WHAT ee2c FOUND. CI asks check-batch.sh the strict question -- no commits waiting to be folded in -- on every push, passing --draft only while the pull request is a GitHub draft. But this project's review cycle STARTS when the draft flag ends, and the cycle prescribes fixup commits. So the check is red through the whole of the review, on every batch, and green only at the end. Five of the last fourteen runs on batch branches failed that way.

WHAT TO BUILD. The strict question moves to where the answer is already known and costs nothing: the working copy, before the merge. The landing gate is the place -- scripts/landing-gate.sh already refuses `gh pr merge` until the review cycle has been recorded against the exact head, and an uncollapsed branch is the same kind of not-ready. It should refuse the merge when `check-batch.sh origin/main..HEAD` does not pass, and say the autosquash line rather than making somebody go and find it.

That turns a full CI round trip into an immediate refusal, and it puts the two merge preconditions in one place instead of one locally and one in a job whose failures nobody reads.

AND CI ASKS THE TOLERANT QUESTION INSTEAD. Option 3 of ee2c: pass --draft always, so the job holds a pull request to the structural rules -- one issue per commit, membership matching the batch epic, no issue landed twice -- without failing on fixups the process asked for. It stays as the only thing holding a FORK to the rule, where no local hook runs, which is why deleting it is not on the table.

WHAT HAS TO BE TRUE FOR THIS TO BE AN IMPROVEMENT RATHER THAN A MOVE:

* The local refusal must fail CLOSED, like everything else in check mode. A missing python3 or an unreadable tracker refuses the merge; that is the direction the gate's own deny_dependency argues for at length, and this is a merge guard rather than the Stop hook's turn guard.
* It must not fire on anything but a merge. check-batch is a whole-branch read and there is no reason to pay for it on an ordinary push.
* It has to say what to run. The gate's existing refusals name the command; this one should carry `git -c core.editor=true rebase --autosquash origin/main` for the same reason.

TESTS, in scripts/landing-gate.test.sh beside the fifteen the stop hook added: a merge refused on an uncollapsed branch, a merge permitted once it is collapsed, and the dependency case that a checker it cannot run refuses rather than permits. The harness already builds throwaway repositories on batch branches, so the fixtures exist.

DOCS. DEVELOPERS.md "When a branch is ready to merge" lists what the gate refuses and gains one more; the same section's four-and-two split -- what main enforces, and the two a person holds to -- is where the moved question belongs, because check-batch being clean is currently one of the two and is about to stop being somebody's honour.

WORTH DOING WITH inventory-tng-83cn's successor work if any: the stop hook, this, and the merge receipt are three refusals in one file that all mean "this batch is not finished", and a reader meeting them separately should still see them as one idea.
notes:
SHARPENED 2026-08-30, after measuring inventory-tng-ee2c properly. Read its notes for the numbers; what changes here is the shape of the fix.

IT IS TWO OBJECTIONS, NOT ONE, and --draft only ever covered the first:

    24 of 31 failures  "N commits are waiting to be folded in"   (--draft downgrades this)
     7 of 31 failures  "in the batch but not landed here"        (--draft does NOT touch this)

So passing --draft always -- which is what this issue originally proposed for CI -- fixes about three quarters of the failures and leaves the rest. A batch built one issue at a time still fails on every push until the last issue lands, draft or not.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD, and it is a cleaner rule than "pass --draft always":

SPLIT THE CHECK ON WHAT THE QUESTION IS ABOUT.

  Structural, asked on every push, stays required:
    - one issue per commit
    - no issue landed twice
    - the commit message rules
  None of these is ever temporarily false. A branch mid-construction still
  holds them, and a fork's pull request is held to them too, which is the
  reason not to delete this job.

  Merge-time, asked once, locally, by the landing gate:
    - is every issue in the batch epic landed
    - is the branch collapsed
  Both are questions about whether the branch is FINISHED. Asking them of a
  branch that is not finished is asking the wrong thing, and getting "no" is
  not a fault -- it is the correct answer to a question nobody should have
  asked yet.

That split needs check-batch.sh to grow a mode that asks only the structural half -- or the two halves to be separable by flag -- so the same script serves both callers. Prefer that over a second script: check-batch.sh already holds the rules and a second reader would be a second opinion, which is the thing scripts/hosts.py exists as a warning about.

THE GATE SIDE IS UNCHANGED from what this issue already describes: refuse `gh pr merge` when the merge-time half does not pass, name the autosquash line, fail closed. It already refuses a merge without a recorded cycle, so this is one more precondition in the place that already holds the others.

AND THE POINT ALI MADE, worth keeping in front of whoever builds this: a pipeline failure should not be a step in the development flow. If the normal way to discover you are ready is that CI stops being red, then red has stopped carrying information -- and the cost is not theoretical. It is why a hanging test got reported as a passing suite three times in one session.
close_reason: check-batch.sh --draft now covers both finished-ness objections, CI passes it always and keeps asking everything structural, and the landing gate runs the strict check before a merge. 41 + 93 cases across the two suites.

title: The one-issue-per-commit check is red on most pull request runs
description:
Raised by Ali on 2026-08-30: despite a7899c4, where the checker was taught to see the rule, and 4839f7f, where DEVELOPERS.md gained the one-issue-per-commit rule, the "One issue per commit" job fails in nearly every pull request run.

HE IS RIGHT, AND IT IS EASY TO MISS. Counted across the fourteen most recent runs on batch branches: five failed. They are invisible to anybody watching `gh pr checks --watch`, because that reports the LATEST run per branch and the failures are on intermediate pushes. Every batch in this repository's recent history has red runs in the middle of it and a green one at the end.

    33299260590  batch/why-the-admin-stands-out      failure
    33299087848  batch/why-the-admin-stands-out      failure
    33287652288  batch/make-the-cycle-deterministic  failure
    33287431536  batch/make-the-cycle-deterministic  failure
    33286032709  batch/two-decisions                 failure

THE CAUSE, from the log of the first of those rather than from reasoning:

    Commits in e20032e..826ae22:
      · f9be0720  inventory-tng-srs3  srs3: Say why the admin is meant to look different
      · batch epic: inventory-tng-17cq
      ✗ 2 commits are waiting to be folded in. Nothing does it on the way in:
      ·   git -c core.editor=true rebase --autosquash origin/main

The checker is doing exactly what it was built to do. It is being ASKED THE WRONG QUESTION.

.github/workflows/ci.yml passes --draft only when the pull request is a GitHub draft:

    scripts/check-batch.sh \
      ${{ github.event.pull_request.draft && '--draft' || '' }} \
      "...base.sha..head.sha"

And check-batch.sh's own usage says what --draft means: "the branch is still under review, where commits waiting to be folded in are expected rather than a fault."

SO TWO NOTIONS OF "UNDER REVIEW" DISAGREE, and the gap between them is the bug. GitHub's draft flag ENDS at `gh pr ready`. This repository's review cycle BEGINS there -- DEVELOPERS.md#pull-requests marks the pull request ready when the batch is complete and green, and only then is it reviewed. Every fixup the cycle prescribes is therefore pushed to a pull request that is no longer a draft, and CI asks the strict question of a branch the process has deliberately left un-collapsed.

The failures are not a checker fault, a flake, or a rule anybody broke. They are the workflow asking "is this ready to merge?" on every push during the phase where the answer is supposed to be no.

WHAT MAKES IT WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN TOLERATING. A check that is red as a matter of routine is a check people stop reading, and this is the one that guards the rule this repository is arranged around. It also costs a full CI round trip to learn something the working copy already knew -- which is inventory-tng-<local enforcement bead>, and the reason that one is linked to this.

THE OPTIONS, and the third is the one this points at:

1. Pass --draft whenever the cycle has not been recorded. CI cannot see that: the receipts are in .claude/ and are gitignored and local. It would need the marker comments, which is a gh call and a second definition of "reviewed" to keep in step with landing-gate.sh.
2. Pass --draft on every `synchronize` and ask the strict question only on `ready_for_review`. Wrong: the last push before a merge is an ordinary synchronize, so the strict question would never be asked at the moment it matters.
3. LET CI ASK THE TOLERANT QUESTION ALWAYS, and enforce the strict one locally, before the merge, where the answer is already known and free. The landing gate already refuses `gh pr merge` until the cycle is recorded and is the natural place to refuse an uncollapsed branch too.

Option 3 is what Ali asked for and it is also the smaller change. Decide it here; the linked issue builds it.

WHAT NOT TO DO: delete the job. It is the only thing holding a FORK's pull request to the rule, where no local hook runs at all. CONTRIBUTING.md is the path that matters for that, and DEVELOPERS.md#what-ci-proves is the argument for why the checkers run in both places.
notes:
MEASURED PROPERLY, 2026-08-30, after Ali sent run 33304076968 as another example and observed that "the development flow waits for it to fail before moving on to the next step". He is right, and it is worse than the first count suggested.

ACROSS EVERY PULL REQUEST RUN THIS REPOSITORY HAS (80 of them, 65 where the job ran):

    34 passed
    31 failed
    -> 48% of runs

Nearly half. And the failures are not one fault but TWO, which matters because the flag that exists only covers one of them:

    24  "N commits are waiting to be folded in"
     7  "in the batch but not landed here: <issue>"

WHAT --draft ACTUALLY DOES, read rather than assumed (check-batch.sh around line 321): it downgrades the folded-in objection from a `fail` to a `note`. THAT IS ALL. The membership objection -- an epic with children that have not landed yet -- is not affected by it at all.

So the two causes map onto the two halves of the documented flow, and the check is red through BOTH:

* WHILE THE BATCH IS BEING BUILT. DEVELOPERS.md says to push each issue as it is finished, "so CI runs per issue rather than once at the end". Every one of those pushes has an epic whose children are not all landed, so membership fails -- and being a draft does not help, because --draft does not cover this one. A four-issue batch fails three times before it can pass once.
* WHILE IT IS BEING REVIEWED. Fixups are what the cycle prescribes, and CI stops passing --draft at `gh pr ready`, which is exactly when the cycle starts.

Green only in the gap between the last issue landing and the first fixup, and again after the final autosquash. The failure is the NORMAL state of the check for most of a batch's life, which is Ali's point exactly: the process is using a red pipeline as an intermediate step rather than as a signal.

WHY THAT IS WORSE THAN NOISE. A check that is red as a matter of routine is one nobody reads, and this one guards the rule the whole repository is arranged around. It also trained me, over this session, to watch only the final run per branch -- which is how a genuine hang in test_shipping.py (inventory-tng-nre8) got reported as a passing suite three times.

THE CONCEPTUAL SPLIT THE FIX SHOULD FOLLOW, and it is clearer than the three options first written here. Two different kinds of question are being asked at once:

  STRUCTURAL, and true at every push -- one issue per commit, no issue landed twice, the message rules. Nothing about the flow makes these temporarily false, so CI should keep asking them on every push and they should stay required.

  MERGE-TIME, and deliberately false until the end -- is the batch complete, is it collapsed. These are questions about whether the branch is FINISHED, and asking them of a branch that is not is asking the wrong thing.

Splitting on that line removes both failure causes without weakening anything, because nothing about the second pair was ever protecting a push -- they protect a merge, and inventory-tng-et6o is where they belong.

KEPT OPEN DELIBERATELY, 2026-08-30. The investigation is finished and its findings are above; what keeps this open is bookkeeping rather than work. Closing it put a second closure into the same .beads diff as inventory-tng-et6o's, and check-commit refused the commit for closing two issues -- correctly. Close it with whatever batch comes next, the way the tracker's own state usually travels.
close_reason: Measured, diagnosed and recorded; the fix landed as inventory-tng-et6o in PR #46.

title: Every sign-in page is unstyled, because nothing overrides allauth's templates
description:
Reported by the project owner on 2026-08-29, with a screenshot of
http://localhost:8000/accounts/reauthenticate/ rendering as bare browser-default
HTML: a "Menu:" bullet list, a serif heading, an unstyled password box.

NOT THE SAME BUG AS inventory-tng-o1uj.1, and the difference is the whole
diagnosis. That one was the Django admin asking for five stylesheets and being
answered 404, because nothing served STATIC_ROOT under gunicorn. It is fixed and
verified: /static/admin/css/base.css answers 200 and the admin draws itself.

These pages are a different thing entirely. Measured rather than assumed:

    curl -s http://localhost:8000/accounts/login/ | grep -ci '<link|stylesheet|<style'
    0

They ask for NO stylesheet at all. Nothing is 404ing; there is nothing to
serve. allauth ships its templates deliberately unstyled so that a project can
put its own frame around them, and this project never has -- so every page
under /accounts/ has looked like this since the day allauth was added. Sign in,
the TOTP challenge, the authenticator setup, the reauthentication prompt in the
screenshot, and every provider page.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. This is the FIRST screen anybody sees. The
README now sends a new contributor to /accounts/login/ before anything else,
and decision 0013 makes it the only way in for an administrator -- a volunteer
organisation asking somebody to type a password into a page that looks broken
is asking for the wrong instinct about the whole system. It is also the one
surface where the app asks for a credential, which is exactly where looking
untrustworthy costs the most.

WHERE THE FIX GOES, established by reading rather than guessed:

* allauth's override point is `allauth/layouts/base.html`, with
  `entrance.html` and `manage.html` extending it. Overriding the first is
  enough to reach every page.
* settings.py TEMPLATES has `"DIRS": []`, so there is no project template
  directory at all yet and one has to be added before anything can be
  overridden. That is the first commit whatever else is decided.
* The stylesheet has to be a file rather than a `<style>` block IF the
  deployed CSP is to stay as it is -- although note `style-src` currently
  carries `'unsafe-inline'` both in settings.py and in
  frontend/nginx.conf.template, so an inline block would work today. Do not
  reach for that without saying so: it is the kind of thing that quietly makes
  the allowance load-bearing and then impossible to remove.
* Whatever the stylesheet is, it is served from STATIC_ROOT through the same
  WhiteNoise that o1uj.1 turned on, so it needs collectstatic and it works in
  the image for the same reason the admin's does.

WHAT IS NOT SETTLED, and wants Ali rather than an answer invented here:

1. HOW FAR TO GO. The cheapest thing that stops it looking broken is a
   readable, unbranded stylesheet -- a width, a font stack, spacing, a form
   that lines up. The most expensive is making these pages look like the
   volunteer app, which means either sharing the frontend's MUI theme somehow
   or reimplementing its colours by hand in CSS, and the second is a second
   copy of a design that will drift.
2. WHETHER THE ADMIN'S LOOK MATTERS TOO. The Django admin now draws itself in
   Django's own style, which is not this project's. guides/worked-examples.md
   session 3 already asks whether that is good enough for a volunteer
   administrator or whether the work belongs in the app; this is the same
   question one screen earlier.

DO NOT let this turn into theming the admin as well without deciding that
first. The narrow version -- these pages stop looking broken -- is worth doing
on its own and is a much smaller change.
design:
HOW THE COLOURS GET SHARED, settled with Ali on 2026-08-30. This supersedes the 'five custom properties, hand-copied' suggestion in the note above, which was the lazy option and was right to be pushed back on.

SYMLINKING IS NOT AVAILABLE, for three reasons and none of them is preference:
* There is nothing to link. theme.ts holds no colour at all -- the values are inside @mui/material's default theme object, under node_modules.
* The build contexts are separate. compose.yaml builds context: ./backend and context: ./frontend, so a link from one into the other dangles inside the image; the other tree is not in the context Docker is sent.
* Wrong language. Django needs CSS and theme.ts is TypeScript.

GENERATE IT INSTEAD, and MUI does most of the work. @mui/material 9.3 accepts cssVariables in createTheme -- confirmed in the installed createTheme.d.ts -- so turning it on makes MUI emit the custom properties itself. A generator then resolves the same theme object the app renders from and writes them out. That is a projection rather than a copy, and it scales the day theme.ts grows a real palette, which a hand-copy does not.

THREE PIECES, AND THE THIRD IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS:
1. cssVariables: true in frontend/src/theme.ts
2. a generator writing the resolved variables to a stylesheet under backend/, collected into STATIC_ROOT like everything else
3. A TEST THAT REGENERATES AND COMPARES, red when the committed file is not what the theme now resolves to

Without the third it is a copy with extra steps. With it, drift is a failing build rather than something somebody has to notice -- the same reasoning as the stop hook in inventory-tng-83cn, and the same reasoning check-docs.sh rests on.

WHERE THE FILE LIVES: committed, following the precedent this repository already set. frontend/capture/ generates the PNGs in guides/images/, they are committed, and the suite that writes them is deliberately kept out of npm test because a suite that edits the working tree is not a suite. Same shape, same argument. Producing it in CI and passing it between jobs is the alternative and buys nothing here.

ONE THING TO VERIFY RATHER THAN ASSUME: cssVariables changes how MUI emits styles in the APP, not only at build time. It is the documented modern path and generally safe, but it is a frontend change with its own verification attached, not a pure build concern. Check it renders unchanged before building anything on top of it.

AND IT MAY STILL BE TOO MUCH MACHINERY. For the five values that exist today, generator plus checker plus wiring is larger than the problem. The case for it is entirely that theme.ts will grow a palette; if it never will, a neutral stylesheet that does not try to match is the honest smaller answer. That is the trade to decide, and it is a different question from the one this bead's description opens with.
notes:
=== ALI'S DECISIONS, 2026-08-30. These are settled; do not relitigate them. ===

1. THE DJANGO ADMIN IS NOT STYLED TO MATCH THE APP, and that is deliberate
   rather than unfinished. His words: if the admin side is usable then do not
   style it to be similar, it SHOULD stand out to make it clear that it is a
   different app and not part of the frontend.

   The reason is worth more than the look. The admin is where nothing validates
   on your behalf and nothing is undoable, and an administrator who has left the
   volunteer app should be able to SEE that they have. A surface continuous with
   the app would hide exactly the boundary worth noticing. Point 2 of the
   description is closed on this, and closed the opposite way from the direction
   it was drifting.

2. THE /accounts/ PAGES ARE STYLED TO MATCH THE APP. This follows from 1 rather
   than sitting beside it: a deliberate contrast only reads as deliberate when
   the other side is consistent. If the admin stands out and the sign-in pages
   also look like nothing in particular, there is no signal in it, only three
   surfaces each looking different for their own reasons.

   The sign-in is the door to both, and it belongs to the app being entered --
   today overwhelmingly the volunteer app, since README sends people to :8080
   where nginx serves the frontend and proxies /accounts. An administrator-only
   door would be its own decision and is not this one.

3. THE COLOURS ARE GENERATED, NOT COPIED. The design field on this issue holds
   the mechanism and why symlinking is not available. What matters here is that
   Ali asked for it directly -- "why can't the copy operation be managed by a
   build script" -- and the answer is that it can, MUI 9.3's cssVariables does
   most of it, and the checker that compares the committed file against what the
   theme resolves to is the part that makes it a projection rather than a copy.

4. THIS GETS A DECISION RECORD, and Ali said so explicitly when asked. It is
   inventory-tng-srs3, and it records decision 1 -- the rule, not the styling --
   because a later contributor will find the admin ugly and improve it with
   entirely good intentions. That is what docs/decisions/ is for.

WHAT REMAINS ON THIS ISSUE after all four: the /accounts/ work itself. A project
template directory (TEMPLATES DIRS is [] today), an override of
allauth/layouts/base.html, the generated stylesheet, and the checker. Nothing
about the admin.

CORRECTION, 2026-08-30, after actually reading frontend/src/theme.ts rather than assuming a theme existed.

THE DESCRIPTION ABOVE OVERSTATES THE DECISION. It offers 'share the frontend's MUI theme somehow' against 'reimplement its colours by hand in CSS, and the second is a second copy of a design that will drift'. There is almost nothing to share and nothing to drift from.

theme.ts is seven lines: createTheme({ colorSchemes: { light: true, dark: true } }). No palette, no typography, no component overrides. main.tsx wraps the app in ThemeProvider and CssBaseline. Counted across frontend/src: 23 sx= props, all spacing and layout; zero styled() calls; zero hard-coded colours; no CSS files of our own.

So the app's appearance is stock Material Design with the OS light/dark preference honoured. Measured against the running stack: dark is background #121212 and text #ffffff, light is background #ffffff and text rgba(0,0,0,0.87), the font stack is Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif at 16px, and it does follow the OS preference. The dark background is CssBaseline, not a choice anybody made here.

WHAT THAT CHANGES. Matching the app is cheap rather than architectural. The 'second copy that will drift' argument does not apply, because there is no first copy. How the values get shared without becoming a copy at all is the design field on this issue.



DECIDED BY ALI, 2026-08-30 -- THE DJANGO ADMIN IS NOT TO BE STYLED TO MATCH.

His words: if the admin side is usable then do not style it to be similar, it SHOULD stand out to make it clear that it is a different app and not part of the frontend.

So point 2 of the description is settled and settled the other way from the direction it was drifting. The admin looking like Django is a FEATURE. An administrator who has left the volunteer app and is editing rows directly should be able to see that they have, and a surface that looked continuous with the app would hide exactly the boundary worth noticing -- the one where nothing validates on your behalf and nothing is undoable. Whoever next finds the admin ugly should read this before improving it.

That narrows this bead to /accounts/ alone, and the design note above applies only there.

AND IT SHARPENS THE ALLAUTH HALF RATHER THAN LEAVING IT ALONE. A deliberate contrast only reads as deliberate if the other side of it is consistent. If the admin stands out and the sign-in pages ALSO look like nothing in particular, there is no signal in it -- just three surfaces that each look different for their own reasons. The argument for making /accounts/ look like the app is therefore stronger under this decision than before it, not weaker: it is what gives the admin something to stand out FROM.

Worth noting the sign-in is the door to both. It belongs to the app being entered, and today that is overwhelmingly the volunteer app -- README sends people to :8080, where nginx serves the frontend and proxies /accounts to Django. If an administrator-only door is ever wanted, that is its own decision and not this one.

PROBABLY WANTS A DECISION RECORD, small as it is. Not for the styling but for the rule: 'the admin is deliberately not themed, because the boundary is worth seeing'. It is exactly the kind of thing a later contributor improves away with good intentions, and docs/decisions/ is where this project keeps the arguments that future work is held against. Ali's call whether it earns one.

title: Batch: make the cycle deterministic
description:
The pair settled with the project owner on 2026-08-29: a Stop hook that refuses to end a turn on a batch that has not been through its review cycle (inventory-tng-83cn), and the documentation it refers to when it refuses (inventory-tng-cj5z).

They ship together because neither is much use alone. The hook without the wording refuses and points at a document that does not say what done means; the wording without the hook is another rule an agent may not follow, which is the failure that produced both.
close_reason: All children completed

title: Batch: two decisions the owner made
description:
Two issues settled by the project owner on 2026-08-29 after the dev-environment work, and landed together because both are the same kind of change: making a shipped configuration tell the truth.

inventory-tng-o1uj.3 asked for a setting that turns the second factor off in development. It is not being built. The seeded integration login already carries a FIXED TOTP secret that survives every database wipe, which is the pain the request was actually about, and it is undocumented where anybody would find it. Documenting it costs nothing and adds no way to turn an access control off, so decision 0013 point 3 stands unamended. The issue was retitled to what is being done rather than closed and replaced, so the argument stays in one place.

inventory-tng-o1uj.4 asked whether a cross-origin arrangement is supported. It is not, and CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS was advertising that it might be.
close_reason: All children completed

title: Write down what a review finding becomes, and what done means for a batch
description:
Settled with the project owner on 2026-08-29, in the conversation that also
raised the Stop hook. Two sentences to add to DEVELOPERS.md, and the value of
both is in a precision that is easy to lose.

ONE: WHAT A REVIEW FINDING BECOMES. The owner's words, and they should survive
into the document roughly as spoken:

  "If an issue is orthogonal or does not align with the current goal of the
  epic then it should be filed. However a fix should not be deferred if a
  review finds that the work done thus far is insufficient to close the epic;
  in that case it MUST add the bead to the epic in progress and it MUST NOT
  consider the epic complete until those newly filed beads are completed."

This sharpens the third row of the table in
DEVELOPERS.md#one-review-pass-findings-filed-per-issue rather than replacing
it. That row already says a finding which is the composition of two issues
becomes a new issue in the same batch; what it does not say is what to do with
a finding that is nobody's composition but still means the epic is not done.

THE PRECISION THAT MAKES IT BIND, and without which it is another honour rule:
it has to be the BATCH epic. scripts/batch-membership.py reads parentage as
batch membership and check-batch.sh refuses a pull request whose landed issues
are not exactly one epic's children -- so a bead parented onto the batch epic
and not landed makes the merge impossible. Parent the same bead onto any other
epic and nothing checks it at all. The wording must say "batch epic" for that
reason, and the reason is worth stating in the document so nobody later
"simplifies" it to "the epic".

Precedent for the other half already exists and should be cited rather than
re-argued: PR #20 deferred four simplify findings into inventory-tng-nb8.15
through nb8.18 and that was correct, because none of them said the batch was
unfinished. PR #41 filed inventory-tng-o1uj.8 the same way. The rule is not
"never defer"; it is "never defer what makes the epic incomplete".

TWO: WHAT DONE MEANS FOR A BATCH. There is currently no definition, which is
how a session can leave a ready, green, unreviewed pull request and describe
it as finished without saying anything false. AGENTS.md already says merging a
mergeable batch/* pull request needs no permission and that an agent working a
batch does not stop to ask. The consequence has never been written down:

  A batch is done when it is merged. Stopping before that is a deviation, and
  the only honest forms of it are "merged" or "stopped at stage N, here is why,
  here is `scripts/landing-gate.sh status`". A ready pull request left
  unreviewed is neither.

Small, and it is the sentence whose absence let a wrong reason go unchallenged.

WHY THIS IS NOT ENOUGH ON ITS OWN, and the honest reason it is filed as a pair:
the failure this documents is an agent not following a written rule. Writing a
better rule does not fix that. The sibling issue is the mechanism; this one is
what the mechanism refers to when it refuses. Land them together or land the
mechanism first.
close_reason: Both written into DEVELOPERS.md: the filing rule sharpens the three-row table and names the BATCH epic as what makes it binding, and a new 'A batch is done when it is merged' section defines the two honest ways to leave one.

title: Refuse to end a turn on a batch that has not been through its cycle
description:
Asked for by the project owner on 2026-08-29, after an agent finished a batch,
left the pull request ready and unmerged, and reported the review cycle as
blocked when it was not. The owner's objection is the right one and is the
reason this exists rather than a rule: "I want to ensure I don't keep returning
to unmerged PRs because of the lack of deterministic steps that ensure
something is done rather than a rule that you may not follow for some reason."

WHAT ALREADY HOLDS, so that this is not built over the top of something that
works. scripts/landing-gate.sh already refuses `gh pr merge` until the cycle
has been recorded against the exact head, refuses `gh pr ready` while checks
are red, refuses a push that would land on main, and refuses a bare force push.
It fails closed. It is registered as a PreToolUse hook on Bash in the tracked
.claude/settings.json, so every clone and worktree gets it.

WHAT NOTHING HOLDS. The moment a session decides a batch is finished and writes
a summary instead of continuing. The gate binds `gh pr merge`; it does not bind
stopping short of it. DEVELOPERS.md says the review pass having happened is the
one part of the bar nobody enforces -- "on your honour" -- and decision 0020
records that trade deliberately. This is that trade being paid, twice, in one
afternoon.

WHAT TO BUILD. A Stop hook: a mode of scripts/landing-gate.sh, registered in
.claude/settings.json beside the PreToolUse entry, that runs when a session
tries to end a turn. It blocks, naming the missing stage, when ALL of:

* HEAD is a batch/* branch
* an open pull request exists for it
* that pull request is NOT a draft
* its required checks are green
* `record` has no receipt for the current head

Ending the turn is what gets refused, so a summary cannot be written in place
of the work. That is the whole point: it is not a reminder, it is a refusal.

THREE CONSTRAINTS, and each is a way this goes wrong if it is missed.

1. IT MUST FAIL OPEN. Every other part of this gate fails closed and should:
   a broken `gh` must not let a merge through. Here the asymmetry reverses. A
   Stop hook that fails closed on a missing `gh`, an unauthenticated one, or a
   rate limit traps the session with no way to end it and no way to fix the
   thing that would release it. It should let the turn end and say loudly on
   stderr that it could not check. The gate's own docstring about failing
   closed needs a paragraph saying why this one does not.

2. IT MUST BE BOUNDED. A hook that blocks unconditionally is an infinite loop.
   It should fire at most once per pull request and head, recording that it
   did, so a genuine "I am stopping deliberately" costs one extra exchange
   rather than the session. Where that record lives wants thinking about: the
   receipt store the gate already keeps is the obvious home, and it is already
   keyed by head.

3. DRAFTS ARE EXEMPT. A batch under construction is a draft by the flow in
   DEVELOPERS.md, and stopping mid-construction is ordinary. Only a ready,
   green, unreviewed pull request is the state this is about.

TESTS. scripts/landing-gate.test.sh exists and is the place. Each of the five
conditions above wants a case that it alone prevents the block, plus one that
the hook fires once and not twice for the same head, plus one that a failure to
reach `gh` lets the turn end rather than trapping it.

DOCS. DEVELOPERS.md "When a branch is ready to merge" lists what the gate
refuses; this is a fifth refusal and belongs in that list. Decision 0020 is
about who merges and why the honour-based part is where it is -- if this
changes that answer, 0020 gets an amendment rather than being left to
disagree with the code.

WORTH DOING WITH the sibling issue about the review-pass wording, which is the
same problem approached from the documentation side.
close_reason: A Stop mode on scripts/landing-gate.sh, registered as a Stop hook in the tracked .claude/settings.json. Fails open, asks once per head, exempts drafts and red checks. 91 cases including the registration itself.

title: Nothing automated ever writes through the proxy
description:
Raised by the code-review pass on PR #40, 2026-08-29, and filed rather than folded into that batch because it is orthogonal to it: the fix there works and is guarded, and this gap pre-dates it and applies to every write path rather than to anything those commits introduced.

WHAT IS MISSING. inventory-tng-o1uj.6 was a defect that refused EVERY write in the application -- the scanning flow of decision 0011 and every administrative screen -- on any stack reached by a port. It reached a green build. Nothing caught it because nothing automated ever performs a write through nginx:

* The backend suite drives Django's test client, which does not go through the proxy and exempts itself from CSRF unless a test asks otherwise.
* CI's 'Compose stack' job brings the whole stack up and checks that pages are served. It never posts anything.
* frontend/integration/ drives a real browser through a real server, which is exactly the right shape -- but its specs sign in and READ. None of them saves a batch.

So the one arrangement that has to work -- browser, nginx, Django, database, all at once -- is asserted by nobody, and the two tests that landed with o1uj.6 bracket it from either side without crossing it. One reads the template as text; the other drives Django directly.

WHAT TO ADD. A Playwright spec that completes the volunteer flow and asserts the ledger moved. seed_integration_data already mints everything it needs -- a login with a published TOTP secret, a volunteer, an item, a location and a label -- so the fixtures are not the work. The sequence is the one guides/worked-examples.md session 2 describes: scan the location label, scan the item label, press Save, then assert the item's balance changed rather than merely that the page did.

Assert the BALANCE, not the screen. A spec that only checks the batch cleared would pass against a server that answered 201 and wrote nothing.

WORTH DOING WITH inventory-tng-o1uj.2, the stale-upstream 502, because both are faults that live in the gap between the containers rather than inside either, and a job that exercises a write through the proxy is what would notice either of them.

AND IT IS THE SECOND TIME. The nb8 epic's notes already record this shape -- 'when asserting something a wrapper outside Django does, drive inventory_tng.wsgi.application' -- after three review findings were invisible to tests that drove Django's Client. This is the same lesson one layer further out: when asserting something nginx does, drive nginx.
close_reason: CI's compose-stack job now performs an authenticated write through nginx, asserts the ledger moved, and asserts a port-less host is still refused so the positive case cannot go vacuous. Verified against the local stack both ways.

title: Say that Podman works, and give somebody a session to follow
description:
Asked for by the project owner on 2026-08-29 while running the app for the first time in a while, and done in the same sitting. Three things, all documentation.

PODMAN AS AN EQUAL. The owner's machine has no docker binary at all, so every command in README's quickstart failed with 'command not found'. DEVELOPERS.md already said Podman works, in one sentence in Prerequisites; README said 'You need Docker'. Both now say either, README gives both command sets in full, and the one thing Podman needs that Docker does not -- its API socket, without which podman compose stops at 'failed to connect to the docker API' -- is written down where somebody meets it. That fact is new; it was found by hitting it.

A HEADING FOR THE FIRST SIGN-IN. The sentence about needing an authenticator app was a trailing paragraph under a table. It is now its own section, because it is a thing to do rather than a note about a thing.

AND THE PORTS WERE WRONG. The service table sent people to :8000, where a correct sign-in ends on a Django 404 -- see inventory-tng-o1uj.5, which is that trap kept as its own issue. Everything now points at :8080, which serves the app and forwards the rest, and every URL in the table was checked against a running stack before it was written.

WORKED EXAMPLES. guides/worked-examples.md is new: three scripted sessions against the seed_demo_data catalogue -- an administrator minting a single sticker and a hundred-count packet sticker, a volunteer taking stock out, and an administrator answering a shelf that disagrees. They exist to be followed on a laptop so that the awkward parts are found by using the app. Each links to the guide that carries the rules rather than restating them, which scripts/check-docs.sh enforced twice during the writing.

Each walkthrough names what to look for, and where the current build stops. They were written against a running stack and every read-only step was verified in it.
close_reason: README, DEVELOPERS.md and the new guides/worked-examples.md all landed; check-docs.sh passes and every URL and anchor was verified against a running stack.

title: Cross-origin credentialed requests cannot work: no Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
description:
Reported by the project owner on 2026-08-29 as a CORS header error seen after
signing in and entering the 2FA code. Investigated the same day. What follows
separates what is proven from what is not, because the second part needs the
owner.

WHAT IS PROVEN. The backend advertises cross-origin access it cannot actually
deliver for anything that carries a session. Against the running compose stack:

    curl -i -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' http://localhost:8000/api/items
      -> access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173
      -> NO access-control-allow-credentials

    preflight OPTIONS on /api/stock/transactions, same origin header
      -> 200, allow-origin, allow-headers, allow-methods all present
      -> NO access-control-allow-credentials

CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS appears nowhere in this repository -- not in
settings.py, not in .env.sample, not in compose.yaml, not in the chart -- so
django-cors-headers leaves it at its default of False. Authentication here is
the session cookie. A browser making a credentialed cross-origin request to an
origin that does not return Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true has the
response withheld from the page and reports exactly the class of error that was
reported.

So CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS is configured in two shipped files -- .env.sample sets
http://localhost:5173 and compose.yaml sets
http://localhost:5173,http://localhost:8080 -- and cannot work for any request
that needs a signed-in user. .env.sample's own comment already admits this
("neither is configured, so that arrangement is unsupported"), which makes
compose.yaml's line the contradiction: it advertises two origins for a mode the
sample says is unsupported.

WHAT IS NOT PROVEN, AND NEEDS ALI. Neither supported way of running the project
should reach this code path, and neither did when driven end to end on this
machine: the SPA only ever fetches relative paths, vite proxies the Django
prefixes (api, admin, accounts, static -- DJANGO_PATHS in vite.config.ts) and
nginx proxies the same set, so the browser sees one origin. Signing in at
:8080, completing TOTP and using the app produced no CORS error at all, and
every request in the nginx log answered 200.

So the reproduction is missing one fact: WHICH URL was open when the error
appeared. Worth asking before any code changes, because the two candidate
causes want different fixes:

* If the app was open on :5173 or :8080 and something still went cross-origin,
  the missing Allow-Credentials above is the bug and the fix is to configure it
  deliberately alongside a trusted-origin list for writes.
* If the app was open on :8000, the SPA is not served there at all and the
  answer is the sibling issue about signing in on the wrong port.

DO NOT simply set CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS = True to make a symptom go away.
Credentialed CORS plus a permissive origin list is how a session gets read by a
page nobody vetted, and this application's read surface is the volunteer data
decision 0012 is about. Either support the cross-origin arrangement properly --
Allow-Credentials, CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS, and a documented origin list that is
never a wildcard -- or drop CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS from the shipped
configurations and say in .env.sample that same-origin through a proxy is the
only supported arrangement. The second is smaller and matches how the project
already works.

Whichever way it goes, .env.sample and compose.yaml have to stop disagreeing
with each other.
notes:
LIKELY SUPERSEDED AS THE EXPLANATION OF THE REPORT, 2026-08-29. inventory-tng-o1uj.6 was found later the same day by driving the volunteer flow to Save, and it is almost certainly what the owner actually hit: Django answers every write with 403 and the words 'Origin checking failed', which is what a person would reasonably report as a CORS error. That one is proven end to end and is P0.

This issue stays open on its own merits and is NOT a duplicate. The missing Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is real and independent of it, and the two want fixing together because a cross-origin arrangement needs the credentials header AND a trusted-origin list -- which is o1uj.6's second half. But the 'which URL were you on' question below matters much less now, so do not block on it.
close_reason: CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS dropped from settings, .env.sample, compose.yaml, the chart and docs/deployment.md. Cross-origin reads are unsupported and now say so instead of advertising a mode that could never work: the session cookie needs Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, which was never set. Verified against the running stack -- a cross-origin read gets no allow-origin header back.

title: Make the second factor an operator's choice, in every environment
description:
Make whether a second factor is REQUIRED an operator's decision, in every environment, and ship config templates that make the intended answer explicit in each.

Read the design field for what to build and why. This description is deliberately short because the issue has been rewritten twice and a long one accumulated contradictions; the history is in the notes.

WHAT IS TRUE TODAY. It is not a config setting and not a partial one. inventory/middleware.py's RequireSecondFactor consults no setting at all -- neither of its helpers reads `settings` -- and RequireSecondLookInTheAdmin is equally unconditional. settings.py's MFA_SUPPORTED_TYPES, MFA_TOTP_ISSUER and MFA_TOTP_TOLERANCE all describe how a second factor works and none of them says whether one is required. Nothing in .env.sample, compose.yaml or infra/helm/ mentions it.

WHAT TO DO. One setting, honoured by those two middleware classes, configurable everywhere with no environment gate and nothing that refuses to start. Off in the local templates, on in the chart's default, and per-environment example values files -- which do not exist yet -- carrying the intended value for a deployed dev environment and for staging, qa and production.

WHY IT IS AN OPERATOR'S CHOICE RATHER THAN A RULE WITH AN EXEMPTION: Ali's call, 2026-08-30. Give operators a choice rather than restrict it, because a more securely built and more capable app even without a second factor is an improvement on what this replaces -- a Google Form writing into a Google Sheet in a personal account.
