Adoption first, then the nudge. The design field carries the consequences of that, including why allauth's MFA has to stay installed and reachable when the requirement is off.

IT AMENDS DECISION 0013 POINT 3, which today says the second factor is required on the local password path with no environment carved out, and names inventory/middleware.py as what makes "required" true. The amendment is part of this issue rather than a follow-up.
design:
SUPERSEDES THE EARLIER DESIGN ON THIS ISSUE, 2026-08-30. Ali read the "only where the host cannot be reached" version and asked for something simpler and differently aimed. That design is gone rather than amended, because its central idea -- a switch the process refuses to honour outside a loopback deployment -- is precisely what he does not want.

HIS DECISION, AND THE REASONING, WHICH IS THE PART TO KEEP:

  "The key point is to give the system operators a choice rather than restrict
  it. A more securely built, more capable app even without 2FA is an
  improvement over what we currently have."

That is an adoption argument and it is a good one. What this replaces is a Google Form writing into a Google Sheet in somebody's personal account -- README says so -- with no second factor, no audit, no referential integrity and no way for the people depending on it to edit it. An inventory-tng with the second factor turned off is enormously better than that on every axis that is not the second factor, and a deployment that will not start because it cannot have one is an inventory-tng nobody runs. Adoption first, then the nudge.

So: CONFIGURABLE IN EVERY ENVIRONMENT. No loopback test, no refusal to start, no environment gate of any kind. An operator who wants the requirement off in production may have it off in production, and that is a supported configuration rather than a hole.

IT IS NOT A CONFIG SETTING TODAY. Established by reading rather than assumed, and unchanged from the earlier investigation: RequireSecondFactor consults no setting at all, RequireSecondLookInTheAdmin is equally unconditional, the three MFA_ settings say how a second factor works and none says whether one is required, and no variable in .env.sample, compose.yaml or the chart touches it.

=== WHAT TO BUILD ===

ONE SETTING, honoured by the two middleware classes. That is the whole mechanism.

OPTIONAL MUST NOT MEAN ABSENT, and this is the design point that serves the nudge. When the requirement is off, nobody is FORCED to enrol -- but allauth.mfa stays installed, MFA_SUPPORTED_TYPES is untouched, and the enrolment pages stay reachable. So:

* somebody who wants a second factor can turn one on for their own account, on a deployment that does not require it;
* an operator can flip the requirement on later and everybody who already enrolled is unaffected;
* turning it on is a configuration change rather than a migration, a redeploy of a different image, or a coordinated enrolment day.

That is what makes a nudge possible at all. Removing allauth.mfa when the requirement is off would make "nudge them towards better security" a rebuild rather than a value change, which is the opposite of the goal.

=== WHERE THE VALUE IS SET, WHICH IS MOST OF THE ASK ===

THERE ARE ONLY THREE CONFIG SURFACES IN THIS REPOSITORY TODAY, and this was checked rather than assumed:

  .env.sample                            the local template
  compose.yaml                           the local stack, values inline
  infra/helm/inventory-tng/values.yaml   ONE chart default; no per-environment files

There is NO deployed-dev template, and no staging or production template either. docs/deployment.md tells an operator to keep their own my-values.yaml and pass --values, and says why -- Helm carries nothing between upgrades, so --set flags are silently dropped on the next one. So what Ali is asking for partly does not exist yet and is part of this issue.

WHAT EACH ONE SHOULD SAY:

  .env.sample                 requirement OFF   (local development)
  compose.yaml                requirement OFF   (the local stack)
  chart values.yaml           requirement ON    (what a deployment gets by default)
  a deployed-dev template     requirement OFF   (new; see below)
  staging / qa / production   requirement ON    (new; see below)

THE PER-ENVIRONMENT TEMPLATES ARE NEW WORK. The natural home is example values files shipped beside the chart -- infra/helm/inventory-tng/examples/ or similar -- that an operator copies as the starting point for their own my-values.yaml. That fits the documented path rather than replacing it: the file they end up passing to --values is still theirs, and these are what it starts as. How many to ship, and whether qa and staging differ in anything but this one value, is worth deciding before writing four near-identical files.

=== TWO THINGS TO KEEP FROM THE OLD DESIGN, AND ONE TO DROP ===

KEEP: the code default is the SAFE one, so a deployment that sets nothing gets the requirement. Every shipped file then sets its value explicitly rather than relying on it. That is decision 0021 point 11's pattern, already applied to the trace sampler and again to CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS in inventory-tng-o1uj.7. It costs an operator nothing -- they are setting a value either way -- and it means the unknown case is the careful one. This is not a restriction: it is which way round the default points.

KEEP: announce at startup when the requirement is OFF, on stderr beside the console-layout line. Decision 0021 point 5 settled that adaptation is never silent. This is a nudge rather than a guard, which is exactly what Ali is after: the operator who turned it off gets a line reminding them it is off, every start, and nothing refuses anything.

DROP ENTIRELY: the loopback test, the refusal to start, and every trace of "only locally". Gone.

=== DECISION 0013 POINT 3 IS AMENDED ===

It currently says TOTP and recovery codes are REQUIRED on the local password path, names inventory/middleware.py as what makes "required" true, and carves out no environment. After this it is required by default and an operator may decide otherwise.

The amendment should carry Ali's reasoning rather than only the new rule, because the reasoning is the part that stops somebody restoring the old one on security grounds without weighing adoption. docs/decisions/0027 is the recent worked example of writing down WHY so a later contributor does not undo it.

=== TESTS ===

1. A password-only session is refused when the requirement is on.
2. It is admitted when the requirement is off.
3. With the requirement off, a user may still enrol a second factor and it is still honoured at sign-in -- the assertion that "optional" did not become "absent".
4. The startup announcement appears when it is off and not when it is on.
5. The chart renders the value, and what an operator sets is what Django reads -- the shape inventory-tng-o1uj.7's tests already use for a new variable.

=== WHAT STAYS ===

The DEVELOPERS.md write-up of the seeded login, from the first pass at this issue. It answers a different half -- one enrolment that survives a database wipe -- and after this lands it serves the person who keeps the requirement ON by choice, which is now a choice rather than the only option.
notes:
HISTORY, because this issue has been rewritten twice and the earlier versions contradict the current one. Only the design field and description are current.

ROUND 1, 2026-08-29. Filed as 'make the second factor configurable, and not required in development', with a long list of constraints -- refused loudly in production, never keyed on DEBUG, impossible to have it off with a real domain in ALLOWED_HOSTS. SUPERSEDED. Those constraints were all the cost of a switch that restricts, and the decision went the other way.

ROUND 2, 2026-08-29. Closed without building anything, on the grounds that seed_integration_data's fixed TOTP secret already solves the friction -- one enrolment surviving every database wipe -- and that documenting it cost nothing and added no way to turn an access control off. SUPERSEDED. That write-up landed and stays (DEVELOPERS.md#signing-in, commit o1uj.3), and it remains useful, but Ali reopened this because the write-up answers a different question from the one he was asking.

ROUND 3, 2026-08-30, CURRENT. Configurable in every environment, no restriction, config templates per environment. Ali's reasoning is in the description and the design.

WHAT SURVIVED ALL THREE: the seeded-login documentation, which is already on main and is not part of the remaining work.

title: Restarting the backend alone makes nginx 502 every proxied path
description:
Found on 2026-08-29 while restarting only the backend to test a settings change
against the compose stack, which is an ordinary thing to do while developing.

WHAT HAPPENS. Restart the backend service on its own -- `compose up -d backend`
or `compose restart backend` -- and every path nginx proxies starts answering
502 and keeps answering it. Not for a moment while the backend comes up: for as
long as the frontend container is left alone. Observed after the backend was
healthy and answering directly:

    http://localhost:8000/api/healthz  -> 200   (backend is fine)
    http://localhost:8080/api          -> 502
    http://localhost:8080/accounts/login/ -> 502
    http://localhost:8080/admin/       -> 502

The frontend's nginx log names the cause exactly:

    connect() failed (113: Host is unreachable) while connecting to upstream,
    upstream: "http://10.89.0.5:8000/api", host: "localhost:8080"

WHY. nginx resolves the name in proxy_pass once, when it loads its
configuration, and caches the address for the life of the worker. The restarted
backend came back on a different container IP, and nginx kept dialling the old
one. `compose restart frontend` fixes it instantly and completely, which
confirms the diagnosis.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE WORKAROUND SUGGESTS. The symptom does not say
"stale address" to anybody who has not met it before -- it says the backend is
down, while the backend is demonstrably up and answering on 8000. The obvious
next move is to look at the backend, which is the wrong container. It cost real
time here and it will cost it again, and it lands on exactly the people this
stack is meant to be easy for. It also punishes the fastest development loop
there is: change a setting, restart the one service, look.

FIXES, in the usual nginx order and all in frontend/nginx.conf.template:

* Give the location a `resolver` pointing at the container DNS and put the
  upstream in a variable, which forces nginx to resolve per request rather than
  at load. The standard remedy. Costs a lookup per request and needs the
  resolver address, which differs between Docker (127.0.0.11) and rootless
  Podman -- so read it rather than assume it, and it may need to be rendered by
  the same envsubst that renders the rest of the template.
* Or set a short `proxy_next_upstream` / re-resolve interval via an upstream
  block with `zone`, which is the tidier form but needs checking against the
  nginx build in nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1-alpine.

Whichever is chosen it has to be verified under rootless Podman specifically,
because that is where the resolver address is least predictable, and this
project now documents Podman as a first-class way to run the stack.

IF IT IS NOT WORTH FIXING, say so in DEVELOPERS.md instead -- one line under
Option A that restarting the backend alone needs the frontend restarted too.
Leaving it undocumented is the only outcome that is clearly wrong.
close_reason: nginx now has a resolver and dials its upstreams through variables, so it re-resolves per request. Verified: the backend moved from 10.89.0.17 to 10.89.0.19 on a restart and every proxied path kept answering with no frontend restart.

title: Mint the device token server-side, and make revoking one mean something
description:
Asked for by the project owner on 2026-08-25, after `inventory-tng-2jzx`
established that the network does admission and a device credential is
therefore for ATTRIBUTION rather than for getting in. The owner's words for
what it buys are "weakly guard against in-network bad actors", and that phrase
belongs in the code, because everything below is worth having and none of it is
a control.

MOST OF THIS IS ALREADY WRITTEN, on `batch/show-the-five-postures` (PR #28),
where it is demo scaffolding that `inventory-tng-81f7.4` is filed to delete.
This bead is the argument for promoting it instead, and it should start by
reading what is there rather than from a blank file:

* `inventory.models.Device` -- `identifier`, `enrolled_at`, `revoked_at`, and a
  docstring that already makes this bead's central argument: "A signature on
  its own can only be withdrawn by rotating the key, and rotating signs every
  device out at once."
* `inventory.permissions.enrolled` -- checks the signature AND then the row,
  `Device.objects.filter(identifier=..., revoked_at__isnull=True)`. Memoised on
  the underlying Django request, because without it one `GET /api/me` made
  seven identical selects.
* `inventory_tng.postures.presented_device` -- the `django.core.signing` reading.

WHAT SIGNING BUYS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT, and getting this wrong is the whole
risk. Signing stops a token being INVENTED. It does not stop one being ASKED
FOR. If `POST /api/devices` answers everybody, an in-network actor wanting more
quota calls it fifty times and holds fifty buckets, and every signature checks
out. So the guard is not the signature, it is whatever constrains minting, and
that has to be built deliberately:

* Throttle the mint endpoint out of a bucket of its own, which PR #28 already
  does at `APPEND_BURST_RATE`, so that a room mistyping cannot spend the
  allowance a volunteer's batch needs.
* RECORD WHAT THE MINT WAS ASKED FROM. Fifty devices minted from one address in
  three minutes is not preventable on a flat network, but it is one query and
  one bulk revoke, and that is the difference between an abuse nobody notices
  and one somebody closes in a minute. This is the cheapest thing on the list
  and it is the one most likely to be left out.

THE REVOCATION RULE, and it is the part that silently stops working. The
signature must never be the authorisation on its own. Verify it, then read the
row, every time. A future change that skips the select "because the signature
already proved it" removes revocation without failing a single test -- so the
test that holds this must revoke a device and assert the NEXT request is
refused, rather than asserting anything about the token.

Two more the owner should be told about rather than discover:

* Refusing a revoked device wants its own reason on the wire, distinguishable
  from "you may not". `postures.ENROLMENT_STATES` already makes this argument
  for enrolment and it is the same one: a wall and a "this device was removed"
  want different screens.
* Rotating `SECRET_KEY` invalidates every token at once. That is the mass
  revocation lever, it is free, and `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` is how a rotation
  happens without one. Worth writing down where a deployer will find it.

RULE 3: this is route 1 throughout. `django.core.signing` mints and checks;
`inventory_tng.debugging` is the copy to follow; use a `salt` of this token's
own so a device token cannot be presented as a debug one. Do not write a token
format, do not compare tokens by hand, do not implement expiry. If anything
here starts to look like arithmetic on bytes, stop and say so.

WHAT IT MATERIALLY CHANGES, so this can be judged rather than assumed: a
device id becomes the rate-limit bucket, which retires the shared-address
bucket that `inventory-tng-81f7.1` and decision 0023 both record; logs become
correlatable per device rather than per NAT; and one row with one flag cuts off
one device on its next request. What it does not do is stop a determined
insider, because re-minting is available. Say the ceiling out loud.
close_reason: POST /api/devices mints with django.core.signing under its own salt; inventory.models.Device is the row; presented_device verifies then reads the row on every request; DeviceNotRevoked refuses a revoked device with code=device_revoked. What constrains minting: DEVICE_ENROLMENT_RATE out of its own bucket, and Device.enrolled_from records the address every mint was asked from. Rule 3 route 1 throughout, never reached.

title: mesh_only is a deployment posture, not a permission class
description:
Recorded from the project owner on 2026-08-25, correcting how `mesh_only`
has been framed everywhere it appears. It is a DEPLOYMENT posture, and the
artifacts currently describe it as an application one.

WHAT WAS WRITTEN. `inventory-tng-81f7.3` implements `mesh_only` as a permission
class comparing the caller's address against VOLUNTEER_ACCESS_NETWORKS, and the
run of show, the decision brief and .env.sample all describe it that way. Read
like that it is a weak control resting on `X-Forwarded-For`, which is exactly
what `inventory-tng-3hgc` is about, and it is reasonable to argue against it on
those grounds. That argument was made in this repository and it was arguing
against the wrong thing.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY MEANT. The whole deployment sits on servers whose routing and
firewall rules WILL NOT carry traffic originating outside the mesh network to
the application at all -- VPN clients included. The app and the reverse proxy
in front of it are not the thing keeping anybody out, and were never intended
to be. The packet does not arrive. The project owner controls the hosts, the
routing and the firewall rules, so this is a posture that can actually be
guaranteed rather than asserted.

WHAT THAT CHANGES, and it is most of the argument:

* The objection from `inventory-tng-3hgc` does not apply. Admission happens at
  L3/L4 and the application never parses a header to decide it. A forged
  `X-Forwarded-For` cannot reach a socket that will not accept it.
* The population reaching the read surface is not the internet. It is mesh
  members, which is small, semi-accountable and a different threat model from
  the one `inventory-tng-81f7` was framed against.
* The remaining cost is reachability rather than permission: a volunteer at a
  hub on mobile data is not refused by the app, they are not on the network.
  That is the real thing to weigh and it should be weighed as an operations
  question.

DEVICE REGISTRATION MAY STILL BE ASKED FOR, and its JOB CHANGES. Under the
spike, enrolment is ADMISSION -- no reading until you enrol -- and the friction
of that is what the demo was built to measure. Under this posture the network
does admission, so enrolment becomes ATTRIBUTION: a device id carried on every
request and written to every log line, which is then the rate-limit bucket and
the revocation handle. A weak guard against an in-network bad actor, and the
owner's words for it are "weakly guard" -- write it down that way so nobody
later mistakes it for a control.

Two consequences worth stating where they will be read:

* Attribution can be minted SILENTLY on first load, the way `telemetry/flag.ts`
  already stores its flag, so it costs no screen and no friction at all. The
  wall only appears on revocation, which is the point of having it.
* A device id is a better rate-limit bucket than an address. `inventory-tng-
  81f7.1` records that a hub of volunteers behind one address shares one
  bucket, and decision 0023 records the same shape for the throttles. Per
  device retires both.

WHAT THIS BEAD IS: propagating the correction, not building anything. Every
place that currently describes `mesh_only` as an application check says so in
its own words and each has to be corrected in its own:

* `inventory-tng-81f7`'s decision brief, and docs/briefs/ where the repository
  copy lives
* the run of show for the demo, ignored/briefs/five-postures-one-config.html
  and the published artifact it deploys to -- act four is the section
* .env.sample's VOLUNTEER_ACCESS and VOLUNTEER_ACCESS_NETWORKS prose, which
  lives on the `inventory-tng-81f7.3` branch rather than on main
* docs/deployment.md, because the routing and firewall posture is a deployment
  fact and that is its canonical home under rule 1
* docs/architecture.md where the access posture is described

AND IT PROBABLY WANTS A DECISION RECORD, either its own or an amendment to
0012, because "the network is the access control and the application is defence
in depth" is a statement future work has to be held against. An application
that assumes it is unreachable from outside is only safe while that is true,
and the failure is silent when it stops being true.

title: check-commit.sh refuses every git commit --amend
description:
Found by the review of PR #29 (inventory-tng-nt1f), which made the commit-msg hook mandatory for everyone and so turned a latent limitation into a daily one.

WHAT HAPPENS. git hands a commit-msg hook the message path and nothing else, so check-commit.sh can never be told it is running under --amend; the flag it documents (scripts/check-commit.sh:18) reaches it only from a person at a terminal. BASE therefore stays HEAD. During an amend the index already equals HEAD's tree, so 'git diff --cached HEAD -- .beads/issues.jsonl' is empty and the closure that is already inside the commit being replaced looks missing.

Reproduced on PR #29's own commit:

  $ git commit --amend --no-edit
    · "nt1f: Install the commit hook from bootstrap"
    ✗ nothing staged closes inventory-tng-nt1f -- run 'bd close inventory-tng-nt1f', then stage .beads/issues.jsonl

HEAD unchanged, and the advice is wrong: the issue is already closed. 'git rebase -i' with reword fails the same way and strands the user mid-rebase being told to run the command the same hook refuses.

WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED IN nt1f. The obvious detection -- if the trailer's issue is already closed by HEAD's own tracker diff, treat it as an amend -- also waves through a genuinely wrong commit: a follow-up that stages nothing for the tracker and claims 'Closes: X' where X was closed by the commit before it. That weakens the rule this repository is arranged around, and choosing how much to weaken it is a decision for a person rather than for a review fix.

WHAT MAKES IT NOT BLOCKING. git rebase runs no commit-msg hook at all -- verified: 'git rebase -i --autosquash' folded a fixup with the hook installed and never called it. So the documented review loop (fixup, then rebase --autosquash) works, and amending is the path with a workaround rather than the path with none.

OPTIONS WORTH WEIGHING. (a) the closed-in-HEAD heuristic above, narrowed by also requiring that the message's summary match HEAD's; (b) accept an amend only when the staged tree is identical to HEAD's; (c) leave it refused and say so in DEVELOPERS.md 'Commits', which today documents amending as ordinary practice at line 1165.
notes:
DECIDED 2026-08-24 by Ali Asad Lotia, from the three options in the description: option (a), the closed-in-HEAD heuristic NARROWED BY A SUMMARY MATCH.

Treat the commit as an amend when both hold: the trailer's issue was closed by HEAD's own tracker diff, AND the new message's summary matches HEAD's summary. Both, never either alone -- the summary match is the whole narrowing, and it is what keeps the rule this repository is arranged around from being weakened: a follow-up that stages nothing for the tracker and claims 'Closes: X' where the commit before it closed X has a DIFFERENT summary, so it is still refused.

Known and accepted gap: a reword that rewrites the summary is refused, because it is indistinguishable from that follow-up on the evidence a commit-msg hook is given. The workaround is the documented review loop -- fixup, then rebase --autosquash -- which runs no commit-msg hook at all. Say so in whatever error the refusal prints, so somebody who hits it is told the way through rather than left guessing.

Option (b), accepting an amend only when the staged tree is identical to HEAD's, was weighed and rejected: it refuses the ordinary 'git add -p; git commit --amend' because staging new work is exactly what makes the tree differ. Option (c), leaving it refused and correcting DEVELOPERS.md:1165, was rejected as the docs half of a fix rather than the fix.
close_reason: Amends are recognised from HEAD: it closed the named issue and the summary is unchanged. Both conditions, so a follow-up claiming the previous commit's closure stays refused. Reword remains refused and the message now names the fixup/autosquash way through.

comments.author: Ali Asad Lotia
comments.text:
HIT, 2026-08-24, while merging PR #30. Narrower than the title suggests, and the detail is worth having.

'git commit --amend --no-edit' on a commit whose message closes an issue was refused with:

  ✗ .beads/issues.jsonl is staged but does not close inventory-tng-614

because the amend re-stages the tracker, the issue's closure is already in the COMMITTED version, so the staged diff closes nothing -- check-commit.sh:168. The commit being amended was itself the one that closed it.

Two other amends in the same session went through untouched, so it is not every amend: it is an amend that restages .beads/issues.jsonl on a commit whose message carries a Closes trailer. Which is a common shape, because the beads pre-commit hook re-exports the tracker on every commit whether or not anything changed.

The way round it was a separate commit with a 'Refs:' trailer rather than 'Closes:', which is honest here but would not be if the amend genuinely belonged to the closing commit.

title: The administrative screens decision 0014 assumes exist
description:
docs/architecture.md names the administrative interface as one of four things not yet built, and NOTHING IN THE TRACKER COVERED IT until this bead. `bd search` for it returned nothing on 2026-08-24. A major feature with no issue is invisible to `bd ready` and to every future session, which is how it stayed unbuilt while its API was finished around it.

WHAT IS ALREADY DONE, read from the code rather than assumed, because it is most of the hard part:

- The write API is complete. Items, locations, categories and labels are created and edited by a caller holding the staff flag; StaffWrites refuses everybody else, and RecentlyAuthenticated makes a destructive write ask who you are again.
- Sign-in is built (decision 0013), and so is the step-up: frontend/src/admin/StepUp.tsx.
- /api/me reports capabilities by RUNNING each view's permission classes through CapabilityProbe, so the client never guesses what it may offer. useCan() in admin/SessionProvider.tsx is the accessor.
- The pattern for an administrative screen EXISTS and is proven: admin/EditItem.tsx is an in-place dialog for correcting a catalogue entry, drawn only when useCan('edit_catalogue') is true (items/ItemRow.tsx:111), with admin/Refusal.tsx and StaleSession beside it for what happens when the server says no. Decision 0014 point 1 is the argument for editing in place rather than in a second application.

So this is not new architecture. It is more of a shape that already works.

WHAT IS MISSING, measured against the CAPABILITIES map in views.py, which is the interface's own vocabulary:

  append_stock       volunteer  -- BUILT (SubmitBar)
  add_volunteer      volunteer  -- BUILT (VolunteerPicker)
  edit_catalogue     admin      -- PARTIAL. The capability covers SIX endpoints:
                                  Item POST/PATCH, Location POST/PATCH,
                                  Category POST/PATCH. Only Item PATCH has a
                                  screen. There is no way to CREATE an item, and
                                  no screen at all for locations or categories.
  print_label        admin      -- NO SCREEN. /api/labels/sheet renders a
                                  printable sheet of stickers server-side and
                                  nothing in the app asks it to.
  revoke_label       admin      -- NO SCREEN. A sticker can only be revoked
                                  through the API or Django's admin.
  merge_volunteers   admin      -- NO SCREEN. Merging is first-class in the data
                                  model (data-model.md) and decision 0015 gives
                                  the 409 that names an unshowable holder, and an
                                  administrator still cannot act on either.

CONSEQUENCE WORTH STATING PLAINLY: an administrator's real tool today is Django's admin. That is the application decision 0014 exists to avoid -- its whole argument is one interface, so that somebody looking at an item's count edits it where they are rather than finding the same item under a different name somewhere else. Every capability above without a screen is that decision not yet honoured.

ALREADY CARVED OUT, so this bead must not duplicate them: inventory-tng-ayu (show open custody at a glance) and inventory-tng-3ez (narrow the label list to a shelf, an item or a print run) are both administrative screens with beads of their own. This one covers what neither does, and should probably become a small epic with children rather than one change.

NOT IN SCOPE: anything about who may do what. That is settled -- decision 0012 for the two populations, 0014 for one interface, 0015 for the merge conflict. This is the screens for decisions already made.
design: Wants breaking into children once the shape is agreed, roughly one per missing capability: creating catalogue entries, locations and categories; printing a sheet of labels; revoking one; merging two volunteers. Each is small on its own because EditItem.tsx, useCan() and StepUp.tsx already establish how an administrative control is drawn, gated and refused. The question worth settling first is navigation: today App.tsx renders one column with no routes at all, so where administrative work LIVES is the one thing these screens cannot each decide for themselves.
acceptance_criteria: An administrator can do from this application everything decision 0014 says belongs here -- create and correct catalogue entries, locations and categories, print and revoke labels, and merge two volunteers -- without opening Django's admin; every control is drawn from a capability rather than a guess; and docs/architecture.md no longer lists the administrative interface as not yet built.
notes:
SPLIT 2026-08-25 into six children. The shape was read off decision 0014 point 1 and the CAPABILITIES map in views.py:1378, not invented.

NAVIGATION IS MOSTLY ALREADY SETTLED, which is the useful finding and the reason five of the six children need no decision before they start. The description asks 'where does administrative work LIVE', and 0014 point 1 answers it for three of the five capabilities by name: 'The item list gains editing, the volunteer picker gains merging, a label gains revocation -- in place, where the thing already is.' Signing in changes what the interface offers rather than navigating anywhere. So the default is NO router and no second surface, and frontend/package.json carrying no routing dependency today is the right starting state rather than a gap.

WHAT IS GENUINELY UNANCHORED is one thing, not five: a sheet of labels spans items and belongs to no single row, so it is the only capability with nowhere obvious to live in a one-column Container maxWidth='sm'. That, and the browse surfaces inventory-tng-ayu and inventory-tng-3ez imply, is the whole of the remaining question -- which makes it a small decision rather than the architectural one the description feared.

title: Install the commit-msg hook from bootstrap, not from a doc
description:
Every commit made in this repository since the checker was written has been unchecked until CI, because the hook that runs it locally was never installed. Found 2026-08-24 after the project owner noticed the "One issue per commit" job failing repeatedly.

WHAT IS TRUE TODAY, read rather than remembered:

  ls .beads/hooks/     -> post-checkout, post-merge, pre-commit,
                          prepare-commit-msg, pre-push. NO commit-msg.
  git ls-files .beads/hooks/  -> those five ARE tracked.
  git config --local core.hooksPath -> .beads/hooks   (LOCAL, so not cloned)

DEVELOPERS.md line 1173 tells a contributor to run `ln -s ../../scripts/check-commit.sh .beads/hooks/commit-msg`. It is a manual step, so it is a step that gets skipped, and nothing anywhere notices that it was.

IT MUST BE commit-msg AND NOT pre-commit, stated because it is the obvious thing to try and it cannot work: git runs pre-commit BEFORE the message exists and passes it no arguments, while check-commit.sh takes the message file as $1 (scripts/check-commit.sh:36) and half of what it checks IS the message -- the summary length, the body line lengths, and whether the Closes: trailer names the issue the staged tracker diff actually closes. commit-msg is the first hook handed that path and it can still refuse.

WHERE THE FIX BELONGS. scripts/bootstrap-dev.sh already IS the one-time setup command this wants: 'From a fresh clone to a database with something in it, in one command', already idempotent by its own header ('Safe to run again: it writes nothing it has already written'), already running `mise trust`, already the documented first step at DEVELOPERS.md:68, and already covered by scripts/bootstrap-dev.test.sh. It has five steps -- Toolchain, Configuration, PostgreSQL, Schema, Something to look at -- and mentions hooks NOWHERE. This is a sixth step in a script that exists, not new machinery.

THE SECOND HALF, and it is the one that makes tracking the symlink insufficient on its own: core.hooksPath is LOCAL git config, and .git/config is not cloned. So a fresh clone has no hooksPath at all, which means neither the new hook NOR beads' own five run until something sets it. bd doctor would normally catch this and cannot here -- it answers 'not yet supported in embedded mode'.

WHAT TO DO:

1. A 'Git hooks' step in scripts/bootstrap-dev.sh: set core.hooksPath to .beads/hooks if unset, ensure the commit-msg symlink, verify it resolves and is executable. Idempotent, in the style of every other step there. Extend bootstrap-dev.test.sh with it.

2. Track .beads/hooks/commit-msg as a symlink, beside the five beads hooks already tracked, so the file arrives with the clone and bootstrap only has to wire hooksPath.

3. A [tasks] section in mise.toml so `mise run setup` invokes bootstrap-dev.sh and `mise tasks` discovers it. mise is already this project's toolchain manager and DEVELOPERS.md's first prerequisite, so this adds discoverability rather than a dependency.

4. scripts/check-setup.sh, wired into the existing 'Guardrail checkers' CI job: assert core.hooksPath points at .beads/hooks and that commit-msg resolves to check-commit.sh. A clone that skipped bootstrap then gets told so plainly, instead of discovering it three commits later through a confusing failure.

5. AGENTS.md gains one line: never `git commit --no-verify` in this repository. A hook that can be stepped past by an agent that meets a refusal is not a guard, and this is the only way past it.

6. DEVELOPERS.md's 'Checking it' stops telling anyone to hand-install the hook, and says it ships.

NOT AUTOMATIC ON DIRECTORY ENTRY. mise supports a [hooks] enter that would run this on every cd, and it was considered and rejected: it runs on every entry so the early exit has to stay genuinely cheap forever, it needs trust before it does anything, and a script that silently rewrites a contributor's git config when they cd into a directory is a different proposition from one they chose to run. Bootstrap is already idempotent and already documented as the first command; point 4 is what catches somebody who skipped it.
design: The checker is not new and is not wrong -- scripts/check-commit.sh does exactly what it should, and CI runs it. What is missing is that it never runs before CI. So this issue changes no rule and no check; it only moves the moment of enforcement from after a push to the commit itself.
acceptance_criteria: A fresh clone that runs scripts/bootstrap-dev.sh ends with core.hooksPath set and commit-msg resolving to check-commit.sh; bootstrap-dev.test.sh covers it; running bootstrap twice changes nothing the second time; CI fails a checkout whose hooks are not wired; AGENTS.md forbids --no-verify; and DEVELOPERS.md no longer asks anybody to install a hook by hand.
close_reason: Closed

title: X-Forwarded-For is believed without a list of proxies worth believing
description:
Found by the code review of PR #28 (inventory-tng-81f7.3). Not caused by it --
the reading is DRF's and predates the branch -- but that branch is the first
thing to make an ADMISSION decision out of it, which is what raises it from a
rate-limiting nuisance to this.

WHAT IS WRONG. `inventory.permissions.client_address` reads the caller's
address the way DRF's throttles do: `X-Forwarded-For` counted back NUM_PROXIES
hops from the right. DRF clamps when the header is shorter than that --
`addrs[-min(num_proxies, len(addrs))]` -- so a header the caller wrote in full
is handed back as the caller's address. PR #28 added a guard that refuses a
header with fewer entries than NUM_PROXIES, and that guard COUNTS ENTRIES,
which are free. Measured against that checkout with the shipped NUM_PROXIES=2:

  X-Forwarded-For: 10.69.0.1            -> '' (refused by the guard)
  X-Forwarded-For: 10.69.0.1,           -> '10.69.0.1'
  X-Forwarded-For: 10.69.0.1, 9.9.9.9   -> '10.69.0.1'

One trailing comma. `client_address`'s docstring now says so rather than
claiming the forgery is closed, and
`test_the_guard_counts_entries_and_entries_are_free` in test_postures.py holds
the measurement so that whoever fixes this is told when the line moves.

WHY IT CANNOT BE FIXED WHERE IT WAS FOUND. No rule reading this header can
tell how many proxies a request actually crossed: every entry is either
appended by a proxy or written by whoever called, and the header does not say
which. Counting hops is a guess about the deployment, and it is wrong in the
dangerous direction exactly when the deployment is wrong -- a request that
reaches Django without crossing NUM_PROXIES proxies, which is what a
misrouted ingress, a health check, or anything on the pod network is.

WHAT THE SOUND VERSION IS. A list of addresses this deployment will believe a
forwarded header FROM -- its own ingress, and nothing else -- and REMOTE_ADDR
checked against it before any of the header is read. That is a statement about
the ingress rather than a line in a permission class, so it needs:

  * a variable beside NUM_PROXIES in .env.sample, with the prose saying which
    way it is dangerous to get wrong, as NUM_PROXIES' own note does
  * the Helm chart and docs/deployment.md, because the value is the cluster's
    and not the application's
  * a decision record, because "which addresses may speak for another" is
    exactly the kind of thing docs/decisions/ exists to hold
  * the throttles too, or deliberately not: the cost of believing a forger
    there is one bucket rather than the roster, and DRF's own reading may be
    the right trade for a rate limit. Say which, rather than leaving the two
    to drift.

WHAT IS AND IS NOT AT RISK TODAY. Nothing on main: every endpoint still asks
for a session, so no admission decision reads this at all. On PR #28's branch
`VOLUNTEER_ACCESS=mesh_only` does, and that branch is a spike that is not
merged. So this is filed as a precondition rather than an incident: it must be
settled before anything ships a posture that admits by address --
inventory-tng-gnhl is the one that would.
close_reason: TRUSTED_PROXIES names the addresses a forwarded header is believed from, and inventory_tng.forwarded.client_address reads it without counting hops. Decision 0023 records why the throttles keep DRF's reading.

title: The credential-free audit reads spellings, not what an anonymous request may do
description:
Found by the code review of PR #26 (inventory-tng-lb95), which added
test_capabilities.py::test_every_endpoint_asking_nothing_of_its_caller_is_one_the_record_argued.
That audit closed the write-only blind spot uq6 fell through. It has two of
its own, both measured by the reviewer against this checkout, and together
they are why it is not yet the whole of decision 0012's consequence.

1. IT ASKS A QUESTION ABOUT CLASS NAMES, NOT ABOUT ADMISSION.
   permissions.open_to_anybody is all(isinstance(p, AllowAny) ...).
   StaffWrites.has_permission returns True for every GET from anybody,
   AnonymousUser included -- its docstring says so ("Reads are left to
   whatever else guards the endpoint"), and the "whatever else" is
   IsAuthenticated. So permission_classes = [StaffWrites,
   RecentlyAuthenticated] -- the project default minus one token -- serves
   every read to an anonymous caller while open_to_anybody answers False and
   the audit records nothing. Measured:
       permission classes: ['StaffWrites', 'RecentlyAuthenticated']
       anonymous GET admitted by every permission: True
       open_to_anybody(LeakyView()) -> False
   Two further spellings escape identically: [AllowAny | IsAuthenticated]
   resolves to one rest_framework.permissions.OR instance, and any custom
   BasePermission whose has_permission returns True. The bug lb95 fixed
   filtered on the METHOD axis; this one filters on the CLASS axis, and it is
   the same shape.

2. IT SEES ONLY THE ROUTES inventory_tng.urls DECLARES ITSELF.
   203 routes resolve; the walk can see 20. Behind accounts/ are 43 patterns
   and behind admin/ are 139. Three answer an anonymous caller today:
       /accounts/login/          -> 200
       /accounts/signup/         -> 200
       /accounts/password/reset/ -> 200
   /accounts/signup/ is an account-creating write reachable with no
   credential. None is among the names the audit holds.

WHY IT MATTERS NOW: inventory-tng-gnhl opens roughly six credential-free
reads over the catalogue, its balances, the volunteer pick-list, the label map
and the resolver. Per inventory-tng-81f7 the rows at stake are volunteer
display names, emails and Slack ids joined to the hardware in their homes.
The edit that opens them is exactly the edit that writes a permission list,
and a list that is not literally [AllowAny] passes the audit unseen.

THE FIX, and both halves already exist in this repository:
  - The spelling-independent probe: CurrentUserView._permitted plus
    CapabilityProbe (views.py:1537-1555) asks
    all(p.has_permission(probe, view) for p in view.get_permissions()) with
    the view built and given a request. Asked of an ANONYMOUS probe, that is
    the version of this audit that cannot be spelled around.
  - The route walk that survives path arguments: test_telemetry.py:369-388
    builds a converter-specimen table, reverses every route including
    <int:pk> and <str:code>, and asserts loudly when a converter has no
    specimen.
Composed, and driven through get_resolver() rather than urls.urlpatterns, one
walk asks each (view, method) whether an anonymous caller is actually
admitted, held against one table of arguments. That subsumes both hardcoded
lists in test_capabilities.py -- ClientFailureView is currently in both,
carrying the same citation 28 lines apart -- and reaches the include()-mounted
routes above.

This is the same walk inventory-tng-s047 is about, so the two should be done
together or this one after it.

UNTIL IT IS DONE, the prose says only what is checked: DEVELOPERS.md and
decision 0012 were narrowed in PR #26 to claim the list in test_capabilities.py
and nothing wider. Widening the claim is part of closing this.
notes:
=== HELD PENDING inventory-tng-81f7.3, added 2026-08-24 ===

This is a REVIEW HOLD, not a real prerequisite, and the distinction matters if you are the one who picks this up when the edge clears.

Nothing in this issue needs anything the demo produces. The dependency is there because the demo builds over the same surface, and this issue's DESCRIPTION may be partly wrong by the time it is unblocked -- built already, superseded, or needing a rewrite to say what is left rather than what was needed. The project owner asked for a mechanism that would not let these be forgotten and would not let them be worked from a stale description.

A dependency was chosen over `bd defer` deliberately. Defer is date-based and needs somebody to guess when; this condition is an EVENT. The edge clears by itself when 81f7.3 closes, which is when the demo has actually been given.

SO THE FIRST THING TO DO WHEN THIS BECOMES READY IS RE-READ IT against what landed, not start work. If the description still holds, carry on. If it does not, revise it before touching code.

title: Demo both access postures, every variant a config value
description:
A spike, deliberately not merged, so inventory-tng-81f7 can be argued from something people have watched rather than something they have been told about. The runbook for whoever stands up and runs it is a separate artifact, linked from 81f7.

WHY IT EXISTS. 81f7 asks a room to choose between five postures whose costs are entirely about how the app FEELS on a first day. Nobody can weigh that from prose. A demo can show it in fifteen minutes, and the arguments this project has measured -- that masking does not separate people, that a search threshold is not a control -- are far more convincing performed than asserted.

EVERY VARIANT IS A CONFIG VALUE. That is a requirement rather than a convenience: a variant that needs a code change cannot be switched in front of an audience, and a variant nobody can switch does not get compared. The surface, all read at startup in the shape of every other knob in settings.py, and all PROVISIONAL:

  ANONYMOUS_PAYLOAD       full | masked | names_only
  VOLUNTEER_ACCESS        open | enrolled_self | enrolled_code | mesh_only
  SEARCH_MINIMUM          0 | 1 | 2 | 3
  ANONYMOUS_READ_RATE     a DRF rate string, or empty for no limit
  CUSTODY_VISIBILITY      anonymous | identified

`masked` is carried DESPITE being measured out on 81f7, and that is the point of it: the measurement says a mask fails to separate 5 of 13 colliding names, and a demo that shows two identical strings where two people should be settles the question in front of everybody in four seconds.

THE CREDENTIAL IS AN OPAQUE TOKEN, NOT A SIGNATURE, and this is the decision that makes the spike affordable. What the room is judging is the FRICTION, and the friction of a token in storage is identical to the friction of a non-extractable key signing every request under RFC 9421 -- same screens, same taps, same wall when you pick up a second phone. The difference is invisible in a room and is entirely about what an attacker can do afterwards. So the demo builds the friction and defers the cryptography, which also keeps it clear of AGENTS.md rule 3: django.core.signing already mints and checks such a token, so nothing here writes crypto. inventory-tng-jro remains where the real thing is argued.

STRIP IDENTIFIERS FIRST, as its own step, because it is independent of everything else and is the piece most likely to be adopted whatever else is decided.

DATA IS SYNTHETIC, NO EXCEPTIONS. Real item names and real locations are fine and make it feel real; PEOPLE ARE INVENTED. A privacy consultation that projects a volunteer's address onto a wall -- possibly with that volunteer in the room, possibly recorded -- has caused the harm it was convened to prevent, and it is not recoverable afterwards. Stripping the payload is what makes an accidental load of real data survivable; synthetic seeding is what stops it happening. Both, not either.

NOT MERGED. 81f7 gates gnhl, and this must not become the decision arriving early with its answer already implemented. Say so on the day.

WHAT IT NEEDS BEYOND THE FLAGS: a Device model and a POST /api/devices, an enrolment screen gated in App.tsx where SessionProvider already wraps everything, a device credential in frontend storage mirroring telemetry/flag.ts, two lines in client.ts's asked(), and one extra field on /api/me so the client can tell 'enrol first' from 'not allowed'. Note that /api/me computes capabilities by RUNNING each view's permission classes through CapabilityProbe, so a new permission class is reported to the frontend with no further work, and PolicyAwareAutoSchema picks it up too.
design: Not merged, and that is the design decision rather than a caveat. inventory-tng-81f7 gates gnhl; a spike that lands first turns a consultation into a ratification. It is built to be watched and thrown away, and inventory-tng-81f7.4 is what makes sure the throwing away actually happens.
notes:
THE RUN OF SHOW for this demo is published, and it is written for whoever presents rather than for whoever builds:
https://claude.ai/code/artifact/76c13c07-ab77-425f-986b-03fe6fe3c27b

Source at ignored/briefs/five-postures-one-config.html, gitignored, redeployable to the same URL. It is also linked from inventory-tng-81f7 beside the decision brief.

READ IT BEFORE BUILDING, because it is what the five settings have to serve. It fixes the ORDER the variants are shown in -- full, masked, names_only, enrolled_self, enrolled_code -- and each act depends on the previous one having removed a tempting answer. Two consequences for the build:

1. SWITCHING MUST BE FAST AND MUST NOT LOSE STATE. The runbook recommends pre-launching every variant on its own port before the meeting and switching tabs, so a value is changed live exactly once to show that it IS a config change. Make that possible: the settings are read at startup, nothing caches across them, and two instances against the same database must not fight.
2. THE masked VALUE IS LOAD-BEARING despite being measured out. Act two shows two seeded volunteers rendering as the identical string. So the seed data needs a deliberate collision -- two volunteers sharing a display name, on the same mail provider, with the same first initial -- and masked must implement the exact rule that was measured: local[0] + domain-initial + TLD.

SEED DATA IS PART OF THIS BEAD, not a step left to the presenter. About 80 invented volunteers, roughly 45% with no address at all so act three can be honest about who typing does not serve, two pairs sharing a display name of which one pair collides under masking. Real item names and real locations; invented people, no exceptions -- the runbook says why and it is the one instruction in it that cannot be waived.

title: Record the never-write-core-crypto rule in AGENTS.md and DEVELOPERS.md
description:
Stated by the project owner on 2026-08-24 as a standing directive, with the explicit instruction that it be recorded even at the risk of violating rule 1. It is already in beads memory under the key never-write-core-crypto, which session hooks inject, and in the agent's own memory store. This bead is the repository half -- the copy a human contributor reads, and the one a fork or a CI runner gets.

WHY IT IS NOT ALREADY DONE: raised while the checkout was on batch/liveness-is-not-readiness with another agent mid-cycle on it. Editing tracked files under a running batch is how two agents' work ends up in one commit (see the running-a-batch memory on the shared index). Do this on its own branch once that one has landed.

WHERE IT GOES, and the duplication is deliberate and authorised:

1. AGENTS.md gains it as a THIRD non-negotiable rule, in full, beside 'One topic, one place' and 'Docs change with the code'. It goes there in full rather than as a link because it is a stop sign, and a stop sign behind a link is not a stop sign. AGENTS.md is CLAUDE.md, CODEX.md and GEMINI.md by symlink, so this reaches every agent.

2. DEVELOPERS.md gains a short pointer from its Definition of Done, so a human contributor meets it on the same path they meet coverage and typing on. One line and a link, not a second copy of the prose.

THE TEXT, so it is not re-derived and softened in the retelling:

  Never write core cryptography. Not a primitive, not a construction, not
  'just' a key-derivation step, a nonce scheme, a padding mode, a signature
  envelope, a token format, or a constant-time comparison.

  1. Use an established library: well known, actively maintained, widely
     deployed, independently audited. Here that means Django's own
     django.core.signing, django.contrib.auth.hashers and
     django.utils.crypto.constant_time_compare first, because they are already
     dependencies; then pyca/cryptography, hmac, hashlib and secrets. In the
     browser it is WebCrypto and nothing else. inventory_tng.debugging already
     signs tokens this way -- copy it rather than inventing beside it.
  2. If the public API does not expose what is wanted, write a thin wrapper
     over that public API. Thin means it arranges calls and validates inputs.
     It never implements the algorithm and never reaches for a private or
     underscore-prefixed name. Once a wrapper contains arithmetic on bytes it
     has stopped being a wrapper and rule 3 applies.
  3. If neither is possible, STOP and say so loudly. Do not prototype it, do
     not leave a TODO, do not put it behind a flag. Name what was needed and
     why neither route reached it, and wait for a person. This is a decision to
     be made very carefully and very deliberately, by a human, with the
     reasoning written into a decision record.

  Why it is absolute: cryptographic code fails silently. Wrong output is
  byte-shaped exactly like right output, so it passes every test in this
  repository and no review here is qualified to catch it. The usual safety net
  -- tests, coverage, a reviewer -- does not exist for this one category, and
  the cost of being wrong is borne by the volunteers whose names, addresses and
  whereabouts the code was protecting.

THE LIVE CASE is inventory-tng-jro and any demo built ahead of it. RFC 9421 message signatures, non-extractable WebCrypto keys and anything resembling a bespoke token format are all inside this rule.
design: Deliberately NOT a decision record. ADRs here carry product architecture -- what the system is and why it is shaped that way. This is a standing constraint on how code gets written, which is what AGENTS.md and DEVELOPERS.md are for. If a case ever reaches rule 3 and a person decides it, THAT decision gets a record; the rule that made them stop does not.
acceptance_criteria: AGENTS.md carries the rule in full as a third non-negotiable; DEVELOPERS.md points at it from the Definition of Done; check-docs.sh passes; no other file restates the prose.
close_reason: Closed

title: A credential-free GET escapes the audit that decision 0012 requires
description:
Found by the review of PR #23 (inventory-tng-uq6).

backend/src/inventory/tests/test_capabilities.py::test_nothing_but_the_two_volunteer_writes_is_open_to_a_volunteer is the audit whose own docstring says 'Decision 0012 requires a new credential-free endpoint to be argued against the record, and that needs something which does not' -- meaning something that does not read the same permission list every other consumer reads.

It filters 'if method not in SAFE_METHODS', so it only ever sees writes. A new endpoint written permission_classes = [AllowAny] on a GET is invisible to it. inventory-tng-uq6 added exactly such an endpoint, /api/livez, and nothing in the repository objected.

Decision 0012's consequences say any endpoint reachable without a credential has to be argued against that record rather than added beside it. That is a rule about READS as much as writes -- inventory-tng-81f7 is the open question about what an anonymous caller may learn about a person, and it exists because the read surface was never the thing 0012 asked about.

THE FIX is a second assertion beside that one, over the credential-free reads: walk urlpatterns, take every view where permissions.open_to_anybody is true, and hold it against a named list the way the write audit does. A new one then has to be added to the list deliberately, which is the moment the argument against 0012 gets written.

RELATED, and cheap to do here: permissions.open_to_anybody's docstring counted the endpoints it covers and was wrong by five -- it said 'three' while the predicate was true of ApiRootView, HealthCheckView, CurrentUserView, ClientFailureView, DebugTraceVerifyView and both spectacular views. inventory-tng-uq6 replaced the count with a description rather than incrementing it again, because two consecutive changes had bumped it by one and left it short. The list the audit above would hold is what makes a count safe to write down again.
close_reason: Closed

title: Readiness probes pin every gunicorn worker when the database blackholes
description:
Found by the review of PR #23 (inventory-tng-uq6), which split liveness onto /api/livez so a database blip stops killing pods. The split is right and does not finish the job: the same symptom is reachable one layer down, through worker exhaustion rather than through the liveness probe.

VERIFIED, not inferred, by the reviewer against the real configuration:

  backend/Dockerfile runs gunicorn --workers 3 with no --worker-class and no
  --timeout, so the defaults apply: SYNC workers, threads=1, timeout=30.

  settings.py DATABASES = {'default': env.db('DATABASE_URL')}. env.db_url_config
  returns NAME/USER/PASSWORD/HOST/PORT/ENGINE and no OPTIONS, so there is no
  connect_timeout, and CONN_MAX_AGE is 0, so every request opens a fresh
  connection.

THE ARITHMETIC. A failover that moves the database's address blackholes SYNs
rather than refusing them, so psycopg.connect() blocks for the kernel SYN
timeout, about 127 seconds. The kubelet hangs up after readiness's
timeoutSeconds, but hanging up does not free the worker: it is blocked inside
libpq and only notices the closed socket when it next writes, so it stays
pinned until the arbiter kills it at 30 seconds.

Readiness fires every 10 seconds and each blocked probe pins one worker for 30:
6 x 30 = 180 worker-seconds demanded per minute against 3 x 60 = 180 available.
That is saturation from probe traffic alone, before one volunteer request.
/api/livez then sits in the accept queue, misses its deadlines, and the
container is killed at about 60 seconds -- every replica together, because they
all dial the same database. Which is inventory-tng-uq6's symptom, reached by a
different road.

THE FIX IS TO BOUND THE CONNECTION rather than to route around it. The
reviewer's suggestion is connect_timeout=2, as a DATABASE_URL query parameter
or in DATABASES['default']['OPTIONS']: it drops readiness's demand from 180 to
about 12 worker-seconds per minute and makes EVERY request fail fast against an
unreachable database, not only the probes. --worker-class gthread or a shorter
gunicorn --timeout each break the arithmetic too, and are worth weighing
against it rather than assuming.

THE NUMBER IS A DECISION, which is why this is a bead and not a line in that
pull request: two seconds is short enough to make a busy-but-reachable database
look unreachable, and whoever picks it is choosing how patient this service is
with its own database. .env.sample, docs/deployment.md and the chart's values
all change with it.

WHILE IN HERE, two smaller things the same review raised about the probes:
there is no startupProbe, so initialDelaySeconds is the only lever for a slow
first boot and it is coupled to the numbers that decide how long a wedged pod
is left alone; and Kubernetes never restarts a container for prolonged
unreadiness, so a pod whose OWN database access is wedged now sits out of the
Service for ever with nothing to page on. Both are named in
docs/deployment.md#health-checks as of that pull request.
notes:
SETTLED BY THE PROJECT OWNER 2026-08-24: connect_timeout is CONFIGURABLE, with a CLEARLY DOCUMENTED DEFAULT OF 5 SECONDS. Not a literal in settings.py -- an environment variable in the shape of every other knob, with .env.sample carrying the prose that says what the number is for and which way it is dangerous to get wrong.

WHY 5 IS THE RIGHT DEFAULT, arithmetic rather than taste, against the probes as uq6 left them (readiness: periodSeconds 10, timeoutSeconds 1, failureThreshold 3; gunicorn: 3 sync workers, threads 1, timeout 30).

TODAY, with no connect_timeout: a failover that blackholes SYNs blocks psycopg.connect() for the kernel SYN timeout, about 127 seconds, capped in practice by the gunicorn arbiter killing the worker at 30. The kubelet hanging up at timeoutSeconds 1 does NOT free the worker -- it is blocked inside libpq and only notices the closed socket when it next writes. Readiness fires 6 times a minute, so 6 x 30 = 180 worker-seconds demanded against 3 x 60 = 180 available. Exactly saturating, from probe traffic alone, before one volunteer request.

WITH connect_timeout=5: a blocked probe pins a worker for 5 seconds rather than 30. 6 x 5 = 30 worker-seconds against 180 available, so probes ask for about 17% of capacity instead of 100%. That is the whole fix.

THE INVARIANT TO WRITE DOWN BESIDE THE DEFAULT, because it is what makes 5 correct rather than merely smaller: connect_timeout MUST stay below readiness periodSeconds. Above it, a probe is still blocked when the next probe arrives and they accumulate, which is the failure this bead describes reappearing at a different number. 5 against 10 leaves a factor of two. Anyone raising connect_timeout has to lower periodSeconds or raise worker count with it, and the document must say so rather than leaving the next reader to rediscover the multiplication.

WHY 5 IS NOT IMPATIENT: a healthy PostgreSQL connect on a cluster network is single-digit milliseconds. 5 seconds is three orders of magnitude of headroom, so it cannot fire in ordinary operation -- it fires only when the database is genuinely unreachable, which is when a fast refusal is what everybody wants.

IT APPLIES TO EVERY REQUEST, NOT ONLY PROBES, and that is an improvement rather than a caveat. settings.py:192 is DATABASES = {'default': env.db('DATABASE_URL')} and env.db_url_config returns no OPTIONS and no CONN_MAX_AGE, so CONN_MAX_AGE is 0 and every request opens a fresh connection. During an outage a volunteer submitting a batch presently waits out the SYN timeout; with this they get a clean refusal in 5 seconds and can retry. The outbox already exists to survive that.

NOT IN SCOPE, noted so it is not swept in: raising CONN_MAX_AGE above 0 is a separate change with its own argument (connection reuse against a failover leaving stale handles), and it is not this bead.
close_reason: Closed

title: MEETING INPUT: what a volunteer's device may read about people
description:
Carries a question that gnhl cannot be built without an answer to, and that nobody in this repository is placed to answer alone.

THE SETTING. Decision 0012 point 3 is accepted: volunteers do not sign in. inventory-tng-gnhl is the work that makes that true, and it is the reason the application cannot yet be put in front of anybody. Point 3's own defences -- an append-only ledger, an actor on every row, rate limits, an administrator who can compensate -- are all about WRITES. The record never asks what the READS contain, because when it was written every read was behind IsAuthenticated and the question did not arise.

WHAT WAS FOUND, read from the code on 2026-08-24 rather than supposed. VolunteerSerializer returns display_name, email and slack_id. VolunteerPicker.tsx renders the whole first page before anybody types (searchPath returns the bare collection for an empty term), so the ordinary first paint of the volunteer screen is fifty people with their addresses. slack_id is on the wire and displayed by nothing. LocationSerializer exposes held_by, and a custody location is named after the volunteer holding stock, so joining it against ItemSerializer.balances gives a named person, an address, and the quantity of hardware in their home. AppendThrottle exempts every safe method, deliberately and correctly, so none of these reads is rate limited at all.

So opening the read surface as gnhl describes would publish the volunteer roster. Roughly fifty to sixty addresses, since 45% of rows carry no identifier -- small, and that is not the point: it is a current, verified, name-to-address list of a named organisation's volunteers.

WHAT IS NOT IN QUESTION. A login and a password for volunteers. That is settled against by decision 0012 and is not reopened here; the options all preserve it.

THE QUESTION IS TWO QUESTIONS. First, what may an anonymous caller learn about a person -- which is answered by what the response carries, and costs a volunteer almost nothing whichever way it goes. Second, whether a device should enrol before it may read, which is inventory-tng-jro brought forward, and costs real friction. They are independent axes and only the first protects the data against a caller who has already enrolled.

BLOCKS gnhl, which should not be built until the first question is answered.
design:
Written to be argued by collaborators and volunteers rather than settled in the repository. Follows the pattern of inventory-tng-8sq: a presented document for people who will not read a decision record, with the repository copy in docs/briefs/ that needs no account -- see docs/briefs/authorisation.md for the precedent and the sentence that explains the duplication.

Outcome is an amendment to decision 0012 or a record of its own; its consequences say any new credential-free endpoint must be argued against that record rather than added beside it, and gnhl opens roughly six.
acceptance_criteria: An answer exists to what an anonymous caller may learn about a person, and to whether reads wait for enrolment, both recorded where gnhl can be built against them. Decision 0012 is amended or a new record supersedes the relevant part of it.
notes:
=== PUBLISHED, two documents, 2026-08-24 ===

THE BRIEF, which carries the argument, the measurements and the questions:
https://claude.ai/code/artifact/e8aa40b6-4220-414b-b5db-a476091ada69

THE RUN OF SHOW, for whoever presents the demo of inventory-tng-81f7.3:
https://claude.ai/code/artifact/76c13c07-ab77-425f-986b-03fe6fe3c27b

Sources are gitignored at ignored/briefs/who-can-see-the-volunteer-list.html and ignored/briefs/five-postures-one-config.html, so either can be redeployed to the same URL. Both are private until shared from the page's own menu.

The repository copies that need no account are not written yet. They follow docs/briefs/authorisation.md's pattern -- that file carries the sentence explaining why a brief and its artifact are the one sanctioned exception to rule 1. Worth writing AFTER the meeting, so they record the outcome rather than the question.

=== SETTLED BY THE PROJECT OWNER 2026-08-24 ===

DECISION 0012 IS AMENDED, AND THE READ-SURFACE POLICY GETS A RECORD OF ITS OWN. Not one or the other. 0012's consequences already require any new credential-free endpoint to be argued against that record rather than added beside it, and gnhl opens roughly six, so the amendment is where that argument goes; the new record is where 'what an anonymous caller may learn about a person' lives, because it is a policy that outlives the six endpoints gnhl happens to open.

THE PAYLOAD HALF IS ANSWERED and is recorded on inventory-tng-gnhl: an anonymous caller gets id and display_name, and somebody sharing a display name identifies themselves by TYPING their own address rather than by reading anybody's. inventory-tng-81f7.2 carries the better answer for the ~45% who have no address on file.

=== RAISED BY THE PROJECT OWNER 2026-08-24: RESTRICT BY NETWORK ===

Added to the brief as a fifth option: NYC Mesh IP space, or the mesh's road-warrior WireGuard setup, documented at https://wiki.nycmesh.net/books/5-networking/page/wireguard-vpn-setup-guide

Worth stating so nobody conflates the two: this is NOT the proposal decision 0012 rejected. That one trusted the Origin header, which a client sets and curl forges byte-identically. A source address is not client-supplied in the same way -- a TCP connection only completes if you can actually receive packets there -- so this is a qualitatively stronger control than the one that was thrown out.

Its limits are the ones every gate shares, plus two of its own. It controls who may ask, not what the answer contains, so it does nothing about the payload. 'On the mesh' is thousands of members by design, plus every public space carrying a mesh connection -- Mil Mundos, Blue Stockings -- so the trusted set is large and deliberately open, which defeats opportunistic scraping but not a targeted one. And the rooftop case is the one that hurts: at an install, before the node is up, the volunteer's phone is on cellular, which is exactly when they want to record what they took.

TWO IMPLEMENTATION TRAPS if it is chosen. It would be enforced at nginx, so the policy would live in deployment configuration rather than in the application -- and 0012's consequence 'both halves must be visible in the API' is then violated, because the generated schema cannot say 'open, but only from these networks'. And any address-based rule must read the client address the same way DRF does (X-Forwarded-For counted back NUM_PROXIES hops, presently 2) or a caller spoofs a mesh address by prepending the header.

=== MASKING MEASURED AND RULED OUT, 2026-08-24 ===

The project owner asked what a masked address does when two people share a mail provider and a first initial. Measured against ignored/NYC Mesh - Inventory Sheet.xlsx, tab QRresponses, 1,861 submissions carrying both a name and an address. Aggregates only -- rule 6 in inventory/sheet/people.py says the workbook is not ours to publish and a table of its people least of all.

53 distinct folded names, 60 distinct addresses.
13 names carry more than one address -- the disambiguation population.
5 of those 13 (38%) are NOT separated by the mask first-char + domain-initial + TLD.
Across all 60 addresses the masked forms collapse to 35 distinct; 40 addresses (66%) share a masked form with somebody else, largest group 4.
52 of 80 distinct name/address pairs (65%) have the first name inside the local part, so a masked address beside a real display name is largely guessable.

Caveat stated rather than buried: 'names carried by >1 address' conflates two people sharing a name with one person using two addresses, which rule 6 says both occur and the sheet cannot separate. So 13 is an upper bound on genuine collisions. The 66% global collision rate does not depend on that ambiguity, and the conclusion does not change.

REPRODUCTION: parse QRresponses columns 'First name' and 'Email Address', fold the name with lower() and whitespace-collapse, group addresses by folded name, and compare mask(e) = local[0] + domain[0] + tld across each group.

=== A SEARCH THRESHOLD IS NOT A CONTROL, measured 2026-08-24 ===

Against the 86 distinct folded names. display_name is matched with icontains, a SUBSTRING match rather than a prefix, so one letter returns 54 of 86.

  minimum length 1 -> 6 searches sweep the whole roster
  minimum length 2 -> 22
  minimum length 3 -> 43, and brute-forcing all 17,576 three-letter combinations is trivial
  capping the anonymous page at 10 with no next link -> 14 / 26 / 43 for the same three

So a threshold is a usability decision and must never be argued as a defence. The full consequence, including what a read limit IS for, is inventory-tng-81f7.1.

=== CHILDREN ===

81f7.1  the read rate limit, sized against the membership oracle and not against enumeration
81f7.2  telling two same-named volunteers apart without naming either
81f7.3  the demo, every variant a config value, deliberately unmerged
81f7.4  pruning those config flags once this bead is settled

BLOCKED BY inventory-tng-lb95: the audit that enforces 0012's credential-free rule filters SAFE_METHODS, so it only ever inspects writes and a new AllowAny GET is invisible to it. gnhl opens roughly six credential-free reads, so that audit needs its read half first.


=== WHY THIS BEAD DEPENDS ON 81f7.3, WHICH LOOKS BACKWARDS AND IS NOT ===

Deliberate, and reinstated on 2026-08-24 after a reviewer read it as tracker corruption and removed it. It was corrupt at that moment and the reviewer was right to act: 81f7.3 still held a parent-child row to this bead AND a blocks edge on it, so bd reported this issue blocked by its own child. The parent-child row is the half that was wrong.

81f7.3 is the DEMO. It has to happen BEFORE the meeting, because it exists to make the meeting decidable. So it is a sibling that blocks this bead, not a child that waits on it -- as a child it inherited a dependency on this bead completing and never appeared in bd ready at all, which would have left the demo invisible to any session looking for work.

The other three children are correctly children: 81f7.1, .2 and .4 all follow the decision rather than precede it.

The edge is worth keeping rather than merely tolerating: it stops this bead being closed -- the decision recorded -- while the demo commissioned to inform it has not been shown.

title: Batch: stickers survive the row they name
description:
Shipping inventory-tng-6pr on its own: deleting an item or a location destroys the labels pointing at it, and those codes are printed on stickers already on shelves.

Membership only; what the issue is about is on the issue.
close_reason: Its only child landed; the batch goes through the review cycle from here.

title: Volunteers still have to sign in, which decision 0012 point 3 says they must not
description:
Decision 0012 is accepted and its point 3 is not built. Volunteers cannot use this application without an account, which is the reason it cannot be put in front of anybody yet.

WHAT IS TRUE TODAY, read rather than remembered:

  backend/src/inventory_tng/settings.py DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES is
  [IsAuthenticated, StaffWrites, RecentlyAuthenticated], so every endpoint
  needs a session unless it says otherwise.

  backend/src/inventory/permissions.py:66 is VOLUNTEER_APPEND = [IsAuthenticated].
  The name and the comment above it say these are the two endpoints decision
  0012 point 3 opens to a volunteer. What they opt out of is the staff flag and
  the step-up, not authentication. views.py:321 and views.py:680 use it.

  Three endpoints are open: the index, the health check and /api/me.

  guides/volunteer.md tells volunteers to ask an administrator for a login and
  calls it 'a gap rather than a plan'. docs/architecture.md#not-yet-built says
  the same to a developer.

WHAT HAS TO OPEN, and it is more than the two writes. The scan flow is useless
without reads: the catalogue and its balances, the volunteer pick-list, the
label map the client prefetches, and the resolver for one scanned code. Every
one of those is IsAuthenticated by the project default. Decision 0012's context
paragraph names this -- 'every endpoint but the index and the health check
requires a session today, the volunteer ones included'.

WHAT ALREADY STANDS IN FOR THE CREDENTIAL: the rate limiting in
inventory/throttling.py, built for exactly this and required by decision 0012's
own consequences. Note that AppendThrottle deliberately exempts reads, because
the endpoint taking a volunteer's name is also the pick-list searched as
somebody types -- so an open READ surface is not covered by what exists and
needs its own answer rather than an assumption.

WHAT FOLLOWS ON ITS OWN: the schema declares each operation's audience from the
view's permissions (PolicyAwareAutoSchema in inventory/api.py, over
permissions.administrators_only and permissions.open_to_anybody), so it will
follow rather than need editing. That is also what makes this assertable.

TESTS THAT INVERT, at least: test_volunteers.py's
test_the_pick_list_requires_authentication asserts today's behaviour and becomes
its opposite. Expect others; the suite has been written against a closed API
throughout.

DOCUMENTS THAT CHANGE IN THE SAME PULL REQUEST: guides/volunteer.md loses its
'Signing in' section, and docs/architecture.md#not-yet-built loses the sentence
about every endpoint needing a session.

NOT THIS ISSUE: inventory-tng-jro, device enrolment. Decision 0012 point 4 is
explicit that enrolled devices are the next step and not the first, deferred
until this flow is in real use and the cost of enrolment friction is known. So
this lands first and jro is argued afterwards, against what was learnt.
design: Decision 0012 point 3 is already the decision, so this implements a record rather than making one -- no new decision record unless the read surface turns out to need an argument the existing one does not make. Decision 0012's consequences say any endpoint reachable without a credential has to be argued against that record, which is the bar for each read opened here.
acceptance_criteria: A volunteer with no account can open the app, search the pick-list, read the catalogue, resolve a scanned code and save a batch. An anonymous caller is still refused every write reserved to an administrator, and the generated schema says so per operation. The two guides and docs/architecture.md no longer describe a sign-in volunteers do not do.
notes:
VERIFIED AGAINST main AT cb5fcb1, 2026-08-24. Everything the description states still holds, read rather than remembered:

- settings.py DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES is [IsAuthenticated, StaffWrites, RecentlyAuthenticated].
- permissions.py VOLUNTEER_APPEND is [IsAuthenticated] -- it opts out of the staff flag and the step-up, NOT of authentication.
- Confirmed by accident while writing a test for something else: after client.logout(), POST /api/stock/transactions answers 403 not_authenticated. The ledger endpoint, which decision 0012 point 3 says a volunteer reaches without an account, refuses an anonymous caller today.

ITS PRECONDITION IS CHEAPER THAN IT WAS. inventory-tng-6pr landed on 2026-08-24, so an item or a location a printed sticker names can no longer be deleted out from under it. Opening the read surface therefore happens over a catalogue whose stickers cannot be destroyed by an ordinary administrative action. That was worth having first.

THE OPEN QUESTION IS STILL THROTTLING THE READS. AppendThrottle.allow_request returns True for every safe method, deliberately -- the endpoint taking a volunteer's name is also the pick-list searched as somebody types, and a limit sized for submissions would be exhausted by typing. So the existing rate limiting, which decision 0012's consequences name as what stands in for the credential, does not cover an open READ surface at all. Now carried by inventory-tng-81f7.1, which also says what such a limit is and is not for.

WHAT IT WOULD OPEN, beyond the two writes: the catalogue and its balances, the volunteer pick-list, the label map the client prefetches, and the resolver for one scanned code. All IsAuthenticated by the project default.

=== SETTLED BY THE PROJECT OWNER 2026-08-24 ===

The payload half of the open question above now has an answer.

AN ANONYMOUS CALLER GETS id AND display_name. No email, no slack_id. slack_id goes with nothing lost at all -- it is on the wire today and rendered by no component; VolunteerPicker.tsx uses it only in identifierField(), which classifies what the USER TYPED and never reads the response. Administrators who sign in keep the full record, so this is two representations keyed on the permission rather than a field deleted from the model.

SOMEBODY WHO SHARES A DISPLAY NAME IDENTIFIES THEMSELVES BY TYPING their own address. VolunteerFilter already matches identifiers exactly and deliberately -- substring is not offered on them -- so this needs no new search behaviour: the address goes IN and only the name comes back. You identify yourself by supplying an identifier, never by reading one.

MASKING WAS CONSIDERED AND MEASURED OUT.
