The reproduction and the numbers are on inventory-tng-81f7; the short of it is that a masked address fails to separate 5 of the 13 colliding names, 66% of all addresses share a masked form with somebody else, and 65% of addresses contain the person's first name anyway, so a mask beside a real name is largely guessable.

NOT A REGRESSION FOR ANYBODY, which is what makes this cheap: the ~45% of rows with no identifier were ALREADY indistinguishable when they share a name, because a null address renders no second line. The better answer for them is inventory-tng-81f7.2 and is deliberately not a condition of this bead.

A SEARCH THRESHOLD IS NOT PART OF THIS. Measured against the 86 folded names: requiring one character lets 6 searches sweep the whole roster, two lets 22, three lets 43, and capping the anonymous page at 10 gives 14/26/43. display_name is matched with icontains, a SUBSTRING match, so one letter returns 54 of 86. A minimum length is a usability decision and must never be argued as a control.

STILL THE MEETING'S TO ANSWER: whether a custody location may be disclosed anonymously (81f7 question 2), and whether reads wait for a gate at all. This bead stays blocked by 81f7 and by inventory-tng-lb95, whose audit has to grow a read half before six credential-free reads land.

title: gunicorn's access line carries the URL, its query string and the user agent, past the allowlist
description:
Found in the review of pull request 19. The third row of DEVELOPERS.md's triage table: it is the composition of nb8.5's allowlist and nb8.6's shipper, and lives in a file neither of them touched.

gunicorn's default access_log_format is '%(h)s %(l)s %(u)s %(t)s "%(r)s" %(s)s %(b)s "%(f)s" "%(a)s"'. %(r)s is the request line -- the concrete path WITH its query string -- and %(a)s is the user agent. Nothing in this repository sets access_log_format; backend/Dockerfile and compose.yaml both pass --access-logfile -, and logs.logging_config routes gunicorn.access to standard output like everything else.

So every request writes event="... \"GET /api/items/4172?volunteer=Ada HTTP/1.1\" 200 ... \"Mozilla/5.0 ...\"" -- the concrete URL and the user agent, which are the two things docs/observability.md's denied list names, using very nearly that URL as its worked example. The allowlist cannot touch it, because it governs FIELDS and this is the message body, which that document says plainly is the author's responsibility.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE NOW THAN IT DID. On main these lines went to a container's output and no further. inventory-tng-nb8.6 ships them to a collector.

THE FIX IS gunicorn's, not the allowlist's: set access_log_format in backend/src/gunicorn.conf.py to something that carries the method and the route-ish path without the query string and without the user agent, or drop the access log entirely now that a server span records the same request with http.route on it. Deciding between those two is part of this issue: the span is strictly better data, and the access line's remaining value is that it exists when telemetry is not configured.
acceptance_criteria: A request with a query string and a user agent leaves neither in any record the backend writes, proven by a test that makes one. docs/observability.md's denied list is true of the whole stream rather than of span attributes alone.
close_reason: gunicorn's access_log_format is set in gunicorn.conf.py: no caller address, no query string, no user agent, and it honours TELEMETRY_PERSONAL_DATA like everything else. Verified against a real gunicorn.

title: A real server produces no server spans: Django is instrumented after the handler is built
description:
Found while standing the compose collector up for inventory-tng-nb8.6, against a real Django serving real HTTP.

MEASURED. With OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT set and the sampler at 1.0, a GET of /api/healthz through a running server produces one trace containing a single SELECT span from the psycopg instrumentation, and no SERVER span at all. Tempo shows rootTraceName=SELECT. There is no HTTP duration or count metric either, and every log record carries an empty trace_id, because there is no request span for one to belong to.

THE CAUSE. DjangoInstrumentor().instrument() does one thing: it inserts its middleware at the front of settings.MIDDLEWARE. Django's WSGIHandler reads that list once, in __init__, through load_middleware(). inventory_tng/wsgi.py builds the handler first and calls telemetry.start() afterwards, so the list is changed after the only reader of it has finished with it. Confirmed directly: after start(), settings.MIDDLEWARE contains _DjangoMiddleware and the handler chain built moments earlier does not.

The same ordering is what gunicorn gets. post_fork calls start(django=False) before the application is imported, which is right; wsgi.py then imports the application and instruments after it, which is not.

WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT. Django's test client builds a handler per request, so a test that instruments and then calls the client gets the middleware -- test_telemetry.py's server-span assertions pass against an arrangement no server has. Any test for this has to hold a handler built the way a server builds one, once, before the request.

THE FIX, roughly: settings have to be configured before instrumenting -- decision 0021 explains why instrumenting with none configured is worse than not instrumenting -- and the handler has to be built after. django.setup() is idempotent and is what get_wsgi_application() calls first anyway, so wsgi.py can do that itself, then start(), then build the application.
acceptance_criteria: A request through a server built the way a deployment builds one produces a SERVER span named for its route, with the database spans beneath it, and the HTTP metrics that middleware emits. The test holds a handler built once before the request, so it fails against the arrangement that shipped.
close_reason: Settings, then instrument, then build. Decision 0021 records the correction; the test holds a handler built the way a server builds one.

title: Batch: the OpenTelemetry SDK, and the settings rule it needed first
description:
Batch membership only, in the sense DEVELOPERS.md#pull-requests gives the word: which issues are in this pull request.

inventory-tng-nb8.14 first, so that the OTEL_ variables nb8.2 adds inherit the rule rather than being five more with the sharp edge. Then inventory-tng-nb8.2, the SDK itself.

Parented here rather than under inventory-tng-nb8 for the reason recorded on that epic: check-batch.sh reads a parent-child dependency as batch membership and nothing else.
close_reason: All children completed

title: An unlisted Host writes a 1.4 KB traceback to the collector, unauthenticated and unlimited
description:
Found reviewing pull request 17. Not a defect in what that branch changed -- it is what giving django.security somewhere to go turned out to buy along with the fix.

MEASURED, on that branch, against a real gunicorn: one request carrying a Host nobody listed produces a JSON record at ERROR of about 1.4 KB, carrying a nine-frame traceback ending in DisallowedHost.

WHY THAT IS A PROBLEM. The ingress is internet-facing, the path takes no credential and nothing rate-limits it, and the nine frames are the same three Django functions every time -- so the traceback carries no information the one-line message lacks. An ordinary host scanner at a few hundred requests a second writes hundreds of megabytes an hour into whatever the cluster ships to, burying real errors; and since nothing outlives a pod (docs/deployment.md#reading-the-logs), it fills the node's disk on the way.

WHAT INVENTORY-TNG-ADJ ACTUALLY NEEDED was the hostname that was refused, which is in the message. The traceback was never the part that was missing.

OPTIONS, none of them chosen here: drop django.security to WARNING without exc_info; keep ERROR but strip the traceback with a filter; or rate-limit the logger. The first is the cheapest and loses least, but it is a deliberate downgrade of a security log and should be decided rather than assumed.

Whatever is chosen, docs/deployment.md#health-checks currently presents the new visibility as pure gain and will need the caveat.
close_reason: The traceback is stripped and the rate is bounded; docs/deployment.md carries the caveat.

title: Batch: structured logging, and the record shape the rest of the telemetry hangs on
description:
Batch membership only, in the sense DEVELOPERS.md#pull-requests gives the word: which issues are in pull request 17.

What it holds: inventory-tng-zya, inventory-tng-nb8.1 and inventory-tng-nb8.12 -- the logging half of the OpenTelemetry epic, inventory-tng-nb8, with no OpenTelemetry in it. If that epic stalls, what shipped here still stands on its own.

Why these three are parented here rather than under nb8: scripts/check-batch.sh reads a parent-child dependency as batch membership and nothing else, which is what DEVELOPERS.md says it means, so an issue cannot be a member of a feature epic and a batch at the same time. nb8 remains the design record and the handover -- its description is where the reasoning lives, and the depends-on chain between its children is untouched, so 'bd ready' still gives the order.
close_reason: All children completed

title: Docs: DEVELOPERS.md, how to read logs while you are working
description:
Ali asked that usable console output be clearly documented in the developer documentation, and this is the half of it that belongs there rather than in docs/observability.md.

THE SPLIT, so rule 1 holds. DEVELOPERS.md owns reading logs while developing: the commands, the environment variables, how to turn one subsystem up to DEBUG, how to follow the backend under compose, how to pipe the JSON stream through the pretty-printer. It sits alongside Code style and Testing and coverage, which is where somebody looks for how to work. docs/observability.md owns the telemetry system itself and where a deployment sends it, and links here rather than repeating it.

WHAT IT HAS TO ANSWER, in the order somebody meets them: I am running Django natively and want readable output. I am running it under compose and want to follow it. I want every SQL query for one endpoint and nothing else. I want to see every function a request called. I have a JSON stream and want to read it.

The commands have to be real -- test_documented_commands.py holds every command any document prints, so a line here that does not run fails the build.
acceptance_criteria: A developer who has never seen the project can get readable logs, raise one subsystem to DEBUG, and follow compose output, using only this section. Every command it prints is exercised by test_documented_commands.py. It does not restate what docs/observability.md says.
notes:
Ali asked whether the developer docs should warn that this needs a wide console. Decided: detection, plus telling the developer what happened -- never silent adaptation.

The docs carry a table of the three layouts, the width each needs, what each one drops, and the DJANGO_LOG_LAYOUT override. nb8.1 makes the process announce its choice at startup, so the documentation explains something the developer has already been told rather than being the only place it exists.

The value being served: a developer must never wonder why their console differs from a colleague's.

WHAT NB8.1 ACTUALLY SHIPPED, so the table documents the code rather than the plan.

Four variables, not five. DJANGO_LOG_LEVEL, DJANGO_LOG_LEVELS, DJANGO_LOG_FORMAT,
DJANGO_LOG_LAYOUT and DJANGO_LOG_CONTEXT -- with the timestamp NOT getting a
variable of its own. The epic asked for one that shortens it; DJANGO_LOG_LAYOUT
already does exactly that, because compact and minimal are time-only. A second
variable doing what the first one does is a second thing to document and to keep
in step. The cost is real and should be stated in the docs rather than hidden:
somebody on a wide terminal who wants only the short timestamp has to take
compact, and loses the logger module path with it.

The three layouts as built: full needs 140 columns and drops nothing; compact
needs 100 and drops the date, the offset and the logger module path; minimal
takes anything narrower and drops the logger column entirely. The announcement
the process prints names the same figures, so the table and the startup line
must agree -- inventory_tng/console.py holds both.

The pretty-printer is scripts/pretty-logs. docs/deployment.md#reading-the-logs
already shows it against kubectl for an operator; what belongs here is the
compose form and the native workflow, linking rather than repeating.
close_reason: DEVELOPERS.md#reading-the-logs-while-you-work, with the layout table and the override

title: Dev environment: a collector in compose, so telemetry has somewhere to go
description:
Ali's requirement: the dev setup ships a working destination, not instructions for building one. It is strictly development, so it is chosen for being one container and no configuration rather than for throughput.

grafana/otel-lgtm is the candidate -- Loki, Tempo, Prometheus and Grafana in a single image, OTLP in on 4317 and 4318, Grafana on 3000, no configuration to write. Verify the image and tag before committing to it; if it has moved, the requirement is the shape rather than that project.

WHAT IT HAS TO DEMONSTRATE, because this doubles as the worked example for server administrators: logs arriving from stdout, metrics and traces arriving over OTLP, and a query in the UI that follows one request end to end. That is the thing docs can point at instead of describing.

Off by default or on a compose profile: a developer who has not asked for telemetry should not pay for a second container, and DEVELOPERS.md#getting-started must not grow a step.
acceptance_criteria: One documented command brings up the collector; a request made against a local backend is findable in the UI with its logs and its spans. It is not started by the default compose up. docs/observability.md prints the command.
notes:
THE IMAGE IS NOT DECIDED. Ali, 2026-08-23: verifying grafana/otel-lgtm is fine, but research the alternatives as part of this issue rather than treating the candidate as the answer. If the research does not produce a clear winner, ask Ali instead of picking one.

What the comparison is against is already in the description -- one container, no configuration to write, OTLP in on 4317 and 4318, and a UI that can follow one request end to end across its logs, metrics and traces. Development only, so throughput and retention are not criteria.

Record what was compared and why the winner won. If it is not grafana/otel-lgtm, the epic's description names that project and will need correcting.
close_reason: grafana/otel-lgtm 0.31.0 behind a compose profile, with scripts/ship-logs for the stdout half. Verified end to end: server span with its queries beneath, HTTP metrics, and the records in Loki.

title: Docs: docs/observability.md, and how a deployment picks a destination
description:
The canonical document for this topic, which does not exist yet -- deployment.md covers deploying and DEVELOPERS.md covers building, and rule 1 means neither grows a second copy of this.

DEPLOYMENT-AGNOSTIC, and this is a requirement rather than a preference. Where this is deployed is not settled: it may be CodeNOW, it may be a Kubernetes cluster NYC Mesh runs itself on Proxmox. docs/deployment.md already gets this right -- it leads with 'standard Kubernetes and CodeNOW' and states there is no CodeNOW-specific code -- and this document has to hold the same shape. A self-hosted cluster is a first-class path, not an appendix, and nothing here may assume a platform that collects container logs for you.

TWO AUDIENCES. A developer wants the compose collector and how to read logs in a terminal. Somebody standing up a cluster wants to know what this project ships (a collector for development only), what it does not (any production destination), and what they have to decide.

THE SURVEY ALI ASKED FOR, because the options differ in where the credential lives and that is the part nobody explains. Direct to a vendor over OTLP with a key in a header; through a collector that fans out, with the key in the collector rather than the application and a disk-backed queue when the destination is down; or stdout scraped by an agent already on the node. Name the trade in each.

FOR A CLUSTER NYC MESH RUNS ITSELF, the docs have to answer concretely: which log agent (Fluent Bit, Vector, Promtail), whether the collector is a DaemonSet, a Deployment or a sidecar, what it costs to run, and what persistence a volunteer organisation actually wants. Self-hosted options worth naming with their real cost: the Grafana stack, an OTel-native single deployable such as SigNoz, and Elastic with Kibana -- the last being the heaviest and the reason to think twice.

THE CHART DOES NOT RENDER A COLLECTOR. Settled in the epic (point 14) rather than left to this issue: a collector is cluster infrastructure shared by everything on the cluster, not a component of this application. Ship the app, document the collector. This issue writes the documentation for standing one up; it does not add a template.
acceptance_criteria: One document, linked from DEVELOPERS.md and docs/deployment.md rather than duplicated into them. A developer goes from clone to a queryable trace using only it. Somebody with an empty self-hosted cluster can stand up logs, metrics and traces from it without reading a vendor's site first. No step assumes a platform that collects for you. The trace sampling knob is documented as Ali asked: the variable, that the code default is a conservative 10%, that every configuration this repository ships sets 100%, and exactly what to change to sample a subset instead.
close_reason: docs/observability.md now carries the destination survey, the self-hosted cluster costs and the sampling knob, and is linked from README, DEVELOPERS.md and deployment.md.

title: Backend: deny-by-default redaction, so telemetry cannot carry personal data
description:
This system holds volunteer data and administrator identities, and telemetry is the easiest place to leak both without noticing, because nobody reads a span attribute the way they read a template.

WHAT COUNTS HERE, concretely: names and email addresses; Google and Slack account identifiers from decision 0013 sign-in; session cookies, CSRF tokens and Authorization headers; passwords, TOTP secrets and codes, password reset links; IP addresses, which are personal data under GDPR and which this system already handles for throttling; and any stable identifier for an unauthenticated volunteer -- inventory-tng-jro would mint exactly one, and a stable pseudonymous id that follows a person across sessions is personal data even though nobody signed in. Pseudonymised is not anonymous.

THE MECHANISM has to be deny-by-default or it will not survive new code. A SpanProcessor that drops any attribute not on an allowlist, and a logging.Filter doing the same for records. An allowlist that has to be edited to add a field is a decision somebody makes on purpose; a denylist is a list of the leaks already found.

A TOGGLE THAT ADMITS IT AGAIN, asked for by Ali 2026-08-23. Deny-by-default is
the resting state, not the only state: an IP address is exactly what somebody
debugging a throttle, a scanner or one volunteer's failing request needs to
see, and a mechanism with no way to look is a mechanism people work around.

WHAT THE TOGGLE IS, and every part of this is load-bearing:

* OFF unless deliberately turned on, in the code and in every configuration
  this repository ships. The chart never sets it on. Turning it on is an act
  somebody performs, not a state a deployment drifts into.
* NAMED, not boolean-vague, and validated the way every other setting in this
  application is -- refused loudly rather than defaulted quietly, so a typo
  cannot leave somebody believing redaction is on when it is off, which is the
  one failure mode worse than not having the toggle.
* ANNOUNCED. The process says at startup, once, that personal data is being
  recorded and by what setting. This repository already refuses silent
  adaptation for a console layout; it must not do less for this.
* MARKED IN THE DATA. Records and spans emitted while it is on carry a flag
  saying so, so that whoever holds the collector can find and purge them later
  without guessing which window was affected. This is the part that makes the
  toggle recoverable rather than permanent, and it is the reason not to leave
  it for the operator to remember.
* SEPARATE FROM THE ALLOWLIST, not a hole in it. The allowlist stays exactly
  as it is; the toggle admits a second, explicitly enumerated group -- the
  personal-data list above -- so what it re-admits is readable in one place and
  nothing joins that group by accident.

WHAT IT IS NOT. It is not a reason to soften the default, not a per-attribute
knob, and not a production setting. inventory-tng-nb8.4 builds a signed,
expiring debug token; tying this to that token instead of to an environment
variable would make it per-request and self-expiring, which is the shape a
production one-off should have. Worth deciding in nb8.4 rather than assumed
here: this issue owes the environment toggle, which is what a developer with a
collector in front of them needs.

WHAT TURNING IT ON MEANS, said plainly in the docs rather than discovered:
telemetry then contains personal data, so wherever it lands inherits that --
retention, access and deletion included. That is a reason to turn it on
briefly and turn it off, not a reason not to have it.

ALSO: route templates rather than concrete URLs (/api/items/{id}, not the id), which OTel's Django instrumentation does for span names but not for query strings; surrogate ids rather than natural ones; and no IP on a span at all -- the throttle needs it in memory, not in a telemetry backend.
acceptance_criteria: An attribute not on the allowlist never reaches an exporter, proven by a test that adds one. Sign-in, the volunteer append path and the label endpoints are each checked for what they emit. docs/observability.md lists what is allowed and why. With the toggle off -- the default -- no attribute on the personal-data list reaches an exporter. With it on, they do, the process has said so at startup, and what it emitted is marked so a collector holder can find it again. A value the toggle does not recognise stops the process rather than being read as off. No configuration this repository ships turns it on, and docs/observability.md says what turning it on makes true of wherever the telemetry lands.
notes:
TWO FIELDS NB8.1 ADDED THAT THIS ALLOWLIST HAS TO ACCOUNT FOR.

'bound' is a list of the key names a record inherited rather than stated. It
carries no values, only names, and the console reader uses it to decide what to
hide -- so removing it does not leak anything but does make 'pretty-logs' fall
back to guessing by name. Allow it.

The 'extra=' allowlist in logs.FROM_LIBRARIES is the same idea one layer down,
already deny-by-default: status_code, duration, params, sql and alias get
through and everything else is dropped, which is what keeps Django's
log_response from putting an HttpRequest -- and the personal data in it -- on
every 4xx and 5xx. Whatever this issue builds should own that list rather than
leaving two allowlists to disagree.

WHAT NB8.2 LEFT ON EVERY SPAN, measured on the branch that shipped it.

A server span from Django's instrumentation carries: http.method, http.route,
http.status_code, http.url, http.scheme, http.flavor, http.server_name,
net.host.port and NET.PEER.IP -- the caller's address, on every request.

That is the personal data this issue exists to keep out, and it is there now.
Nothing leaves the process yet because no endpoint is configured anywhere this
repository ships, and docs/deployment.md#telemetry carries a blockquote telling
a deployment not to set one until this lands. Deleting that blockquote is part
of closing this.

There is a test that FAILS the day you fix it, on purpose:
test_a_span_still_carries_the_client_address_until_the_redaction_lands in
backend/src/inventory/tests/test_telemetry.py. It is the reminder; delete it.

Note the attributes are the OLD HTTP semantic conventions -- http.status_code
rather than http.response.status_code. Whether to set OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN
and target the stable names instead is worth deciding here rather than
discovering later, because the allowlist has to name them either way.

DECISION 0021 CONTRADICTS THIS UNTIL YOU FIX IT. Its "No personal data,
enforced by an allowlist" section is already on main and says deny-by-default
with no exception; the epic'''s point 12 has been amended and that record has
not. Closing this issue means amending docs/decisions/0021-telemetry-over-otlp.md
in the same change -- the toggle, why it exists, and the conditions on it --
because a decision record that describes the previous decision is worse than
none.

Take care with rule 1 while doing it: 0021 argues WHY the toggle exists and
what it costs; docs/observability.md describes the variable and how to use it.
scripts/check-docs.sh will object if the argument appears in both.
close_reason: Deny-by-default across spans, metrics and log records, with the enumerated toggle, its four conditions, 0021 amended and docs/observability.md created.

title: Backend: OpenTelemetry traces and metrics over OTLP
description:
The SDK, the exporters, and the two instrumentations that cover most of it.

PACKAGES, matched to what is pinned: opentelemetry-distro, opentelemetry-exporter-otlp, opentelemetry-instrumentation-django, opentelemetry-instrumentation-psycopg (psycopg 3 -- the psycopg2 package is the wrong one, backend pins psycopg[binary]==3.3.*), opentelemetry-instrumentation-logging.

THE GUNICORN TRAP, decided: the SDK starts in a post_fork hook in a gunicorn config file, NOT by wrapping the command in opentelemetry-instrument. gunicorn pre-forks and a BatchSpanProcessor's exporter thread does not survive fork, so a master-initialised SDK leaves every worker buffering spans and exporting none. This is the single most common way a Django + gunicorn OTel setup silently produces nothing.

CONFIGURATION is the standard environment: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES. No endpoint set means the SDK is not started at all, so a checkout with no collector behaves exactly as it does today.

METRICS: what Django and psycopg give free is HTTP server duration and count by route and status, and DB client duration. The deliberate ones -- ledger appends accepted and rejected by reason, throttle rejections, label print runs and sheets consumed, sheet import rows staged against committed, second factor challenges -- are their own issue.
acceptance_criteria: A request produces a server span with its DB queries beneath it, exported to a collector. Workers export after fork, proven by a test or a documented manual check. No endpoint configured means no SDK and no overhead.
notes:
SAMPLING, settled with Ali 2026-08-23. The rate is configurable, not fixed at 100%.

The code default is a conservative 10%. The reasoning is what happens when nobody sets anything: an unconfigured deployment pointed at a collector somebody else sized should not be the thing that overwhelms it. A default that is safe when ignored is worth more than a default that is correct when attended to.

Every configuration this repository ships then overrides it to 100% explicitly -- .env.sample, compose, and the chart's values -- because at this traffic volume 100% is what we actually want and an explicit setting is visible where a silent default is not.

DOCUMENTATION IS AN ACCEPTANCE CRITERION, not a nicety. Ali was specific. What has to be stated: the variable's name, that the default is 10%, that the shipped configurations set 100%, and how to lower it to sample a subset -- with the value to change and where. It goes in docs/observability.md (nb8.7), which owns telemetry configuration; DEVELOPERS.md links rather than repeats.

The standard OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER / OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG environment is the first thing to reach for, since configuration here is otherwise the standard OTEL environment. Check it composes with the custom debug-flag sampler in nb8.9/nb8.4 before committing to it -- the sampler that honours the W3C sampled bit has to wrap the ratio sampler, not replace it.
close_reason: telemetry.py starts the SDK from gunicorn post_fork and the app ready hook; no endpoint means no SDK; sampling defaults to 0.1 and ships 1.0

title: Backend: structured JSON logs to stdout, and a readable console rendering
description:
Builds on inventory-tng-zya, which gives Django a LOGGING block at all. This decides the shape of a record and how a person reads one.

ONE PIPELINE, TWO RENDERINGS. structlog is the proposed dependency: a single processor chain feeding either a JSON renderer or a console renderer. The property that matters is that dev and deployed records differ only in how they are drawn, never in what they contain -- so what you debug against is what production emits. It bridges stdlib logging, so Django's own loggers (django.request, django.security, django.db.backends) render the same way as ours, and its bound context is how trace_id, span_id and a request id reach every record without being threaded through call arguments.

The no-dependency alternative -- a logging.Formatter subclass of about sixty lines -- is real and should be weighed, given this repository justifies every dependency it takes. structlog earns it by being one dependency for both renderings rather than two.

RENDERED ON READ, NOT ON WRITE, wherever a collector is watching. In compose and deployed the process writes JSON only, because that is what the collector parses and because Ali asked compose to demonstrate the real arrangement. Readability is then a read-time concern: a small pretty-printer the developer pipes logs through. That way there is one format in the system and no restart to make output legible. Native development, which has no collector and no pipe, defaults to the console renderer.

WHAT THE CONSOLE RENDERING HAS TO DO, because 'colourised' is not a specification. Fixed columns so the eye can follow one down the page: time without the date, a fixed-width level, the logger name truncated FROM THE LEFT so the informative tail survives and the message always starts in the same column, then key=value pairs. Colour only when the stream is a TTY, and NO_COLOR honoured, so piping to grep, less or a file gives clean text. Function entry and exit from inventory-tng-nb8.3 rendered as arrows with depth indentation rather than prose, which is the only way that volume is survivable.

PER-LOGGER LEVELS, which is what separates usable from merely present. DEBUG everywhere means django.db.backends prints every query and the tracer prints every call. An environment variable setting levels per logger -- inventory.sheet=DEBUG,django.db.backends=DEBUG over an INFO default -- lets a developer turn up only the subsystem they are working on.

GUNICORN WRITES ITS OWN ACCESS LOG and will emit plain text beside our JSON, which breaks a collector's parsing. It has to be brought into the same dictConfig.
design:
DECIDED with Ali on 2026-08-23.

TIMESTAMP: full ISO-8601 with offset by default -- 2026-08-23T14:32:07.412-04:00 -- not time-only. The deciding argument is that a container logs UTC while the reader's terminal is not, so a bare time is actively misleading rather than merely terse; a line pasted into a bead should also be self-locating. An environment variable shortens it for anyone who wants the 17 columns back.

WIDTH is a real constraint once the timestamp costs 29 columns: 63 are gone before the message starts. Two mitigations rather than a warning. Indentation from the function tracer caps at a configurable depth (default 8, two spaces each) and shows depth as a number beyond it -- nesting stops being countable by eye at about six anyway. And the layout is chosen from shutil.get_terminal_size(): full at 140 or more, compact below that (time-only, logger trimmed to its last segment), minimal below 100 (no logger column). Forceable by environment variable. Render-on-read helps here: the pretty-printer runs in the reader's terminal and detects the real width, which a process writing into a pipe cannot.

KEY-VALUE CONTEXT IS BOUND, NOT PASSED, which is the answer to keeping it easy. Middleware binds request_id, method, templated path, status, trace_id, span_id and the surrogate user id for the life of a request; the @traced decorator from nb8.3 binds the function and its span; process identity is bound once at startup. A developer writing log.info('something happened') with no keys still gets all of it, and only ever types the keys specific to that line.

The rendering side of the same decision: the console renderer hides always-present keys by default, because request_id repeated on forty lines is noise. One summary line per request carries them; individual records show only their own; a flag shows everything when chasing a correlation.

STRUCTLOG is accepted as the dependency.
acceptance_criteria: A JSON line parses and carries level, logger, message, timestamp, trace_id, span_id. The console rendering is legible in a terminal and colourless when piped. Piping compose's JSON through the pretty-printer is documented and works. Per-logger levels are settable from the environment. gunicorn's access log is in the same format as everything else. Tests cover both renderings.
notes:
NO SILENT ADAPTATION. Ali's constraint, 2026-08-23: output that changes shape on its own without saying so is magic, and a developer must not have to wonder why a colleague's terminal shows a column theirs does not.

So the layout is announced, not merely chosen. At startup the console renderer emits one line naming the detected width, the layout it picked, what that layout drops, and the variable that overrides it -- for example:

  console layout: compact (terminal 118 cols; full needs 140)
  dropped: full timestamp, logger module path.  Override: DJANGO_LOG_LAYOUT=full

It appears once per process at startup, not per record, and only when rendering for a terminal -- never in the JSON stream.

The three layouts, what each drops, and the override belong in DEVELOPERS.md as a table (inventory-tng-nb8.12), so the behaviour is documented rather than discovered. The rule this is an instance of: a developer should always be able to tell why their output looks the way it does.

ADR 0021 IS WRITTEN, AND IT LANDS IN THIS COMMIT. Settled with Ali 2026-08-23. The epic description is currently the only record of fourteen settled decisions, and a bead description is not in the repository: scripts/check-docs.sh cannot see it, and a contributor looking for why the logging is shaped this way will not find it. docs/decisions/0021 holds the decisions; docs/observability.md (nb8.7) describes the system; DEVELOPERS.md (nb8.12) covers reading logs while working. Take care that 0021 argues and the other two describe, or check-docs.sh will object and be right.

TRACE_ID AND SPAN_ID BEFORE THERE IS A TRACER. The acceptance criteria above ask a JSON line to carry trace_id and span_id, but the SDK and opentelemetry-instrumentation-logging arrive in nb8.2, which depends on this issue. The chain is not reversed and should not be: the record shape is decided before anything fills it in. What this issue owes is the FIELD CONTRACT -- a processor that reads the current span context and binds empty values when no SDK is running -- so that nb8.2 makes the fields non-empty without changing the shape of a line. A test here asserts the keys are present and empty; the test that they are populated belongs to nb8.2.
close_reason: structlog pipeline with JSON and console renderers, per-logger levels, gunicorn in the same dictConfig, scripts/pretty-logs, decision 0021

title: The landing gate is not in the repository, and fails open three ways when it is
description:
AGENTS.md now lets an agent merge without asking, and names the recorded review cycle as the condition that makes that safe. That condition rests on .claude/hooks/landing-gate.sh, which is weaker than the rule assumes. All verified:

NOT IN THE REPOSITORY. .gitignore:45 ignores .claude/hooks/, and 'git ls-files .claude/' returns only settings.json and skills. The tracked .claude/settings.json is {"hooks": {}}; the PreToolUse registration lives in gitignored .claude/settings.local.json at an absolute /home/lotia path. A fresh clone, a fork, a CI runner and every .claude/worktrees/agent-* checkout get the permission and none of the mechanism. AGENTS.md is CLAUDE.md, CODEX.md and GEMINI.md by symlink, and Codex and Gemini run no Claude Code hooks at all.

RECORD VERIFIES NOTHING. landing-gate.sh:44-59 stamps whatever head gh reports and writes stages: ["code-review", "simplify"] as a hardcoded literal. An agent that has run no review at all can record and merge.

FAILS OPEN THREE WAYS. set -uo pipefail with no -e. jq missing: deny() emits nothing and exits 0, permitting a merge with no receipt. python3 missing: the matcher's stderr is discarded and an empty verdict is read as nothing-to-guard. gh failing, rate-limited or unauthenticated: pr_head() swallows the error with 2>/dev/null, current is empty, and the head comparison at line 199 is skipped -- so a receipt from a superseded head permits the merge. Nothing surfaces that the gate has stopped working.

BYPASSED BY ORDINARY INDIRECTION. The matcher only sees the literal token gh in command position: gh api -X PUT .../merge, env gh, command gh, /usr/bin/gh, bash -c, and a pipe into xargs all walk past it. The script concedes this ('a guardrail, not a security boundary'), which was a fair trade only while a human ask was the real control. It no longer is.
design: Decide what this is meant to be. As a guardrail against forgetting it is fine as it stands and the rule should not lean on it. As the thing that makes merge-without-asking safe it has to be tracked, wired in .claude/settings.json rather than a gitignored local file, fail closed on every missing dependency, and record evidence that the stages ran rather than a literal. Those are different pieces of work and the first question is which one is wanted.
acceptance_criteria: The gate ships with the repository and is wired in tracked settings; a missing jq, python3 or gh denies rather than permits; record stores evidence rather than a hardcoded literal; a test covers each failure mode. Or: AGENTS.md stops claiming the gate is what makes merging safe.
notes:
VERIFIED AGAINST main, 2026-08-24. Every claim in the description holds:

  git ls-files .claude/     ->  .claude/settings.json and .claude/skills only
  .gitignore:45             ->  .claude/hooks/
  cat .claude/settings.json ->  {"hooks": {}}

So the mechanism AGENTS.md rests its merge-without-asking permission on is not in the repository, and the tracked settings register no hook at all.

AND IT WAS EXERCISED WHILE UNFIXED. Three pull requests were merged on 2026-08-24 -- #20, #21 and #22 -- each on the strength of `landing-gate.sh record`. The cycle genuinely ran on all three, but the gate could not have known: it stamps stages: ["code-review", "simplify"] as a literal and verifies nothing. That is the concrete cost of this issue rather than a hypothetical, and it is worth stating in whatever fixes it.

ONE OPERATIONAL GOTCHA found while using it, worth keeping whatever else changes: `landing-gate.sh record <pr>` must be run as ITS OWN command. Piping it -- `record 22 | tail -2 && gh pr merge ...` -- takes the pipeline's exit status, the record does not take effect, and the merge is then refused with "No review cycle has been recorded", which reads like the record failed rather than like the shell ate it. The script's own message says "Step 5 last, as its own command"; that is why.
close_reason: The gate ships in scripts/, is registered in tracked .claude/settings.json, fails closed on every missing dependency, and records the artifacts it found on the pull request rather than a literal. 37 cases, one per failure mode. Wiring check-setup.sh to verify the interpreter is left to inventory-tng-pg63, which owns that question for the commit hook already.

title: EPIC: OpenTelemetry throughout, and logging as an acceptance criterion for all new work
description:
Read this issue first. It is written to be enough on its own -- no prior conversation is needed to pick up any child.

=== WHAT EXISTS TODAY ===
Nothing. Established by reading the code, not assumed:
- settings.py configures no LOGGING and no ADMINS, so with DEBUG=false Django's default config sends records to a console handler filtered out by require_debug_true and a mail_admins handler with no recipients. Nothing reaches any destination. inventory-tng-zya covers the immediate consequence: every traceback is lost in production.
- There is not one getLogger in the application code.
- DRF configures no logging of its own. It does not arrive with the framework.
- No metrics anywhere. /api/healthz runs a trivial query and says ok.
- The frontend has exactly one console.error, in scan/decodeLoop.ts. It runs in a volunteer's browser and is seen by nobody.
- OpenTelemetry appears in the tree only as a transitive Playwright dev dependency.

=== THE GOAL ===
Extensive telemetry -- logs AND metrics -- over OTLP so any compatible destination can receive it. One request must be followable from a click in the browser through nginx into Django and its queries. New work after the retroactive sweep is expected to be logged and instrumented, checked by tooling rather than by review attention.

=== SETTLED. Do not relitigate these without asking. ===
1. LOGS: structured JSON on stdout, collected externally. Not OTLP direct from the app -- a log written to stdout survives the process dying, kubectl logs keeps working, and no telemetry pipeline sits in the request path.
2. CONSOLE: the same records rendered readably for a terminal. structlog is the accepted dependency: one processor chain, two renderers, so dev and deployed differ only in drawing, never in content.
3. RENDER ON READ where a collector is watching. In compose and deployed the process writes JSON only; readability comes from piping through a pretty-printer in the repo. Native development, which has no collector, defaults to the console renderer.
4. TIMESTAMPS are full ISO-8601 with offset. A container logs UTC while the reader's terminal does not, so a bare time misleads.
5. NO SILENT ADAPTATION. Layout is chosen from terminal width AND announced at startup, naming what was dropped and the override. A developer must never wonder why their console differs from a colleague's.
6. CONTEXT IS BOUND, NOT PASSED. Middleware binds request_id, method, templated path, status, trace_id, span_id and a surrogate user id; @traced binds the function; process identity is bound at startup. A developer writing log.info('x') with no keys still gets all of it.
7. BACKEND SDK starts in a gunicorn post_fork hook, NOT by wrapping the command in opentelemetry-instrument. gunicorn pre-forks and a BatchSpanProcessor's thread does not survive fork, so a master-initialised SDK exports nothing. This is the most common way such a setup silently fails.
8. THE BROWSER EXPORTER posts to a same-origin path proxied by the frontend's nginx. frontend/nginx.conf.template sets connect-src 'self' and that policy is not to be widened.
9. THE DEBUG FLAG sets the W3C sampled bit; a custom sampler honours it. It must NOT be a bare ParentBased sampler -- that hands an unauthenticated client control of what the backend records, and with function-level tracing it is a work-amplification vector. Gated by a signed expiring token (inventory-tng-nb8.4).
10. AT DEBUG, every function invoked is recorded, as spans rather than flat lines.
11. LOGS ARE 100% OF TRAFFIC at INFO. TRACE SAMPLING IS CONFIGURABLE, settled 2026-08-23. The code default is a conservative 10%, so a deployment that sets nothing cannot flood a collector it did not size for. Every configuration this repository ships -- .env.sample, compose, the chart values -- overrides that to 100% explicitly, so the intended behaviour is what runs and the safe behaviour is what happens in its absence. The knob is to be CLEARLY documented: the variable, the default, the shipped value, and how to lower it to sample a subset.
12. NO PERSONAL DATA IN TELEMETRY BY DEFAULT, enforced deny-by-default. IP addresses are personal data. So is a stable identifier for an unauthenticated volunteer -- inventory-tng-jro would mint exactly one, and pseudonymised is not anonymous. AMENDED 2026-08-23, Ali: there is a toggle that admits it again, because an IP address is exactly what somebody debugging a throttle or one volunteer'''s failing request needs, and a mechanism with no way to look is one people work around. Off by default and in every shipped configuration, refused loudly if mistyped, announced at startup, and what it emits is marked so a collector holder can purge it afterwards. The conditions are inventory-tng-nb8.5'''s; the point is that deny-by-default is the resting state rather than the only state.
13. DEPLOYMENT TARGET IS NOT SETTLED. It may be CodeNOW or a Kubernetes cluster NYC Mesh hosts itself on Proxmox. Nothing here may assume a platform that collects container logs for you. A self-hosted cluster is a first-class path.
14. THE HELM CHART DOES NOT RENDER A COLLECTOR. A collector is cluster infrastructure shared by everything on the cluster, not a component of this app. Ship the app, document the collector separately. Recorded here rather than decided again in nb8.7.
15. docs/decisions/0021 IS WRITTEN, settled 2026-08-23. The points above are decisions and belong in the repository, where scripts/check-docs.sh can see them and a contributor can find them without reading a tracker. It lands in the first batch, folded into the nb8.1 commit. Once it exists, 0021 is the record of WHY; docs/observability.md (nb8.7) describes the system; DEVELOPERS.md (nb8.12) covers reading logs while working. Three topics, three homes.

=== STILL OPEN ===
- Which image the dev collector uses. grafana/otel-lgtm is the candidate, not the decision: nb8.6 both verifies it is still current AND researches the alternatives, and asks Ali rather than guessing if it cannot decide between them.
- Current Helm chart names, to be read at implementation time rather than from recall.

=== ORDER ===
Dependencies are wired, so 'bd ready' gives the answer. The chain is zya, then nb8.1, then nb8.2, and everything else hangs off those. Children are prefixed Backend, Frontend, Dev environment, Docs or Both, and labelled.

=== WHY IT MATTERS ===
The probe bug fixed in inventory-tng-adj presented as a crash loop against a healthy database for one reason: DisallowedHost reached no log. That is this epic's absence, priced.
design: Backend: opentelemetry-distro, opentelemetry-exporter-otlp, opentelemetry-instrumentation-django, opentelemetry-instrumentation-psycopg (psycopg 3 -- the psycopg2 package is wrong, backend pins psycopg[binary]==3.3.*), opentelemetry-instrumentation-logging, structlog. Frontend: @opentelemetry/sdk-trace-web, instrumentation-fetch, instrumentation-document-load, exporter-trace-otlp-http. Configuration is the standard OTEL_ environment; no endpoint set means no SDK and no overhead.
notes:
Design agreed with Ali over 2026-08-22 and 2026-08-23. He asked that these
issues be pickable up without the session that produced them, which is why
the description above is long: it is the handover.

WHY CHILDREN LEAVE THIS TREE AS THEY SHIP. A parent-child dependency means
batch membership and nothing else -- DEVELOPERS.md#pull-requests says so and
scripts/check-batch.sh enforces it, refusing a pull request whose landed
issues
are not exactly one epic's children. So an issue cannot be a member of this
epic and of the batch shipping it at the same time, and when a batch is
formed
its issues are re-parented onto a Batch: epic. inventory-tng-pfz0 was the
first,
taking zya, nb8.1 and nb8.12.

Nothing about the design is lost by that. This description is the handover,
and
the depends-on chain between the children is untouched, so bd ready still
gives
the order. What is lost is the tree: read the ORDER section rather than the
child list once batches start shipping. Worth Ali revisiting if the tree
turns
out to be the thing people actually navigate by.

=== THE SWEEP IS DONE, 2026-08-24 ===

Every child this epic planned has shipped. In order: zya, nb8.1 and nb8.12 in
batch pfz0; nb8.2, nb8.4, nb8.5, nb8.6, nb8.7 and the iqff follow-ups in the
batches between; and nb8.9, nb8.3, nb8.8, nb8.10 and nb8.11 in batch hqi8,
merged as PR #20. The ORDER section above is now history rather than a plan.

WHAT THE LAST BATCH COST, because it is the honest measure of the design. Its
review found 23 defects and /simplify found 20 more. The pattern worth carrying
forward: nearly every review finding was a place where a docstring or a decision
record stated a guarantee the code did not keep -- 'always, from every device',
'NOTHING RUNS UNLESS A TOKEN IS HELD', 'does NOT count against the token's rate
limit'. The prose was the specification and it ran about a dozen places ahead of
the code. Three of the sharpest were invisible to the tests because the test
drove Django's Client rather than the WSGI application that actually charges,
which is the iqff.1 defect recurring; when asserting something a wrapper outside
Django does, drive inventory_tng.wsgi.application.

WHAT REMAINS ARE FOUR FOLLOW-UPS, all raised by /simplify against PR #20 and
deferred from it deliberately: nb8.15 (the debug flag expiring does not stop the
SDK -- a defect, and the sharpest of the four), nb8.16, nb8.17 and nb8.18. Each
carries its own argument. Nothing depends on anything else, so bd ready gives
the order and priority is the only thing separating them.

The epic stays open only to hold those four.

title: Every traceback is lost in production: Django's default logging has nowhere to send them
description:
settings.py configures no LOGGING and no ADMINS, so Django's DEFAULT_LOGGING applies. Its two handlers are mutually exclusive by design:

- console  -- filter require_debug_true
- mail_admins -- filter require_debug_false, and needs ADMINS

DEBUG must be false in production, so console is filtered out; ADMINS is empty, so AdminEmailHandler sends nothing. Every record on the django logger and its children therefore reaches no destination at all.

CONSEQUENCE. django.request logs unhandled exceptions at ERROR with exc_info. In production that traceback is written nowhere. What a deployment actually sees is gunicorn's access line -- 'POST /api/... 500' -- with no stack, no exception type, and no request context. The same silence hid DisallowedHost for the whole of inventory-tng-adj: verified by putting a bad Host to the real settings module with DEBUG=False, which answers 400 and writes nothing.

Also lost: django.security.* (host and CSRF failures), django.db.backends warnings, and anything the application logs once it starts logging.

This is scoped deliberately small -- give Django a LOGGING block that writes structured records to stdout, where a container runtime can collect them, and cover it with a test. The full telemetry story is a separate piece of work and should not hold this up.
acceptance_criteria: A LOGGING setting sends WARNING and above -- including django.request tracebacks and django.security -- to stdout with DEBUG=False. A test asserts a traceback reaches a handler under DEBUG=False. docs/deployment.md says where a deployment reads them.
notes:
READ inventory-tng-nb8 FIRST. This issue is the first move in that epic, and doing it without the epic risks solving it twice: nb8.1 immediately follows with structlog, a JSON renderer and a readable console rendering, so the LOGGING block written here should be the shape that grows into that rather than a formatter thrown away a week later.

The minimum this issue owes on its own: with DEBUG=false, a django.request traceback and a django.security record both reach stdout. Everything about renderers, structure and terminal layout belongs to nb8.1.

Kept as a separate issue because it is a live production bug -- tracebacks are being lost now -- and should not wait behind the design of the rest.
close_reason: LOGGING configured in settings.py via inventory_tng.logs; tests in test_logging.py; docs/deployment.md#reading-the-logs

title: Deleting an item or a location destroys stickers already on shelves
description:
Found by an inventory administrator reading guides/administrator.md on 2026-08-22.

Label.item and Label.location are on_delete=CASCADE, while StockMovement's links are PROTECT. So an item or location that has never moved stock CAN be deleted from Django's admin -- the red Delete button is on both pages, since only AppendOnlyAdmin and StagedAdmin refuse deletion -- and doing so silently destroys every Label row pointing at it.

Those codes are printed on stickers that are already on shelves. The code is opaque, so it cannot be worked out again, and Label.code is unique and unchangeable by design. Scanning one afterwards resolves to nothing, for ever.

The guide said 'there is no delete, and there should not be'. It was wrong about the button and right about the intent; it has been corrected to warn instead. This issue is the guard that should make the warning unnecessary.

FIX, to be argued: PROTECT rather than CASCADE, or refuse deletion in the admin for any row a live label points at, so that retiring is the only way out. Whichever, it needs a test that a label survives an attempt on the item it names.
close_reason: Both of a label's foreign keys are PROTECT, so a row a sticker names cannot be deleted out from under it.

title: An item's search does not read its identifiers, so the table does nothing
description:
Found twice on 2026-08-22, independently: by the rule-1 codebase survey for inventory-tng-65l, and by an inventory administrator reading guides/administrator.md and trying to act on it.

ItemFilter.search in backend/src/inventory/views.py is CharFilter(field_name='name', lookup_expr='icontains'). ItemIdentifier is imported by no serializer and no view; there is no endpoint that returns one. A scan resolves a LABEL code, not an identifier.

So the whole point of the identifier table -- 'a volunteer types what they call the thing and it resolves' -- is not true of the app a volunteer uses. It is true only of Django's admin, whose ItemAdmin.search_fields includes identifiers__value.

That makes docs/data-model.md's 'a scan or a typed string resolves to exactly one item' a statement about an intention. guides/administrator.md said the same thing and has been corrected to what is true today; this issue is the code that would make the original sentence honest.

DEPENDS ON THE RULE 1 DESIGN. inventory-tng-65l decision 6 already settled how this has to be indexed: add text_pattern_ops on the normalised column and lower the search term in Python before querying with __startswith, because Django's __istartswith compiles to UPPER(col) LIKE UPPER(...) and matches no index. Decision 5 -- search identifiers, display items -- is the rule this implements, and the survey named the two guard tests that must come with it, since nothing currently stops a future annotation leaking a raw identifier value into a pulldown.
notes:
VERIFIED AGAINST main, 2026-08-24, and unchanged:

  views.py:932  search = CharFilter(field_name="name", lookup_expr="icontains")
  grep ItemIdentifier across serializers.py and views.py -> no hits at all

So the identifier table is reachable only through Django's admin, exactly as the description says, and nothing a volunteer or an administrator uses in the app reads it.

WORTH KNOWING BEFORE STARTING: inventory-tng-6kyb (raised 2026-08-24) is about ItemIdentifier.item still being CASCADE, so deleting an item destroys its identifiers. That is a different fault, but it touches the same model and carries an open decision -- whether the guard covers every kind or only the printed ones (barcode, legacy_nycm) and not alias. If both are done together, decide that once.
DOCS THAT MOVE WITH THIS, noted in the simplify pass on PR 38 so neither is discovered late:

- docs/data-model.md says 'A scan or a typed string resolves to exactly one item'. Rule 2 means that sentence becomes true in this change or is corrected in it.
- guides/administrator.md was already corrected to what is true today -- 'its search reads item names and nothing else, and nothing there ever shows an identifier' -- and carries an interim instruction ('Until it is closed, add the identifier AND check that the item's own name is one somebody would think to type') plus a naming of this bead. All three go back when this lands.

Decision 5 of docs/decisions/0026-what-makes-two-strings-one-identifier.md is the rule this implements and decision 6 is how it must be indexed.
SEARCHES BOTH, DISPLAYS NAMES -- settled in decision 5 of docs/decisions/0026-what-makes-two-strings-one-identifier.md rather than left to this bead, because reading the rule the other way is a regression.

An item created through the app has no ItemIdentifier row at all (inventory-tng-w4dg). So a search that consulted identifiers INSTEAD of Item.name would make every item added in the app permanently unfindable, with no route in the interface to repair it. Searching both is safe whether or not w4dg is ever done; searching identifiers alone is safe only after it.

Decision 5 is about what is OFFERED, not what is matched: one product appears three times because three labels are drawn, not because three strings were searched. ItemAdmin already searches name and identifiers__value together while displaying name.

REQUIRED TEST, and it is the assertion that would have caught this: create an item through the API with exactly the fields frontend/src/admin/CreateItem.tsx sends -- name, category, unit_of_measure, minimum_stock, reorder_quantity, and no identifier -- and then find it by typing its name. Nothing asserts that today.
A TEST THAT BELONGS HERE, moved out of inventory-tng-udz6.4 during the simplify pass on PR 39 because it could not fail before this bead lands.

'One item appears once however many identifiers it has' -- three strings meaning one thing must not become three rows to choose between. While ItemFilter searches Item.name only, the identifiers a test creates are read by nothing and the assertion is indistinguishable from the plain name-search test three tests above it. It becomes a real assertion the moment search reads identifiers, and a join over identifiers is exactly what produces the duplicates, so write it as part of this.

The guard that DID land in udz6.4 is test_the_item_list_never_answers_with_an_identifier_value, in test_catalogue_api.py: it mints a mis-cased identifier and scans the response recursively, substring-wise, so a composed label like 'LiteBeam (litebeam)' fails it. Keep it passing.

title: Publish the images, and let the chart pull them
description:
Found by a deployment review on 2026-08-22, following docs/deployment.md as somebody with a namespace and no other knowledge.

docs/deployment.md says 'helm upgrade --install ... --set image.tag=v0.1.0' and the chart renders ghcr.io/lotia/nycmesh-inventory-tng-backend:v0.1.0. Nothing in this repository has ever pushed an image: both CI image jobs use 'push: false', there are no git tags, and no workflow logs into a registry. So the migrate hook Job goes ErrImagePull, Helm blocks until --timeout, and the release fails.

Worse if the package is private: 'grep -rn imagePullSecret infra/helm/' returns nothing, so there is no way to supply a pull secret without editing the chart.

Also worth settling: ghcr.io/lotia is a personal namespace shipped as the default for an organisation's inventory system.

FIX: publish on tag, add imagePullSecrets to both Deployments and the Job, and give docs/deployment.md the build-and-push step it does not have.

title: Liveness probes the database, so a brief outage kills every pod
description:
Found by a deployment review on 2026-08-22.

backend-deployment.yaml points BOTH probes at /api/healthz, and that view executes SELECT 1. Readiness should: a pod that cannot reach the database should leave the Service. Liveness should not.

A managed PostgreSQL failover taking 70 seconds fails liveness three times at periodSeconds 20, so the kubelet kills every backend pod at once. They restart into a still-recovering database, fail again, and back off exponentially. A one-minute blip becomes a fifteen-minute outage with no pods running, and whoever is paged sees CrashLoopBackOff against a database that is by then perfectly healthy.

FIX: liveness must prove only that the process is alive. Keep /api/healthz on readiness. docs/deployment.md 'Health checks' presently states the database check as a feature and warns of nothing, so it changes with the chart.
notes:
VERIFIED AGAINST main, 2026-08-24, and unchanged:

  infra/helm/inventory-tng/templates/backend-deployment.yaml:41-46
    livenessProbe  -> /api/healthz, initialDelaySeconds 10, periodSeconds 20
  :47-52
    readinessProbe -> /api/healthz, initialDelaySeconds 5,  periodSeconds 10

  views.py:145  HealthCheckView.get runs `SELECT 1`

Both probes hit the endpoint that touches the database. With the default failureThreshold of 3 and periodSeconds 20, roughly 60 seconds of database unavailability kills every backend pod at once.

CRITICAL, BUT CONDITIONALLY: nothing is deployed and the target is not settled (see the deployment-target memory), so this cannot bite today. It becomes critical the moment anything runs on a cluster, and it is a chart change rather than application work -- which makes it cheap to do before that happens rather than during an incident.

docs/deployment.md's "Health checks" presently states the database check as a feature and warns of nothing, so it changes with the chart.
close_reason: Liveness asks /api/livez, which touches nothing; readiness keeps /api/healthz and its query. The chart says which and why, and writes out the arithmetic a restart depends on.

title: Batch: setup, the two user guides, and the checks that keep them true
description:
The documentation batch: inventory-tng-61c (setup instructions for a developer and for an administrator), inventory-tng-pfw (a guide for volunteers and one for inventory administrators, with generated screenshots) and inventory-tng-a1k (the mechanism that fails the build when either goes stale).

Batched because a1k is the check over what the other two write, and because all three are read by the same person in the same sitting: somebody who has just been handed this system.
close_reason: All children completed

title: Make the setup and user guides fail the build when they go stale
description:
A separate bead rather than a line in each of the other two, because it is one mechanism serving both and because it is the part most likely to be dropped if it rides along.

THE PROBLEM IS NOT NEW HERE AND THE REPOSITORY ALREADY KNOWS IT. CLAUDE.md's second non-negotiable rule is that documentation changes with the code, and DEVELOPERS.md says of its own setup guide: 'This guide is expected to work. If a command here fails on a clean machine, that is a bug in the guide.' Nothing checks either claim. Three review passes across three batches found hand-written figures that no longer matched anything, and the answer that worked -- inventory-tng-o86.2 -- was not a rule but a test: it reads the fenced blocks out of docs/briefs/sheet-classifiers.md and fails when a block's labels are no longer the ones its code emits. That is the pattern to copy, twice.

FOR THE SETUP INSTRUCTIONS: execute them. The commands are already in fenced bash blocks, so the same trick applies -- extract them and run them on a clean machine in CI. A guide whose commands are run on every push cannot rot silently, and the failure names the line that is wrong. Decide how far this goes: the developer path is a container away and is plainly automatable; the administrator path needs a cluster and may only be checkable as far as 'helm template renders and the values the document names exist'. Say which parts are covered and which are not, in the document, so a reader knows which half has been proven.

FOR THE USER GUIDES: the screenshots are the perishable part, and they perish silently -- a renamed button leaves a picture that is merely wrong, with nothing failing. Two candidate mechanisms, and the bead should choose with reasons: regenerate the screenshots in CI and fail if they differ, which catches everything but is noisy on any pixel change; or assert that the elements the guide describes still exist, by driving the same Playwright scene and checking each label and control the guide names, which is quieter and catches the change that matters. The second is probably right, and it composes with the first being run on demand.

THE THIRD THING, and the one a checker cannot do: neither guide should be able to describe a role that no longer exists or omit a flow that now does. That is a review question, so it belongs in the Definition of Done rather than in CI -- and DEVELOPERS.md#definition-of-done is the single place to say it.

Do not build a documentation framework. Two tests and a CI job, in the shape the repository already uses.
acceptance_criteria: A change that breaks a documented setup command fails the build and names the command. A change that renames or removes a control the user guide describes fails the build and names the control. The Definition of Done says which documents a change has to be weighed against, and the guides themselves say which parts of them are machine-checked.
close_reason: Closed

title: A user guide for volunteers, and one for inventory administrators
description:
Two roles, two documents, because the two share almost nothing. Both as short as they can be and no shorter.

THE VOLUNTEER'S GUIDE covers one flow and its edges: scan a printed QR code, build a cart, save it, and know what happened. The edges are where a guide earns its keep -- what a per-line complaint means and how to fix one line without losing the rest; what the warning 'worth a stock count' is telling them; and the outbox, which is new and which nobody will guess at. A batch saved with no signal is held, the cart comes back empty so the next armful can be scanned, and the held batch is drawn at the top of the screen until it is in or refused. Decision 0011's amendment says why it works that way. Also worth a line: every printed QR opens the form preset to Checking Out, so returning something is not the same gesture as taking it.

THE INVENTORY ADMINISTRATOR'S GUIDE covers the things only they can do: the catalogue and what an identifier is for (a volunteer types what they call the thing, and it resolves); volunteers, and specifically merging duplicates -- a merge sets merged_into, leaves the ledger untouched, and is how the import's flagged rows get settled; the sheet_flag column on a volunteer and the one on an item, both of which are questions the import could not answer and which are answered by being emptied; locations; printing labels; and reading a balance, including that it is derived from movements and never stored.

SCREENSHOTS. Take them with the Playwright setup that already exists rather than by hand: playwright.config.ts, frontend/integration/, and seed_integration_data, which exists precisely to give the browser suite a fixed scene. A script that drives the seeded scene and captures each step is the mechanism, and it means the screenshots can be regenerated rather than re-taken. Run it headless.

FORMAT. Markdown under docs/, consistent with everything else here, with the images committed beside them. Two things to decide rather than assume: where the images live and what that does to the size of the repository, and whether the guides belong under docs/ with the architecture and the decisions or somewhere a non-developer would think to look. The reader of these two documents is not the reader of the rest of docs/, and that is worth a moment's thought.

Keep them succinct. The existing documentation in this repository is discursive because its audience is people changing the code; these two are for people using it while standing at a shelf.
design: Depends on inventory-tng-24q for the import's flags, which the administrator's guide has to explain, and on the offline outbox from inventory-tng-ykw, which is already on main.
acceptance_criteria: A volunteer who has never seen the system can complete a scan-and-save, including a failure and a save with no signal, by following the guide alone. An inventory administrator can resolve an import's flagged volunteers and items, print a label, and read a balance the same way. Every screenshot is generated by a script that can be re-run.
close_reason: Closed

title: Setup instructions a developer and an administrator can each follow start to finish
description:
Two audiences, and the current documentation serves neither completely.

A DEVELOPER running it locally. DEVELOPERS.md already has three options (all-in-Docker, native with Postgres in a container, devcontainer) and they broadly work, but a developer who follows them lands on an empty database: no catalogue, no items, no volunteers, no labels. The only seed that exists is seed_integration_data, which is deliberately gated behind an acknowledgement flag because it creates a login whose password is published in this repository -- correct for the Playwright suite and wrong as a general starting point. So the first honest thing to fix is that there is nothing to look at.

The compose setup should be MINIMALLY PRIVILEGED and should be seen to be. Worth deciding and documenting: rootless podman as a first-class path (the images are already fully qualified so it resolves without extra configuration), a non-root user in the container, a read-only root filesystem where it will hold, dropped capabilities, and no privileged ports. Whatever is chosen, the compose file should show it rather than a comment claiming it.

AN ADMINISTRATOR deploying to staging or production. docs/deployment.md and infra/helm/inventory-tng exist. What is not written down as a followable sequence is the bootstrap: which environment variables have no default and why (DJANGO_SECRET_KEY is the pattern -- see docs/architecture.md), how the migrate Job relates to the web pods, how the first administrator account comes into being, and that decision 0013 requires a second factor on the local password path so the very first sign-in cannot complete without an authenticator app. That last one is exactly the kind of step that is obvious to whoever built it and a wall to everybody else.

BOOTSTRAPPING THAT IS NOT AUTOMATED, to be enumerated honestly and then judged one by one: mise trust and mise install; copying .env.sample; the Postgres 18 volume note for anyone who ran this before August 2026; creating a superuser; enrolling that superuser's second factor; and now the sheet import, which is five commands in a required order (stage_sheet, mint_items, import_volunteers, post_ledger) or the one that composes them, import_sheet.

WEIGH AUTOMATING IT TO ONE COMMAND. The bar is that it composes commands that already exist rather than becoming a framework of its own. A script that runs mise install, writes .env from the sample, brings up Postgres, migrates, creates an administrator, seeds a small honest catalogue and prints the URL and what to do next is a good trade. A bespoke installer with its own configuration language is not. If the answer is that some step genuinely cannot be automated -- and the second factor may be one -- the script should say so at the point the human has to act, rather than the documentation saying it somewhere else.

The audience for the result includes end users too, indirectly: a volunteer or an inventory administrator meets this system only if somebody could stand it up.
design: Depends on nothing, but should be written AFTER inventory-tng-24q lands, because the import commands it has to document are part of that batch.
acceptance_criteria: A developer with neither the repository nor the toolchain can go from a clone to a working system with something in it, and an administrator can go from an empty cluster to a first sign-in, each by following one document without asking anybody. Every bootstrap step that is not automated is named in the place the reader needs it, and the decision not to automate it is stated.
close_reason: Closed

title: The importer bead still specifies from retracted figures
description:
inventory-tng-2dg gained all six classifier dependencies, and its own description still specifies the import from three figures the batch retracted.

It says '41 match nothing today ... Each becomes an ItemIdentifier row'. The brief re-partitions those: nine are case-only variants that already resolve under the sheet's case-insensitive lookup, and 32 match nothing. Minting 41 aliases would create nine rows for strings that were never broken, in the system built to stop strings being identity.

It says '~18.7% of rows are corrections, and must import as adjustments'. The brief records that 18.7% reproduces under no rule tried and that its original method is unrecorded.

It says '102 name spellings across 65 emails', which reads as a headcount and is not one.

It also points at docs/data-model.md#migrating-the-existing-sheet for a breakdown that has moved to the brief. The commit that swept 8sq and o5t for retracted figures missed the one bead the six classifiers were filed to unblock.
acceptance_criteria: 2dg states no retracted figure, cites the brief for anything rule-dependent, and its alias sizing matches the brief's partition.
close_reason: 2dg now cites the brief for each rule-dependent figure and sizes the alias table from the partition rather than from the retracted 41.

title: Move classifier-dependent figures out of decision 0008
description:
Decision 0008's Context carried eleven figures, and three review passes over one batch each found some of them unreproducible -- including two the corrections themselves introduced. The pattern is structural rather than careless: a derived statistic living as prose in a decision record has no method attached, so nobody can re-run it and everybody quotes it.

Four of the five Context bullets need a rule before they can be counted at all: which strings are unresolvable, which notes are corrections, which name a place, which name a job. Those rules are not documentation. Each is a decision the sheet importer must make about every historical row, so the rule and the figure it produces belong together and belong with the code.

0008 keeps only what needs no rule -- 52 items, 3,439 submissions, 2,455 against 984, 145 item strings, 102 name spellings -- and links to docs/briefs/sheet-classifiers.md for the rest. The brief states each rule beside its figure and names the command that will emit it.
acceptance_criteria: Decision 0008 states no figure that requires a classifier, the brief holds each rule beside the number it produces, and every claim the strip-down contradicted elsewhere in the record is corrected in the same change.
notes:
Six classifiers filed (2xb, e1p, 6gm, utc, a82, 5r2), each blocking both inventory-tng-2dg and the reporting command inventory-tng-6s9. The one thing no classifier can recover -- whether hardware came back -- is recorded as a non-goal on inventory-tng-8sq so it is not attempted a third time.

--- FOURTH REVIEW PASS APPLIED 2026-08-21 ---

Six defects, all in the restructure rather than in the figures, all fixed here: 0008 claimed the brief states each rule when four of six sections record that no rule is settled; the population definition was stripped out of 0008 along with the classifier figures and has been restored to the Context where the counts depending on it live, with the brief linking rather than repeating; the brief filed 145 item strings and 102 name spellings under 'needs no rule' when both are counts of distinct strings whose thing-count needs a case rule; the mesh-room figures were quoted without the compound predicate that produces them, and three plausible readings differ by 12%; kx6's notes blamed the burst gap on the submitter key when it is set entirely by the windowing rule; and two classifiers blocking P2 work were filed at P3.
close_reason: 0008 keeps only classifier-free counts; the rules and their figures live in docs/briefs/sheet-classifiers.md, and the six classifiers plus the reporting command are filed under the sheet-classifier label.

title: Re-verify every figure in decision 0008 against the workbook
description:
Decision 0008's Context is the project's most-cited evidence: the item-string mess, the check-out imbalance, the corrections share and the notes-field overloading are all quoted from it, into beads, into the stakeholder guide, and into arguments that have already changed the design once.

Four figures outside the record were checked in the course of inventory-tng-2zx and three were wrong -- a claimed 54% of check-outs carrying a note is 61%, a claimed 13% naming a node is nearer 5%, and a zip-tie distribution was out on every row. The fourth is inside 0008 itself: the Context says 'Sean mesh room 131 broome st alone accounts for 175 submissions' and that exact string appears 97 times, with roughly 156 across four spellings of the same room.

That is a poor enough hit rate that the remaining figures cannot be assumed. Each one in Context and Consequences gets reproduced from ignored/NYC Mesh - Inventory Sheet.xlsx or corrected: the 52 items and 3,439 submissions, the 145 distinct item strings and the 41 matching nothing at 160 occurrences, the 52 retired NYCM codes, 102 spellings of 65 people, 1,557 rows without an email, 2,455 check-outs against 984 check-ins, 18.7% corrections with its four enumerated counts, 136 submissions citing an NN number across 62 distinct, the 175 above, and the Consequences claim that 76% of submissions fall inside a ten-minute burst with a largest of 24.

The denominator needs settling first: the workbook's QRresponses tab holds 3,456 data rows against the record's 3,439, and every percentage depends on which filter produced the smaller number.
acceptance_criteria: Every numeric claim in decision 0008 is either reproduced from the workbook by a stated method or corrected in the record, and the method is written down so the next reader can re-run it rather than trusting the number.
notes:
VERIFICATION COMPLETE 2026-08-21. Every numeric claim in decision 0008 was counted against the QRresponses tab of the export. The population question is settled: 3,439 is the rows carrying a direction, 2,455 Checking Out plus 984 Checking In, with 17 further rows having neither. That is now stated in the record so the next reader does not have to rediscover it.
