DRF answers a FIELD refusal with a field-keyed map and no detail at all -- {"name": ["item with this name already exists."]} -- which is what POST /api/items sends for the commonest mistake there is, Item.name being unique. So an administrator who types a name already in the catalogue is told a number, and so is every field refusal EditItem can provoke: a negative minimum stock, a reorder quantity of zero, a category that would make a loop.

IT WILL GET WORSE BEFORE IT GETS BETTER. inventory-tng-2oba.2 adds location and category writes, whose refusals are almost all field ones -- location_held_by_iff_custody, the tree-cycle guard, the unique name within a parent. inventory-tng-2oba.4 adds merging, where the sentence that matters most is a NON-field error: "X still holds the custody location 'Y'. Move the stock recorded there and retire it, or hand it to somebody else, before merging or retiring them." guides/administrator.md warns an administrator about that exact case, and the app would answer it with "The inventory service answered 400."

WHAT TO DO. Widen detailOf to read the shapes DRF actually sends, in one place rather than in each screen: a string detail where there is one; otherwise the messages under non_field_errors; otherwise the messages under the fields, which is what names the field the person has to go back to. The batch endpoint keeps its own shape (BatchRejectedSerializer) and is not this -- SubmitBar reads errors[] itself and must go on doing so.

WHAT TO PIN. A test per shape, in api/client.test.ts, and one in administrator.test.tsx that refuses a create with the body the server really sends rather than one carrying detail. That second one is the point: the existing test "says the other kind of no as a sentence" stubs a detail body, so it is green over a screen that says nothing.
close_reason: Closed

title: The app carries a device token and never acts on what the server says about it
description:
Raised by the simplify pass on PR #34 and filed rather than folded in: the
server half is inventory-tng-t9of and it landed complete, and this is a client
change that could not have been written before it.

WHAT IS THERE. frontend/src/device/credential.ts mints once from main.tsx and
api/client.ts sends X-Device on every request. GET /api/me answers a "device"
field with one of four words -- none, enrolled, revoked, unknown -- and NOTHING
IN THE APP READS IT. frontend/src/api/capabilities.ts's Me type does not even
declare the field.

THREE THINGS TO DO, and they are separable:

1. ACT ON "unknown". This means the browser is holding a string this server has
stopped honouring -- a key rotated away from, a row deleted, a mangled copy.
credential.forget() already exists, is exported, and is imported by nothing;
calling it on this answer and letting the next load mint again is the whole
fix. Without it the browser presents a dead string for ever and the attribution
this feature exists for is silently off for that device.

2. SAY SOMETHING ON "revoked". inventory_tng/devices.py and
permissions.DeviceNotRevoked both argue that a wall and a "this device was
removed" want opposite screens, and the server does its half: the refusal
carries code=device_revoked rather than the general forbidden, and /api/me
answers before anything has been refused. The client draws neither. Decide what
it draws -- a sentence with a way to enrol again is the obvious one -- and do
NOT replace the app with a gate: a revoked device still holds a batch in the
outbox, and losing that is the thing this system exists not to do.

3. SEND THE HEADER ON THE FAILURE-REPORT PATH. frontend/src/telemetry/report.ts
posts to /api/client-failures with a bare fetch and debugHeaders() rather than
through api/client.ts, so no X-Device arrives -- and that endpoint is the ONE
place in this API that reaches AppendThrottle.get_ident today, being the only
one that names AllowAny. So the per-device bucket inventory-tng-t9of built
cannot apply anywhere it is currently reachable. AppendThrottle.get_ident says
so in its own docstring and names this bead. Check why report.ts avoids the
client first -- it may be deliberate, to keep a report from recursing through
the thing that reports failures -- and if it is, carry the one header rather
than routing the call.

WHAT TO PIN: a test that a browser told "unknown" stops sending the old token,
and one that a revoked device still sees its held batch.

title: The admin still deletes an ItemIdentifier, which frees a string 6kyb protected
description:
Found by the review of PR #33, and its own issue because it predates that batch.

ItemIdentifierInline sits on the item change form and ItemIdentifierAdmin
(backend/src/inventory/admin.py) is registered as a plain SimpleHistoryAdmin, so
an identifier can be removed from either place. Nothing stops it: no model holds
a foreign key to ItemIdentifier, so nothing PROTECTs it.

WHY THAT MATTERS AND IS NOT MERELY UNTIDY. item_identifier_unique_normalised_value
makes the normalised string unique across the table, so removing a row FREES the
string. It can then be typed against a different item, and a barcode already
printed on an object -- or a label already on a shelf whose scan resolves through
it -- afterwards answers with the wrong item rather than with nothing. That is the
exact harm inventory-tng-6kyb made ItemIdentifier.item PROTECT to prevent, and
guides/administrator.md states it in those words. Answering wrongly is worse than
answering nothing, which is why this is P2 and ls6d is P3.

SIBLING, NOT DUPLICATE: inventory-tng-ls6d is the same shape on Label, and
inventory-tng-k2sg is the same shape on Item and is done. All three want the same
helper by now -- k2sg wrote has_delete_permission plus a get_actions that drops
delete_selected by name, and a third copy of that pair is the point at which it
should be extracted rather than retyped.

ARGUE IT RATHER THAN SWEEPING: k2sg was explicit that each model is its own
argument. The argument here has a wrinkle k2sg did not: an identifier typed
against the WRONG item is a real thing an administrator must be able to undo, and
today deleting it is how. So the fix is probably not a bare refusal -- it may be
that correcting the item field is the supported move and the delete is what goes,
or that a delete is right and the inline is not. Decide it, and say which in
guides/administrator.md's Delete section, which now carries decision 0024 beside
it.

WHAT TO PIN: whatever is decided, a test that the chosen path is the only one, and
a line in the guide. MAY_CASCADE in tests/test_models.py is where a deliberate
destruction is recorded with its reason.
close_reason: Closed

title: The frontend suite fails on node 26, and nothing says which node to use
description:
Two halves of one snag, hit on 2026-08-25 by an agent running the frontend
suite in a shell that had the system's node rather than this project's.

THE FAILURE. `npm test` under node 26 fails roughly 247 of 410 tests with
`Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'clear')` -- `window.localStorage`
undefined under jsdom 30. It fails identically on unmodified `main`, so it is
environmental rather than any branch's defect. mise.toml pins `node = "24"`,
CI pins 24 in two places in ci.yml, and frontend/Dockerfile builds on
`node:24-bookworm-slim`, so nothing that matters is currently broken -- this is
a trap for whoever's shell resolves node differently, and it cost an agent a
run to work out.

A LEAD RATHER THAN A DIAGNOSIS, and it needs reproducing before it is believed:
jsdom exposes `localStorage` only for a non-opaque origin, so a missing
`environmentOptions.url` on the vitest environment is the usual cause of it
being `undefined`. Why node 26 surfaces it and node 24 does not is the part
actually worth finding out, because the answer decides whether this is a
one-line config fix or a dependency bump.

ORDER MATTERS AND IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE OBVIOUS ONE. Do not raise the pin
first. The failure IS on 26, so pinning to 26 spreads it to CI and to every
contributor instead of fixing it. Fix the suite, prove it green on 24 AND on
26, and only then decide whether the pin moves. Node is a build and test
dependency only -- decision 0002 and frontend/Dockerfile's own comment, "There
is no Node runtime in production" -- so the pin has no production consequence
either way, which is an argument for being relaxed about moving it and none at
all for moving it first.

THE SECOND HALF, and it is the cheaper one: nothing in DEVELOPERS.md tells a
contributor what to do when their shell has the wrong node. `mise exec -- npm
test` works from any shell regardless of whether mise has activated in it, and
that sentence belongs beside the test command it rescues. mise.toml already
carries a `[tasks]` block, so a task is the other option and probably the
better one.

SCOPE, EXPLICITLY: the fix stays inside this repository. The project owner has
asked that nothing outside the repository root be changed -- no shell
configuration, no PATH, no mise global state. `mise exec --` is the answer for
exactly that reason.
design:
FIVE WAYS TO FIX THIS PER-REPOSITORY, since the project owner has ruled out a
system-wide PATH change: they want the toolchain controlled per repository, not
globally. All of these live inside this repository root. Measured 2026-08-25.

1. `[settings] activate_aggressive = true` IN THIS REPOSITORY'S mise.toml.
   VERIFIED, and it is the direct answer. mise has a setting for exactly this
   failure -- it pushes a tool's bin path to the FRONT of PATH rather than
   letting later modifications win. Measured with it set in the project file:

       node install dir  position 18 -> 4
       /usr/bin          position  7 -> 19
       mise exec -- sh -c 'node --version'   v26.7.0 -> v24.19.0

   That last line is the one that matters: it is the child-process case, which
   is what an npm script and vitest spawning node both are.

   NOT FULLY PROVEN: this was measured through `mise env` and `mise exec`, which
   is what the tooling and CI use. Whether a BARE `npm test` in an interactive
   shell that activated mise before entering the directory also picks it up
   depends on the activation hook re-reading project settings on a directory
   change. Likely, since the hook calls `mise env`, but it was not tested and
   must not be claimed. One command in an interactive shell settles it.

   Worth arguing in the commit rather than slipping in: a repository asserting
   a mise setting overrides a preference on the contributor's machine. The case
   for it is that it only reorders THIS project's own pinned tools ahead of
   system ones, which is what pinning them was for.

2. THE `engines` RANGE CURRENTLY PERMITS THE BROKEN VERSION. frontend/
   package.json says `"node": ">=24"`, so node 26 satisfies it and npm says
   nothing. Narrowing it to `"24.x"` and adding `.npmrc` with
   `engine-strict=true` makes `npm ci` refuse. Cheap, and it is a layer rather
   than a fix: engine-strict gates INSTALL, not `npm test`, so it catches a
   fresh clone and not the case that actually bit.

3. A PREFLIGHT ON THE TEST SCRIPT, and this is the one that makes the failure
   legible for good. A `pretest` reading `process.version` against the pinned
   major and exiting with ONE line -- "this repository pins node 24, you are on
   26" -- turns 247 unexplained `localStorage` failures into a sentence.
   Independent of mise, of PATH, of whose machine it is, and it works in CI.
   It costs a dozen lines and it is the difference between a minute and an
   afternoon, which this has now cost two agents in one day.

4. FIX THE UNDERLYING INCOMPATIBILITY, which is the main body of this bead and
   the only option that makes the mismatch stop MATTERING. The pin is still
   wanted for reproducibility afterwards, but nobody loses a run to it.

5. ALREADY IN THE REPOSITORY AND WORTH NAMING: .devcontainer/devcontainer.json
   exists, and mise.toml pins `devcontainer-cli`. A container is the maximal
   per-repository toolchain and needs no new mechanism at all. Heavy for a test
   run; the right answer for somebody who wants no local toolchain.

RULED OUT, so nobody re-derives them:

* `mise run` with a task in mise.toml -- a task inherits the same environment,
  so it has the same defect unless 1 is done. Fixing 1 fixes tasks for free.
* direnv with a committed `.envrc` -- genuinely per-repository, but it is a new
  dependency and a `direnv allow` on every clone to reach the same place 1
  reaches with three lines already-installed mise reads.

RECOMMENDED: 1 and 3 together, with 4 as the actual repair and 2 folded in
while package.json is open. 1 makes it work for anybody using mise; 3 makes it
explain itself for everybody else, for ever.
notes:
MEASURED ON THE OWNER'S MACHINE, 2026-08-25, correcting this bead as first
written. It said `mise exec -- npm test` works from any shell. IT DOES NOT, and
the reason matters because it makes the obvious workarounds fail too.

    mise exec -- node --version            -> v24.19.0
    mise exec -- sh -c 'node --version'    -> v26.7.0

`mise exec -- <tool>` resolves the tool itself and is right. Anything that
re-does a PATH lookup in a child process -- a shell, an npm script, vitest
spawning node -- is wrong, because the PATH mise hands that child APPENDS its
tool directories instead of prepending them. From `mise env`, by position:

    7   /usr/bin
    18  ~/.local/share/mise/installs/node/24/bin

So /usr/bin/node wins for every child process. mise resolves this project's
config correctly -- `mise ls --current` reports node 24.19.0 from mise.toml --
and the fault is purely the ordering of the environment it constructs. node is
the only pinned tool that also exists in /usr/bin, which is why it is the only
one that misbehaves and why this went unnoticed.

`mise run` is therefore NOT the fix either, and a task added to mise.toml would
inherit the same environment. That kills the option this bead suggested second.

WHAT ACTUALLY WORKS, verified:

    env PATH="$(mise where node)/bin:$PATH" npm test    -> node v24.19.0

THE REAL FIX IS THE PATH ORDERING and it is OUTSIDE this repository, so it is
the owner's to make and must not be attempted from here -- they have said so
explicitly. What this bead may do is document the explicit-prepend form beside
the test command in DEVELOPERS.md, and say why it is there, so that the next
contributor whose shell resolves node differently loses a minute rather than an
afternoon. That is worth doing whether or not the ordering is ever fixed,
because a contributor's shell is not this repository's to assume.

CONFIRMED BY THE PR #32 AGENT INDEPENDENTLY: it hit exactly this, reported that
`mise exec --` was insufficient, and had to prepend the install bin directory
by hand to get a green frontend suite.
close_reason: Root cause was node 26 defining globalThis.localStorage itself; vitest skips window keys the global already has, so jsdom's Storage was never installed. Repaired in src/test-setup.ts. Suite green on 24 and 26 (423 tests). Guardrails: [settings] activate_aggressive in mise.toml, a pretest note naming the version, DEVELOPERS.md. engines left at >=24 deliberately -- 26 is now proven green, so narrowing would refuse a working version.

comments.author: Ali Asad Lotia
comments.text:
MEASURED 2026-08-25, answering the project owner's question directly: can the
shell `mise exec --` spawns be given the prepend as an environment parameter?

YES on the invocation, NO in the config's [env] block:

    MISE_ACTIVATE_AGGRESSIVE=1 mise exec -- sh -c 'node --version'   v24.19.0
    mise exec -- sh -c 'node --version'                              v26.7.0
    [env] MISE_ACTIVATE_AGGRESSIVE = "1" in mise.toml                v26.7.0
    [settings] activate_aggressive = true in mise.toml               v24.19.0

The [env] form fails for the reason it looks like it should work: the setting is
consumed while mise is BUILDING the environment, so a value placed inside that
environment is read one step too late. [settings] is where it is read in time,
and that is the per-repository form worth committing.

`_.path` with a `{{ config_root }}` template was tried as a third route and did
not reach the front of PATH. Not pursued -- [settings] already does it, and a
hand-maintained bin directory is a second thing to keep correct.

title: An item leaves the catalogue by going inactive, so the admin should stop offering Delete
description:
Asked for by the project owner on 2026-08-25 while reviewing
`inventory-tng-6kyb`: fold the Django admin into the change 6kyb made.

WHAT 6kyb LEFT. `ItemIdentifier.item` and `VendorOffer.item` are `PROTECT` now,
joining `Label.item` from `inventory-tng-6pr`. So Django's admin still renders a
Delete button on `Item` which refuses with `ProtectedError` for any item that
has ever been catalogued, printed or priced, and quietly succeeds for a row
somebody created a minute ago by mistake.

That is a button whose behaviour cannot be predicted from looking at it, on the
one screen an administrator reaches for when the app will not do something.
`guides/administrator.md` already says an item leaves the catalogue by going
**Active: no**, and 6kyb rewrote that section to say the refusals are the
intention rather than a limitation. The admin is the last place still
contradicting it.

THE SHAPE: `has_delete_permission` returning False on `ItemAdmin`, and the bulk
`delete_selected` action off with it -- the action is a separate path and
turning off one without the other is the usual mistake here. `Item.active` is
what remains, and it is already on the change form.

SIBLING, NOT DUPLICATE: `inventory-tng-ls6d` is the same shape one model over --
the admin offering a Delete on a LABEL that the API refuses. The two want the
same helper and probably the same commit's worth of thought, so read it first;
they are filed apart because the label case has a live API refusal behind it
and this one has a database constraint.

DO NOT let this become a general "no deletes in the admin" sweep. Each model is
its own argument and `MAY_CASCADE` in test_models.py is where a deliberate
exception is recorded with its reason.
close_reason: ItemAdmin.has_delete_permission is False and delete_selected is dropped by name in both action locations. Admin page tests for the PROTECT refusals retargeted to Location, which still has the button; guides/administrator.md says an item has no Delete.

title: Batch: the follow-ups from the 6kyb review and the toolchain snags
description:
Holds the follow-ups agreed with the project owner on 2026-08-25, after the
bug sweep in `inventory-tng-p7ic` landed. Filed together and parented together
because the owner asked that they be the NEXT batch rather than five loose
beads that `bd ready` scatters among forty others.

Two of them are corrections to this repository's own tooling and are cheap.
Two are `inventory-tng-6kyb` follow-ups that the owner asked for while
reviewing it. One is the device-token design, which is the largest and is the
one with a dependency worth reading before starting.
close_reason: Four of the five landed in batch/toolchain-and-admin. inventory-tng-t9of was unparented rather than dropped: --parent means batch membership, and it ships in its own batch.

title: Let compose up give a stack with something in it
description:
Asked for by the project owner on 2026-08-25: bringing the stack up should be one command whichever container runtime a developer has, and should leave an application with data in it rather than empty screens.

WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE, so this is smaller than it sounds:
- compose.yaml:148 already runs 'python manage.py migrate --noinput' before gunicorn, so the SCHEMA is created by 'compose up'. This issue is not about migrations.
- scripts/bootstrap-dev.sh:35-41 already picks 'docker compose' or 'podman compose' and dies with a useful message when neither is there, so the runtime question is settled for the bootstrap path. What is NOT settled is that a developer following Option A in DEVELOPERS.md never runs bootstrap at all.
- compose.yaml already has the pattern this wants: the 'collector' service sits behind 'profiles: [telemetry]' so that a developer who has not asked for it pays nothing.

WHAT IS MISSING. Nothing seeds. 'compose up' produces a migrated, empty database, so every screen a developer opens is blank -- which is the exact thing DEVELOPERS.md says bootstrap exists to prevent ('puts an invented catalogue in the database so that no screen you open is blank'). Option A and Option B therefore do not arrive at the same place, and only one of them is a single command.

THE DESIGN QUESTIONS, none of which should be answered by whoever picks this up without deciding them deliberately:

1. DEFAULT-ON OR BEHIND A PROFILE. Default-on is what makes 'one command' true and is the point of the request. Against it: the collector precedent in this same file argues for opt-in, and default-on changes what 'compose up' does for everybody who already uses it. A one-shot service with 'restart: no' that exits after seeding is the shape either way.

2. IDEMPOTENCE IS REQUIRED, not optional, because the service runs on every 'compose up'. seed_demo_data.py needs checking for this; seed_posture_demo.py is explicitly idempotent and is the model to copy.

3. IT MUST NOT SEED STOCK. The two ledger tables refuse UPDATE and DELETE (decision 0016), so invented movements cannot be taken out again. Whatever runs here must be the catalogue-and-people seed only. seed_posture_demo's '--with-stock' is precisely what must not be wired in.

4. THE LABEL CODES ARE THE HARD PART, and are the reason this is not a five-line change. DEVELOPERS.md is explicit that the last thing bootstrap prints is the two label codes the seed made, that those codes are the stickers a scanner resolves, and that NOTHING ELSE PRINTS THEM. A seeder inside compose buries them in 'compose logs backend' where nobody will look. Options: have the service print them prominently and say so in DEVELOPERS.md; add a 'manage.py show_label_codes' that can be run any time; or make the seed write them somewhere durable. Doing this without answering it trades one blank-screen problem for a worse can't-scan-anything one.

5. WHAT COMPOSE STILL CANNOT DO. createsuperuser asks for a password at a terminal, so an administrator account cannot be made unattended. Option A therefore still cannot fully replace bootstrap, and DEVELOPERS.md should say what Option A does and does not leave you with rather than implying parity.

ACCEPTANCE. A developer with only podman, or only docker, brings the stack up with one command and opens an application with a catalogue, people and resolvable label codes in it. Running the same command again changes nothing. No ledger rows are written. DEVELOPERS.md's Option A says what you get and what you still have to do by hand, and the 'Compose stack' job in CI covers the new service.

title: DESIGN: where work that belongs to no single row goes
description:
The one navigation question the administrative screens cannot each answer, and it is much narrower than inventory-tng-2oba first supposed.

WHAT IS ALREADY ANSWERED. Decision 0014 point 1 settles the placement of three capabilities by name -- editing on the item list, merging in the volunteer picker, revocation on a label -- and its principle settles two more: a location and a category are fields on an item, so they are made where an item names them. Signing in changes what the interface offers rather than navigating anywhere, and frontend/package.json carries no routing dependency, which under that principle is correct rather than missing.

WHAT IS NOT ANSWERED. A sheet of labels belongs to no single row: it spans items, and /api/labels/sheet renders it server-side. So does 'show me open custody' (inventory-tng-ayu) and 'narrow the label list to a shelf, an item or a print run' (inventory-tng-3ez). Three browse-and-act surfaces with no anchor in a one-column Container maxWidth='sm' laid out for somebody standing at a shelf with a phone.

THE QUESTION, stated so it can be answered once: does this application grow a second surface for work that is not about the row in front of you -- and if so, is it a route, a drawer, an expandable panel, or a tab -- or does each such surface find an anchor and stay in the column?

WHAT MAKES IT WORTH DECIDING BEFORE THE SHEET IS BUILT. Whatever is chosen, three issues adopt it. Retrofitting a navigation shape across three screens costs more than choosing one now, and choosing it inside whichever of the three happens to be built first is how the other two inherit a decision nobody argued.

CONSTRAINTS THAT SHOULD BIND THE ANSWER. The volunteer flow is the reason this app exists and must not be made worse to accommodate administration -- 0014 accepted rebuilding the editing surface as the largest piece of work in the plan, not as a licence to reshape the app around it. And the layout is mobile-first because the user is holding a phone at a shelf.

OUTPUT: an entry in docs/decisions/, since this binds three issues and the next person to add an administrative surface.
close_reason: Closed

title: Merge two volunteers from the picker
description:
merge_volunteers maps to VolunteerDetailView PATCH. Merging is first-class in the data model (docs/data-model.md) and decision 0015 defines the 409 that names an unshowable holder -- and an administrator can still act on neither from this application.

WHERE IT LIVES. 0014 point 1 again names it: 'the volunteer picker gains merging'. volunteers/VolunteerPicker.tsx is where duplicates are noticed, because that is where somebody types a name and sees two of them. That is the moment to offer the merge, not a separate people-management screen.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. inventory-tng-24q.6 is 'a volunteer whose spelling moves is minted twice', and inventory-tng-65l is the DESIGN issue about one product, one spelling. Duplicates are a known, recurring condition of this data rather than an exception, so the tool for resolving them is not a nicety.

DECISION 0015 IS THE HARD PART, not the merge itself: the 409 names a holder the caller may not be allowed to see, and the interface has to say something true and useful without leaking it. Read 0015 before designing the error path -- that is where this issue's real work is.

Destructive, so 0014 point 5 applies.

ACCEPTANCE. An administrator can merge two volunteers from the picker, is re-authenticated first, the 409 is rendered in a way that does not disclose what 0015 says it must not, and the surviving record is the one the model says it should be.
close_reason: Closed

title: Revoke a label where the label is
description:
revoke_label maps to LabelResolveView PATCH. A sticker can be retired only through the API or Django's admin today.

WHERE IT LIVES. 0014 point 1 names this one outright -- 'a label gains revocation'. A label is already resolved and shown in this app when one is scanned or deep-linked (frontend DeepLink and the scanner path), so the control belongs on that resolution, gated on useCan('revoke_label'). Nothing new to navigate to.

TWO THINGS TO GET RIGHT. It is destructive, so 0014 point 5 applies: admin/StepUp.tsx and the RecentlyAuthenticated permission make it ask who you are again. And a revoked label must read as revoked afterwards rather than as missing -- a sticker somebody is holding in their hand should explain itself, which is the difference between a useful refusal and a dead end.

RELATED BUT NOT THIS: inventory-tng-ls6d is the admin offering a Delete the API refuses; worth reading alongside, because the answer there informs what this control should NOT offer.

ACCEPTANCE. An administrator can revoke a scanned label in place, is re-authenticated first, and a subsequent scan of it says what happened.
close_reason: Closed

title: Make a location or a category where an item names one
description:
The other four of edit_catalogue's six endpoints: Location POST/PATCH and Category POST/PATCH. There is no screen for either, so both are Django-admin-only today.

WHERE THEY LIVE, and this is the design point. Neither a location nor a category is a thing anybody navigates to in a stock-taking app -- they are fields on an item. So the in-place answer 0014 point 1 asks for is not a locations screen; it is 'add a new one' inside the item editor, at the moment somebody discovers the shelf they need is not in the list. Correcting one is the same control reached from the same place.

That keeps the one-column layout and avoids inventing a management surface for two small vocabularies, which is what a second application would have done.

WORTH DECIDING WHILE BUILDING IT: whether a location or category that nothing references can be deleted here, or whether that stays with Django's admin. The API exposes POST and PATCH only, so the honest default is no deletion, and saying so is better than a control that 404s.

ACCEPTANCE. An administrator can add and correct a location and a category without leaving the item they were working on; both controls are drawn from the capability; a volunteer sees neither.
close_reason: Closed

title: Batch: the guardrails that bit us
description:
Six bugs in scripts/, five of them found by being hit rather than by being looked for, and four of them hit during the single session that merged PR #30.

WHY THEY ARE ONE BATCH RATHER THAN SIX TICKETS. They are the same kind of defect in the same place: a guardrail that is right about the rule and wrong about the circumstances it runs in. check-commit.sh cannot see that git is amending; landing-gate.sh cannot see that its own source is mid-rebase; the documented rebase assumes a terminal; check-commit.sh assumes python3 and assumes .git is a directory; check-docs.sh assumes it can read what DEVELOPERS.md says it reads. Each is cheap on its own and expensive together, because the tax is paid on every batch by every contributor, and because a guard that misfires teaches people to reach for --no-verify.

THE EVIDENCE IS UNUSUALLY GOOD, and it is written on the issues rather than inferred: h0hr refused an amend of the commit that had just closed inventory-tng-614; ghqk blocked every Bash command in a session twice, once from conflict markers in the shell and once from markers inside the matcher's inlined python; 4md is why that rebase had to be run with GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true.

ACCEPTANCE. Each child closes with its own commit and its own tests, and DEVELOPERS.md stops describing behaviour none of them has.
close_reason: All six children merged in PR #31 (rebase, six commits). The batch is landed; the epic carried nothing but membership.

title: DECISION: let the required checks hold the review cycle, rather than a hook on this machine
description:
Found by the simplify pass on PR #30 (finding A2). Closer to a decision than a cleanup, because taking it deletes most of scripts/landing-gate.sh and revisits an ADR.

WHAT THE GATE DOES CLIENT-SIDE. record, status, clear, the receipts file, pr_head, the recorded-vs-current head comparison, the --repo/merge-elsewhere refusal and the 'gh api .../pulls/N/merge' case all exist to attest ONE fact: both review markers are on this pull request, at this head.

GITHUB CAN HOLD THAT FACT ITSELF, WITH MACHINERY ALREADY IN THIS REPOSITORY. scripts/repo-settings.sh:47 derives the required status contexts from the job names in .github/workflows/ci.yml, and :146-160 sets strict: true and enforce_admins: true on main. So a CI job that reads the pull request's own reviews and comments for the '<!-- review-cycle: ... -->' markers becomes a REQUIRED, un-waivable check automatically, just by existing and being named. strict: true gives the head-freshness property for free -- the thing the receipts file exists to provide.

WHY THAT IS A DIFFERENT KIND OF GUARD. No command spelling can route around a required check. The entire regex surface -- and inventory-tng's sibling issue about replacing it with a tokenizer -- exists only because a client-side hook has to recognise the command before it runs. A server-side check does not care how the merge was spelt, which machine it came from, or whether the hook was installed at all. It also covers the case the hook structurally cannot: a person merging from the GitHub web UI.

WHAT IT WOULD TAKE.
- ci.yml triggers only on push and pull_request, so a marker posted AFTER the last push would never re-run the job. It needs issue_comment and pull_request_review triggers.
- statuses: write permission.
- The never-reported-yet state has to read as blocking rather than as broken, which is the same fail-closed reasoning inventory-tng-3sp applied to the hook.

WHAT IS STILL CLIENT-SIDE AFTERWARDS, AND MUST NOT BE DELETED WITH THE REST. The bare 'git push --force' rule from inventory-tng-614 is not server-enforced for batch/* branches -- branch protection covers main only -- so that arm stays exactly where it is. Same for the local UX value of refusing early rather than after a round trip.

WHY IT TOUCHES AN ADR. docs/decisions/0020-who-merges.md reasons about a client-side guard and reads as 'as real as a client-side guard can be'. If a server-side guard is reachable with the machinery already here, 0020's trade is not the trade it describes, and the record should say so either way -- including if the answer is 'we know, and we still want the local one'. That is a decision for a person, which is why this is filed rather than done.

NOT BLOCKING the tokenizer issue: if this is taken, the tokenizer work mostly evaporates, so someone should look at this one first.

title: Tokenize the command line rather than growing a ninth regex for it
description:
Found by the simplify pass on PR #30 (findings A1, A3 and A4, which are one restructure rather than three).

WHAT IS THERE NOW. scripts/landing-gate.sh's matcher approximates a shell parser with eight regex fragments -- QUOTED, SHELL_C, ASSIGN, WRAP, GIT_FLAGS, SEP, prog() and numbered() -- and every review round has added one. The branch's own comments say so four times over: 'found by the review of PR #30' appears against leading VAR=value assignments, against subshells and brace groups, against git -C, and against a quoted REST URL.

WHY THAT IS THE WRONG ALTITUDE. Each addition closes the spelling somebody thought of. None of them closes the class. A guard that has needed nine patches to read a command line is not converging on correctness; it is enumerating an infinite set. The suite now asserts 30 guarded spellings, which reads as thoroughness and is really a record of how many were missed.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD. shlex.shlex(cmd, posix=True, punctuation_chars=True) with whitespace_split=True is stdlib and does the whole job. Verified against the suite's own cases:

  'GH_TOKEN=x env gh pr merge --rebase 7'   -> ['GH_TOKEN=x','env','gh','pr','merge','--rebase','7']
  'if true; then gh pr merge 7; fi'         -> ['if','true',';','then','gh','pr','merge','7',';','fi']
  '{ gh pr merge 7; }'                      -> ['{','gh','pr','merge','7',';','}']
  'echo 7 | xargs gh pr merge'              -> ['echo','7','|','xargs','gh','pr','merge']
  "bd create --title='gh pr merge 7 fails'" -> ['bd','create','--title=gh pr merge 7 fails']
  'git -C /tmp/repo push --force origin x'  -> ['git','-C','/tmp/repo','push','--force',...]
  'gh api -X PUT "repos/o/r/pulls/7/merge"' -> ['gh','api','-X','PUT','repos/o/r/pulls/7/merge']

Tokenize once; split on operator tokens for command position; drop leading WORD= tokens and known wrapper words; match on argv. The regex pile becomes a small word list. The false-positive protection comes free too: --title=... is a single token and never command position, so the strip-quoted-spans-then-search-them-anyway dance goes away.

TWO LIMITS, BOTH VERIFIED, BOTH MUST BE HANDLED.
1. shlex does not understand heredocs: <<'EOF' yields the delimiter and then the body as ordinary tokens. The explicit heredoc-stripping rule stays.
2. shlex raises ValueError on unbalanced quotes. That MUST map to a refusal, not a permit -- it is the same fail-closed rule as the matcher's sys.exit(2), and getting it backwards reintroduces the hole inventory-tng-3sp existed to close.

A3, THE SAME FIX'S SECOND HALF. The push command line is currently parsed twice in two languages: python emits 'push ' + everything after the token as a text blob, and the shell re-splits it with its own remote/refspec/HEAD logic, inheriting none of the first parser's quoting care. Once the matcher has tokens, it should emit a structured verdict (action, pr, push argv) and the shell should do only the part that needs git -- symbolic-ref.

A4, WHY IT BECOMES TESTABLE. scripts/ pairs a shell driver with a sibling Python module every other time it needs one: check-docs.sh/check-docs.py, check-telemetry.sh/check-telemetry.py, repo-settings.sh/ci-check-names.py, check-batch.sh/batch-membership.py. landing-gate.sh is the only one that inlines it, six times, and the ~140-line matcher can only be reached through the hook envelope. Move it to scripts/landing-gate.py and the tokenizer gets unit tests instead of end-to-end ones. The shell keeps deny/deny_dependency, which is the part that deliberately has no dependencies.

WHY IT IS NOT BEING DONE ON THAT BRANCH. It is a rewrite of the core of a security guard, and doing it in the last commit before a merge is how the ninth bypass gets introduced while the eighth is being removed. The 64-case suite is the regression net and it should be run against a branch of its own.

ACCEPTANCE. Every one of the 64 existing cases passes unchanged; unbalanced quotes are a case, and it refuses; the heredoc rule keeps its case; the matcher lives in scripts/landing-gate.py with its own suite.

title: A landing-gate.sh that will not parse blocks every Bash command
description:
Found while landing inventory-tng-3sp, by hitting it.

WHAT HAPPENS. The gate is now registered as a PreToolUse hook on Bash in tracked .claude/settings.json, so it runs before every Bash tool call. A rebase left conflict markers in scripts/landing-gate.sh, bash refused to parse it, the hook exited non-zero, and Claude Code blocked the tool call:

  PreToolUse:Bash hook error: line 8: syntax error near unexpected token '<<<'

Every Bash command in the session, not only the guarded ones. Including the git commands needed to finish the rebase that broke it. The way out was the Read and Edit tools, which is fine for an agent that has them and is a dead end for one that does not.

WHY IT IS NOT SIMPLY 'FAIL CLOSED WORKING AS INTENDED'. The fail-closed direction inventory-tng-3sp built is deliberate and should stay: a gate that cannot READ a command must refuse it. This is a different case. The gate is not failing to judge a command; it is failing to load at all, and it is doing so in a way that takes the whole session with it rather than the commands it guards. The prefilter in check mode exists to keep a missing python3 from blocking unrelated commands, and this walks straight past that reasoning because it happens before any of the script runs.

THE CASE IT HAPPENS IN IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. A conflicted or half-written landing-gate.sh is exactly what a rebase, a merge, a bad edit or an interrupted checkout leaves behind, and the commands somebody needs next are git commands.

OPTIONS WORTH WEIGHING. (a) register the hook as a tiny stable shim that syntax-checks the gate and refuses only the guarded commands when it will not parse -- but that shim is then the thing that must never break, which is the same problem one level down and it is at least much smaller; (b) let the hook wrap the gate so a non-zero exit becomes a deny of the guarded verbs only, which needs the prefilter duplicated in the wrapper; (c) accept it, and say so in DEVELOPERS.md beside the rest of the gate's failure behaviour, so somebody who meets it knows to fix the file rather than to hunt for what they typed.

Whichever is taken, DEVELOPERS.md 'When a branch is ready to merge' currently promises 'Nothing else in this repository is blocked' -- which is true of the refusal path and not true of this one.
notes:
DECIDED 2026-08-25 by Ali Asad Lotia, on a recommendation argued out with Claude: options (b) and (c) together, and NOT (a) the shim.

WHAT IS BEING BUILT. The gate recuses itself at the point where it would refuse for not having been able to read something: if its own source is mid-conflict, it permits, because the commands somebody needs next are exactly the ones it guards. On the deny path only, so the hot path pays nothing. Plus the DEVELOPERS.md sentence promising 'Nothing else in this repository is blocked', which is true of the ordinary refusal and false of this.

TWO THINGS MEASURED DURING THE DECISION, recorded so neither is re-derived:

1. bash exits status 2 on a syntax error, and 2 is precisely Claude Code's 'block this tool call' code for a PreToolUse hook. Mode 1 takes the session down by a COINCIDENCE OF EXIT CODES rather than by any decision in this file. Any other non-zero exit is a non-blocking error and the command proceeds.

2. 'source' of a syntax-broken file returns 2 and leaves the caller alive -- but bash executes a sourced file incrementally, so statements before the error DO run. Verified: an 'echo' ahead of the markers printed. A shim that sourced the gate could therefore load half of it, hit an early 'exit 0', and permit silently. That is worse than the bug being fixed, so the cheap version of the shim is off the table and only the 'bash -n' version was ever really on it.

WHY NOT THE SHIM. Not cost of context -- measured at zero, since the gate prints nothing on the permit path and a shim would print nothing either. It is proportionality. The hook runs only inside Claude Code and only in this project, so no human at a terminal can hit this. The population is an agent editing landing-gate.sh itself, mid-rebase, without Read and Edit tools. It has happened twice, both times recovered in minutes with those tools. Against that, the shim is a permanent second file that must never break -- smaller, so less likely, but the property has moved rather than gone -- plus 'bash -n' over 841 lines on every Bash command in every session forever.

THE HOLE THIS LEAVES, STATED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER. A conflicted SHELL half still blocks a Bash-only session; only the embedded-python half is fixed.

WHAT REOPENS THIS. Either of: a third occurrence in the bash-syntax mode, or the gate being registered anywhere with a wider reach than this one project. Both are reasons to build the shim, and the argument above is then already made and does not need repeating.
close_reason: Option (b)+(c) as decided: the gate stands down when git reports an operation in flight AND its own source carries conflict markers, checked only on the deny path so the hot path is unchanged. DEVELOPERS.md no longer promises that nothing else is blocked. The shell-half mode is uncovered and said so; ghqk's notes carry the reopen triggers.

comments.author: Ali Asad Lotia
comments.text:
HIT AGAIN, 2026-08-24, while merging PR #30 -- and by a second cause, which widens this issue.

The first report was conflict markers from a rebase making bash refuse to parse the file. This time the file parsed fine: 'git rebase --autosquash' left markers inside the EMBEDDED PYTHON of the matcher, so python exited non-zero and the gate took its (correct, deliberate) deny_unavailable path -- 'The landing gate could not find out, so it is refusing this.' Every Bash command in the session, including the git commands needed to finish the rebase that caused it.

So the trigger is not 'the shell script will not parse'. It is 'the file is mid-rebase', and the fail-closed path inventory-tng-3sp built turns that into a total session block by design. Both halves of the file -- shell and inlined python -- are equally able to cause it.

WHAT GOT ME OUT, both times: the Read and Edit tools, resolving the conflict by hand until the matcher parsed again, then git rebase --continue. That works for an agent with those tools and is a dead end for one with only Bash, which is exactly the population this hook is registered for.

WORTH NOTING FOR WHOEVER TAKES THIS: inventory-tng-4xd8.1 moves the matcher out to scripts/landing-gate.py. That does not fix this -- it moves the same failure from one file to two -- unless the fix is specifically 'a gate whose own source is mid-conflict is a gate that recuses itself'. The obvious shape is to detect .git/REBASE_HEAD, .git/MERGE_HEAD or conflict markers in its own source and permit rather than refuse, which is the one place fail-open is right: mid-rebase, the guarded commands are the ones needed to escape.

comments.author: Ali Asad Lotia
comments.text:
TWO CORRECTIONS FOUND WHILE BUILDING IT, both worth having on the record.

1. THE FIRST DRAFT OF THE FIX WAS WRONG, and the suite caught it against this very repository. It treated REBASE_HEAD as evidence that a rebase was in flight. git does not remove that file when a rebase finishes, so it is present in any checkout that has ever rebased -- including this one, right now. The effect was that the first of the two conditions was permanently satisfied, leaving the whole guard resting on 'does my source contain markers', which is the single condition the decision explicitly rejected. The in-flight signals that are actually reliable are the rebase-merge and rebase-apply DIRECTORIES; MERGE_HEAD, CHERRY_PICK_HEAD and REVERT_HEAD are removed on completion and can be trusted. There is now a case asserting that a leftover REBASE_HEAD does not stand the gate down.

2. THE SCOPE IN THE DESCRIPTION AND IN MY EARLIER COMMENT IS TOO BROAD FOR ONE OF THE TWO MODES. 'Every Bash command in the session' is right for markers in the SHELL half: bash exits status 2, which is the harness's block code, so nothing runs. It is NOT right for markers in the inlined python, which I asserted in the comment above without checking. Measured against a deliberately conflicted copy: ls -la, git status and git rebase --continue all PERMIT, because the bash prefilter answers before the matcher is ever started. Only a command mentioning gh or push as a word reaches the matcher and gets refused.

That makes the python-half mode meaningfully less severe than reported -- the escape commands were never blocked by it. It does not change the fix, which stands the gate down wherever the matcher fails and the source is conflicted, but it does mean the remaining uncovered case (the shell half) is the more serious of the two rather than the lesser. Anyone weighing the shim again should weigh it on that.

title: Batch: the landing gate is real
description: The gate AGENTS.md rests its merge-without-asking permission on, made into something a rule may rest on: tracked, registered in tracked settings, failing closed on every missing dependency, recording the artifacts it found rather than a literal, and enforcing the one ask-first row that nothing implemented.
close_reason: Both children shipped in PR #30: the gate is tracked, registered in tracked settings, fails closed on every dependency, records the artifacts it found rather than a literal, and enforces the --force row. Two rounds of review found nineteen more findings, all fixed here except three filed on: 8nqo (what makes a review current), 4xd8.1 (tokenize rather than a ninth regex), x0jp (let required checks hold the cycle).

title: Decide whether a hooks fault may stop bootstrap short of a database
description:
Raised by the review of PR #29 (inventory-tng-nt1f) and deliberately left as it is, because the instruction that shaped it was explicit: a core.hooksPath somebody else set must not be overwritten in silence -- it must be said and the run must stop.

WHAT THAT COSTS. The Git hooks step sits ahead of PostgreSQL, the migrations and the seed, and reports its faults with die under 'set -euo pipefail'. So a contributor whose core.hooksPath already points elsewhere cannot get a working database out of this repository's one documented setup command. Verified: with core.hooksPath set to .githooks, only 'mise trust' and 'mise install' ever ran -- no container, no migrations, no seed. The script's own header promises 'From a fresh clone to a database with something in it, in one command', and CLAUDE.md names stale or blocking setup as the biggest barrier to new contributors.

TWO MORE PATHS REACH THE SAME DIE with nothing to do with anybody's configuration: a clone with core.symlinks off (Windows, or a filesystem without symlinks) and a checker that lost its exec bit (exFAT, NTFS, core.fileMode=false). nt1f already reordered the step so those two are refused BEFORE git is repointed, rather than after -- so the worst of it, being left aimed at a directory the script has just called broken, is gone. What remains is that they stop the run.

THE ALTERNATIVE the review argued for: note the fault and carry on, and let scripts/check-setup.sh be the thing that refuses, since reporting is what it is for and it is already wired into CI. Against that: a note in the middle of thirty lines of closing message is a note nobody reads, and the person then commits unchecked -- which is the whole fault nt1f existed to fix.

A middle route worth weighing: keep die for a hooks path somebody deliberately set, and downgrade the two mechanical failures (no symlink, no exec bit) to notes, since neither is a decision anybody made.

title: Decide what beads' five hooks may cost every commit
description:
Raised by the review of PR #29 (inventory-tng-nt1f). That change points core.hooksPath at .beads/hooks from bootstrap, which arms beads' five shims for every contributor -- not only the commit checker it was about. The shims were tracked before, but inert for anyone who had never run bd, because bd is what used to write that setting.

MEASURED on a fresh clone (git 2.55.0, bd 1.1.2):

  git commit   4 ms   ->  113-126 ms
  git switch   5-9 ms ->  46-52 ms

Per commit: git 4 ms, beads pre-commit 45-49 ms, beads prepare-commit-msg 37-45 ms, check-commit.sh 30-32 ms. So roughly 85 of the 113 ms is 'timeout 300 bd hooks run' twice. post-checkout now fires on every checkout, switch and clone; post-merge on every pull. In a clone with no beads database those calls still cost about 45 ms each to do nothing, and with bd absent from PATH the three extra 'env sh' forks still take a commit from 4 ms to 37-42 ms.

nt1f took the documentation half of this: bootstrap now says the pointer arms beads' hooks too, and DEVELOPERS.md 'Checking it' says what else stops and starts running. What it did not take is the judgement.

TWO THINGS TO DECIDE.

1. Is roughly a tenth of a second per commit the right price for beads staying in step? It may well be; it should be a decision rather than a side effect of a setup script.

2. BEADS_HOOK_TIMEOUT defaults to 300 in the shims, so a wedged bd blocks a commit for five minutes with no indication of why. Exporting a small value -- five seconds, say -- costs nothing when bd is healthy and turns a hang into a slow commit. This half looks like a plain improvement whatever is decided about the first.

title: check-commit.sh reads the tracker through an unguarded python3
description:
Found by the review of PR #29 (inventory-tng-nt1f). Before it the checker was opt-in and a broken interpreter cost one confusing manual run; it is now on every commit for everyone.

scripts/check-commit.sh:88 pipes the staged tracker diff through an inline 'python3 -c' behind mapfile, under 'set -uo pipefail' with no -e and no check on the result. A python3 that is missing or broken produces no closures, and the script then accuses an honest commit:

  with python3:     · closes inventory-tng-nt1f          (passes)
  python3 -> false: ✗ .beads/issues.jsonl is staged but does not close inventory-tng-nt1f

Nothing in the output mentions python3. scripts/report.sh:79 'relay' exists for exactly this -- its own header says 'a reader that crashed prints nothing' -- and check-commit.sh is the one checker not using it.

Hooks inherit whatever PATH the invoking shell had, and mise.toml pins python 3.14 rather than installing one globally, so somebody committing from a GUI git client, or from a shell where mise was never activated, on a machine with no system python3, is locked out of committing and told to close an issue that is already closed.

SEPARATELY, and measured on the same pass: python3 is spawned even when .beads/issues.jsonl is not staged and the diff is empty -- 18.8 ms of the checker's 30.0 ms. Guarding the call with [[ -n "$staged_tracker" ]] gave byte-identical output at 12.1 ms. Worth taking with the same change, since this now runs on every commit.

Neither check-setup.sh nor bootstrap-dev.sh asks whether the hook's interpreter is reachable; whether they should is part of this.
close_reason: The reader's exit status is checked and exit 2 names python3 instead of accusing the commit; the interpreter is not started at all when nothing is staged for the tracker (30.0 ms to 13.4 ms measured); and check-setup.sh now reports an unreachable python3 rather than leaving it to be found at the first refused commit.

title: check-commit.sh's merge escape is unreachable in a worktree
description:
Found by the review of PR #29 (inventory-tng-nt1f), which armed this hook for every clone.

scripts/check-commit.sh:59 tests -f "$REPO_ROOT/.git/MERGE_HEAD" and "$REPO_ROOT/.git/CHERRY_PICK_HEAD". In a linked worktree 'git rev-parse --show-toplevel' returns the worktree root, where .git is a FILE holding 'gitdir: ...' rather than a directory -- so both -f tests are permanently false and the 'Not an issue being landed' exit is unreachable.

Verified: in a worktree, 'git cherry-pick --continue' after a conflict is refused with '✗ nothing staged closes <id>', while the identical operation in the main checkout prints 'Not an issue being landed (merge, revert or cherry-pick). Nothing to check.'

Plain merges survive by accident, because their subject begins with 'Merge' and message_is_git_own catches them -- the file test contributes nothing there. A merge committed with a custom -m, or any conflicted cherry-pick, is refused.

This repository's agents work in .claude/worktrees/, so it is the ordinary case here rather than an exotic one.

FIX. 'git rev-parse --git-path MERGE_HEAD' is worktree- and GIT_DIR-aware and answers with the right path in both layouts. Same for CHERRY_PICK_HEAD. Needs a case in scripts/check-commit.test.sh built on a real worktree; testlib.sh's new_repo would want a companion that adds one.
close_reason: git rev-parse --git-path replaces the .git-is-a-directory assumption, so the escape for git's own commits works in a linked worktree, the main checkout and under a relocated GIT_DIR alike. Four cases on a real worktree, verified failing against the old path.

title: A database that answers the dial and then goes quiet still pins a worker
description:
Found by the review of PR #27 (inventory-tng-39ng), which bounded the CONNECT
and deliberately stopped there. The finding is right and the bound is not the
whole of the failure it was aimed at.

DATABASE_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS is libpq's connect_timeout, which covers the
dial: TCP, TLS and authentication. Once those complete it is spent. The
readiness endpoint then runs `SELECT 1` (backend/src/inventory/views.py,
HealthCheckView.get) on a socket with no deadline of any kind on it, and
nothing in this repository sets one -- there is no statement_timeout, no
tcp_user_timeout and no keepalive setting anywhere in backend/, infra/,
compose.yaml or .env.sample, so libpq inherits the operating system's
keepalive idle time, which is about two hours.

SO THE PINNED WORKER COMES BACK for every fault that lets the handshake finish
and then stalls: a checkpoint or IO stall, a lock pile-up, a pgbouncer at
max_client_conn accepting and queueing, a promoted standby still in recovery,
or a partition that lands after the connection is up. The probe gets through
the 5-second dial and then blocks on the read until the gunicorn arbiter kills
the worker at 30 seconds -- which is exactly the arithmetic 39ng removed, at
6 x 30 = 180 worker-seconds against the 180 a three-worker pod has, reached by
the other half of the connection's life.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT, and each is a number somebody picks rather than a fix to
apply:

- OPTIONS['options'] = '-c statement_timeout=...' on the connection, which
  bounds every query this process makes and not only the probe's. That is the
  strongest and the most invasive: a legitimately slow query -- the sheet
  import, an admin page over the ledger -- is cancelled by it, so the number
  has to clear the slowest thing this application does on purpose. Measure
  before choosing.
- A timeout on the probe's own query alone, leaving everything else unbounded.
  Narrower and it protects exactly the traffic 39ng was about, at the cost of
  the connection's settings differing by caller.
- tcp_user_timeout or explicit keepalives, which bound the socket rather than
  the statement and so catch a partition but not a stall.

39ng's owner settled connect_timeout and nothing else, and each of the above
changes what happens to a query somebody is waiting on, which is not a change
to make on an agent's judgement. docs/deployment.md#health-checks names this
bead where it says the bound covers the dial.

title: No startupProbe, and no page for a pod stuck unready
description:
Left over from inventory-tng-39ng, which bounded the database connect and
deliberately did not touch the probes themselves. Both of these were raised by
the review of PR #23 (inventory-tng-uq6) and both are already written up as
known behaviour in docs/deployment.md#health-checks, so neither is invisible --
what is missing is a decision, and each needs a number somebody picks.

1. THERE IS NO startupProbe. infra/helm/inventory-tng/templates/backend-deployment.yaml
   gives liveness initialDelaySeconds 10 and readiness 5, so the only lever for
   a slow first boot is that delay -- and it is welded to the numbers that decide
   how long a WEDGED pod is left alone, because they are the same fields. A
   startupProbe separates the two questions: how patient to be with a container
   that has not finished starting, and how quickly to kill one that has stopped
   serving. The cost is a third probe to keep in step with the arithmetic in
   docs/deployment.md#health-checks, which is quoted rather than derived and is
   held by backend/src/inventory/tests/test_chart.py.

   The number to pick is failureThreshold x periodSeconds -- the longest first
   boot this deployment will tolerate. Nobody has measured a cold start of the
   backend image against a cluster's image pull, so that measurement is the
   first piece of work here.

2. KUBERNETES NEVER RESTARTS A CONTAINER FOR PROLONGED UNREADINESS. Since
   inventory-tng-uq6 split liveness onto /api/livez, a pod whose OWN database
   access has wedged -- a leaked socket, exhausted descriptors, a stale DNS
   answer only it holds -- answers /api/livez for ever, fails readiness for
   ever, and sits out of the Service with no restart and no CrashLoopBackOff.
   Capacity drops by a replica silently. That trade is right (a failover must
   not kill every pod at once) and it leaves nothing to page on.

   The options, none of them free: an alert on kube_pod_status_ready being 0
   past some window, which needs a monitoring stack this cluster does not have
   yet; or a liveness probe that fails only on a fault local to the pod, which
   is the distinction /api/healthz cannot draw today.

Both are deferred rather than dropped: 39ng's owner settled connect_timeout and
nothing else, and each of these changes what the kubelet does to a running pod,
which is not a change to make on an agent's judgement.

title: Batch: an open read is argued too
description:
Two issues that ship together because one of them cannot ship alone.

inventory-tng-lb95 adds the audit over credential-free endpoints that
decision 0012's consequence asks for, and is what inventory-tng-gnhl is
blocked on.

inventory-tng-1ks is a tracker-only closure: it was closed as a duplicate of
inventory-tng-qdbm with the note that it would ride out with the next
landing, and it cannot, because check-commit.sh permits one issue to move to
closed per commit and every landing closes one of its own. It lands as its
own commit here, which is what makes this branch two issues rather than one.
close_reason: All children completed

title: Prune the demo config flags once the decision is made
description:
Filed at the same time as inventory-tng-81f7.3 and on purpose: the flags that make the demo possible are the flags that rot if nobody is told to come back for them. This is that instruction, written while the reasons are fresh rather than reconstructed later from a diff.

THE PRINCIPLE, and it is the one that governs feature flags generally: a flag exists to defer a decision. Once the decision is made the flag is not an asset, it is a second code path nobody exercises, a branch in every test that touches it, and a paragraph in .env.sample describing a choice nobody has. Keeping it is not free and not neutral -- it is a standing invitation for the unchosen branch to drift until it no longer works, discovered by whoever next tries to flip it.

WHEN THIS RUNS: after inventory-tng-81f7 is settled and its outcome recorded. Not before -- the flags are load-bearing until then.

WHAT IT MUST DO, for EACH of the five, by name:

  ANONYMOUS_PAYLOAD       full | masked | names_only
  VOLUNTEER_ACCESS        open | enrolled_self | enrolled_code | mesh_only
  SEARCH_MINIMUM          0 | 1 | 2 | 3
  ANONYMOUS_READ_RATE     a rate string, or empty
  CUSTODY_VISIBILITY      anonymous | identified

Decide one of exactly two outcomes. COLLAPSE: the chosen value becomes the only behaviour, the flag goes, and every other branch goes with it. Or REMOVE: the whole flag and everything under it goes, because the demo answered a question that needed no code kept.

THERE IS NO THIRD OUTCOME. A flag is not kept because it still works, because it might be useful, or because removing it is a diff. A flag kept needs an argument written down, held to the same bar as a coverage exclusion in DEVELOPERS.md -- and 'we might want to switch it back' is not one, because the decision record is what switches it back.

FILE A REMOVAL BEAD PER FLAG rather than doing five removals in one change. Each is a separate behaviour change with its own tests and its own documentation, and check-batch.sh wants one commit per issue anyway.

WHAT A REMOVAL HAS TO REACH, because a flag is never only a flag -- this list is the reason the bead exists rather than a reminder to tidy up:

  - settings.py, the env() call and its default
  - .env.sample, the variable AND the prose explaining a choice that no longer exists
  - every branch on the value: serializers keyed on it, permission classes, viewset overrides
  - the frontend half -- a branch in a component, a field read off /api/me, a type in api/types.ts
  - tests asserting the UNCHOSEN branches, which is the bulk of it and the part most often left behind
  - the generated schema: backend/openapi.yaml is checked in, so a permission class that goes changes it
  - CAPABILITIES in views.py if an operation stopped existing
  - the Helm chart and docs/deployment.md if the variable was plumbed through
  - any decision record that described the flag as present tense

VERIFY BY GREP, NOT BY MEMORY. When the last removal lands, the flag names should return nothing anywhere in the tree -- and that grep belongs in the final bead's acceptance, because a flag half-removed is worse than one kept: the documentation says it exists and the code ignores it.

WORTH SAYING WHY THIS IS FILED AT ALL. Nothing enforces it. No checker finds a stale flag, and the demo will have been a success by then, which is exactly when this is easiest not to do.
design: Deliberately filed BEFORE the demo is built, not after. A cleanup bead written once the flags are already familiar gets scoped to what somebody remembers; this one names all five while the reason for each is still the reason it was added.
acceptance_criteria: Every one of the five flags has been collapsed or removed, each by its own bead; a grep for each flag name returns nothing in the tree; no .env.sample entry, test, schema fragment or document still describes a choice that no longer exists; and any flag kept carries a written argument.

title: Tell two volunteers of the same name apart without naming either
description:
The follow-up half of the decision the project owner took on 2026-08-24, recorded on inventory-tng-gnhl: an anonymous caller gets id and display_name and nothing else, and somebody who shares a display name identifies themselves by TYPING their own address rather than by reading anybody's. This bead is what would serve the people that leaves out.

WHO IS LEFT OUT, and it is not a small group. Volunteer.NULL_WHEN_BLANK records that 45% of the historical rows carry no identifier at all. Typing an address finds nobody when you never gave one. Where two such volunteers also share a display name, nothing distinguishes them.

WORTH BEING CLEAR THAT THIS IS NOT A REGRESSION gnhl introduces. VolunteerPicker.tsx renders the address as a list item's , and a null one renders no second line, so two identifier-less volunteers of the same name are ALREADY indistinguishable on screen today. Showing addresses never served that 45%; it served the subset who had one, shared a name, and remembered which they used. So this bead is an improvement on today rather than a repair of gnhl -- which is why it is P2 and separate rather than a condition of gnhl landing.

THE SHAPE: show something that is not an identifier. When they were added (Volunteer.created_at) and/or the last stock location they recorded at, reachable from StockTransaction.actor. It works for EVERYBODY, because being on the pick-list at all means having moved something, and it is useless to a harvester: a month and a stock room are not contact details.

THE GUARD THAT MAKES OR BREAKS IT, and it must be a test rather than a comment: the hint MUST NEVER name a custody location. A custody location is somewhere a volunteer is personally holding stock and location_held_by_iff_custody guarantees it says who, so a hint reading 'last at <somebody's home>' is inventory-tng-81f7's third scenario reached by a different route -- it would publish which named volunteer has hardware at home, which is the exact harm the whole consultation exists to prevent. Filter Location.Kind.VOLUNTEER_CUSTODY out, and assert it.

MEASURE BEFORE BUILDING. The meeting (inventory-tng-81f7) asks whether picking the wrong person actually happens. If nobody has ever done it, this is worth less than it costs. The workbook can bound it: 86 distinct folded names, 13 of them carrying more than one address -- but that conflates two people sharing a name with one person using two addresses, and rule 6 in inventory/sheet/people.py says both occur and the sheet cannot separate them. So the true collision count is unknown and smaller than 13, and the meeting is the instrument, not the spreadsheet.

COSTS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: the last-recorded location is a per-row lookup across the page, so it wants an annotation on the queryset rather than a walk -- the pick-list is under a hundred but ITEMS already shows what the house does about N+1 on a phone.
design: Not part of gnhl. gnhl's own acceptance is that no personal identifier reaches an anonymous caller, and it meets that without this. Folding this in would grow gnhl by a queryset annotation, a serializer field, a custody-kind guard and its tests, for a group the current app does not serve either.
acceptance_criteria: Two volunteers of the same display name are distinguishable in the picker without any identifier reaching an anonymous caller, including when neither has an address on file; a test asserts no custody location can ever appear in the hint.
notes: CORRECTION to the description above, where a shell ate a word: the sentence should read 'VolunteerPicker.tsx renders the address as a list item's SECONDARY line (the secondary prop at VolunteerPicker.tsx:148), and a null one renders no second line'. Nothing else in the description is affected.

title: Anonymous reads need a rate limit, and it is for the oracle not the roster
description:
Falls out of inventory-tng-81f7 and is needed by inventory-tng-gnhl. Filed separately because the sizing argument is easy to get wrong in the obvious direction.

AppendThrottle.allow_request returns True for every safe method, deliberately: the endpoint taking a volunteer's name is also the pick-list searched as somebody types, and a limit sized for submissions would be exhausted by typing. So the read surface gnhl opens has no limit of any kind.

WHAT A READ LIMIT IS AND IS NOT FOR, measured 2026-08-24 against the 86 distinct folded names in the workbook. display_name is matched with icontains, which is a SUBSTRING match and not a prefix, so a single letter returns 54 of 86.

  minimum search length 1 -> 6 searches sweep the whole roster
  minimum search length 2 -> 22
  minimum search length 3 -> 43, and brute-forcing all 17,576 three-letter combinations is trivial
  capping the anonymous page at 10 with no next link -> 14 / 26 / 43 for the same three

So a rate limit does effectively NOTHING against copying the roster: 43 requests is under a second even at a strict limit, and a minimum search length is a usability decision rather than a control. Whoever sizes this must not size it as though it were the defence against enumeration, because that argues for a limit tight enough to break typing while still not stopping a sweep.

WHAT IT IS ACTUALLY FOR is the membership oracle. VolunteerFilter matches identifiers EXACTLY, so 'search=someone@example.org' answering count 1 or count 0 tells a caller whether a given address belongs to a volunteer. That attack needs one request per address checked -- ten thousand addresses is ten thousand requests -- and it is the one case where a limit converts the attack from seconds into hours of conspicuous traffic. Size it against that, and against a human typing, and nothing else.

NOTE the bucket. AppendThrottle derives from UserRateThrottle so the key is the client address while nobody is signed in. A hub of volunteers shares one address, and .env.sample's NUM_PROXIES note says which way that is dangerous to get wrong.
design: Not APPEND_THROTTLES. DRF keys a bucket on the scope and the client, so sharing a scope means sharing a budget, and searching while typing would eat the allowance a volunteer's actual submission needs -- which is the reason ReportThrottle was given a scope of its own rather than reusing the append one. Read ReportThrottle's docstring before choosing; the argument there is the same argument.
acceptance_criteria: Anonymous reads carry a limit sized against the membership oracle and against a person typing; it does not refuse an ordinary keystroke-by-keystroke search; the rate is configuration in .env.sample with a comment saying what it is and is not for; and a test covers a search being refused.
notes:
=== HELD PENDING inventory-tng-81f7.3, added 2026-08-24 ===

This is a REVIEW HOLD, not a real prerequisite, and the distinction matters if you are the one who picks this up when the edge clears.

Nothing in this issue needs anything the demo produces. The dependency is there because the demo builds over the same surface, and this issue's DESCRIPTION may be partly wrong by the time it is unblocked -- built already, superseded, or needing a rewrite to say what is left rather than what was needed. The project owner asked for a mechanism that would not let these be forgotten and would not let them be worked from a stale description.

A dependency was chosen over `bd defer` deliberately. Defer is date-based and needs somebody to guess when; this condition is an EVENT. The edge clears by itself when 81f7.3 closes, which is when the demo has actually been given.

SO THE FIRST THING TO DO WHEN THIS BECOMES READY IS RE-READ IT against what landed, not start work. If the description still holds, carry on. If it does not, revise it before touching code.

=== WHAT inventory-tng-81f7.3 ALREADY BUILT, and why this issue is still open ===

Added 2026-08-24, after the demo spike landed on `batch/show-the-five-postures` (PR #28).

That branch ALREADY CONTAINS an implementation of this issue: `AnonymousReadThrottle` in inventory/throttling.py, scoped `anonymous-read`, off unless `ANONYMOUS_READ_RATE` names a rate, attached to the pick-list rather than spread across every read, and derived from `AnonRateThrottle` so a signed-in administrator is not counted at all. Its docstring makes exactly the argument this bead was filed to preserve -- that a read limit does almost nothing against copying the roster (43 requests, measured) and is decisive against the address-by-address membership check.

SO WHY IS THIS STILL OPEN. Because PR #28 IS DELIBERATELY NOT MERGED. It is a spike that inventory-tng-81f7 gates, and if the consultation goes another way the branch may be thrown away and this work goes with it. Nothing here is on main.

WHAT WHOEVER PICKS THIS UP SHOULD ACTUALLY DO, therefore, depends on what happened to that branch:
- If #28 was merged or its throttle was lifted onto main, this issue is largely DONE and wants closing or narrowing to whatever is left -- check whether the rate reached .env.sample with prose, and whether a test covers a search being refused.
- If the branch was discarded, the implementation is still worth reading before rewriting it from this description. `git show 5095785 -- backend/src/inventory/throttling.py` on that branch.

The sizing argument in the description above stands either way and is the part that must not be lost: this limit is for the membership oracle, NOT for enumeration, and sizing it as though it were the defence against enumeration argues for a limit tight enough to break somebody typing while still not stopping a 43-request sweep.

title: Deleting an item destroys its printed identifiers and its price history
description:
Found by the review of PR #22 while fixing inventory-tng-6pr, and its own issue because it predates that change.

6pr made Label.item and Label.location PROTECT, so a sticker's row cannot be deleted under it. Two other things printed or recorded about an item are still CASCADE:

  ItemIdentifier.item   backend/src/inventory/models.py:374
  VendorOffer.item      backend/src/inventory/models.py:424

WHAT THAT COSTS. Verified on the 6pr branch: an item with a legacy_nycm code NYCM-ER-LBEG2 and a barcode 0123456789012, with no label and no movement, deletes cleanly -- the admin offers the confirm button and names nothing -- and both identifiers go with it. A barcode is printed on the thing itself, so this is the same class of loss 6pr closed for stickers, on a different artefact. ItemIdentifier.value_normalised is unique table-wide, so the freed string can later attach to a DIFFERENT item, which is worse than losing it.

VendorOffer is the same shape against a different promise: its own docstring says "Prices are appended rather than overwritten, so a historical purchase price stays recoverable". One delete of an unlabelled, unmoved item wipes the series, and unlike a sticker there is no physical artefact to notice the loss by.

FIX: PROTECT on both, with a test each, exactly as 6pr did for labels.

BUT ARGUE THE SHAPE FIRST, because doing this makes an item with any identifier undeletable, and the importer mints identifiers for every row it stages -- so after a sheet import essentially no catalogue row could be removed. That may be right; it may want the guard on printed kinds only (barcode, legacy_nycm) and not on alias. 6pr deliberately did NOT narrow to live labels and the reasoning there is worth reading before deciding differently here.

WORTH DOING WITH IT: guides/administrator.md currently tells an administrator that a row nothing is printed for can be deleted. That sentence is only safe once this is fixed, and 6pr had to soften it for exactly this reason.
close_reason: ItemIdentifier.item and VendorOffer.item are PROTECT, unnarrowed, matching 6pr; guides/administrator.md and docs/data-model.md say what that now refuses.

title: Batch: the telemetry follow-ups the sweep's review raised
description:
The four issues /simplify raised against PR #20 and that were deliberately deferred out of it: nb8.15, nb8.18, nb8.17 and nb8.16. Membership only; what each is about is on the issue.

Each was re-confirmed against main at cb5fcb1 before this batch was formed, and two of the four had their specification corrected in the process -- nb8.17's central premise was wrong, and nb8.16's proposed template does not fit two of its eight commands. Read the NOTES on each, not only the description.

ORDER, and the reason for it: nb8.15 first because it is the only bug and because it reshapes flag.ts, start.ts and Recording.tsx; nb8.18 second because its second half touches flag.ts and wants to see that reshaping; nb8.17 third because it is small and independent; nb8.16 last because it is the largest and because it interacts with the checker nb8.11 added.
close_reason: Its last child landed; the batch goes through the review cycle from here.

title: Frontend: the debug flag expiring does not stop the SDK
description:
Found by /simplify on PR #20 (the telemetry sweep), deferred out of that batch because it is a defect rather than a cleanup.

frontend/src/telemetry/flag.ts says the client-side LIFETIME exists so that 'the indicator goes away and the app stops paying for an SDK on a phone in a basement'. Nothing implements it. When the hour elapses mid-session, asked() starts answering null -- so the X-Debug-Trace header on API calls stops -- while the provider keeps batching spans and posting them, and the badge keeps showing.

That is the same half-stop that inventory-tng-nb8.8's Stop button fix was written to close, arriving through the timer instead of the button. start.stop() now exists and is the teardown to call.

WHAT IS ALSO WORTH FIXING WITH IT: 'is this device recording' is currently held in three places that nothing reconciles -- flag.asked() has the token and its expiry, start.ts has 'started', and Recording.tsx copies a boolean into component state at mount. start.recording() is documented as 'what the indicator asks' and nothing asks it. One owner in start.ts that Recording subscribes to (useSyncExternalStore, or a useRecording hook) would let expiry and the button tear down through the same path, and would stop the badge disagreeing with the SDK.
notes:
CONFIRMED against main at cb5fcb1, 2026-08-24. Every claim holds, and two things are worse than the description says.

VERIFIED:
- flag.ts:20-23 does promise it: 'this side keeps its own so the indicator goes away and the app stops paying for an SDK on a phone in a basement'.
- Nothing implements it. There is no timer anywhere in frontend/src outside the decode loop; asked() checks 'stored.until <= now' only when something calls it.
- api/client.ts calls flag.asked() per request, so the header does stop.
- start.ts holds 'started' and a 'teardown' closure, set once by start() and cleared only by stop(). Nothing re-checks expiry.
- Recording.tsx:21 is useState(recording) at mount and is never re-evaluated.
- start.stop() exists and is exported. Its only caller in the application is Recording.tsx:41, the button.
- start.recording() has ZERO callers outside the test file. report.ts:27 has a local function of the same name that builds the debug header -- a different thing, easily mistaken for a caller.
